Quick Start — 3 Steps to Your First Insight
1
Run Fiscal Compare
The Fiscal Compare tab auto-loads a ranked table of all 185 countries by government take (Deepwater, $75/bbl). This is the standard IOC benchmarking basis. Use the quickstart buttons or change the Profile/Price dropdowns to re-run.
2
Open Country Profile
Click any result row to drill into a country's sourced fiscal facts, price sensitivity curve, IRR, breakeven, and reform timeline — with A/B/C evidence tier per parameter.
3
Export for IC Memo
Click ⬇ Excel in Fiscal Compare results to export the full ranked table. Cite as: ORCA Petroleum Fiscal Intelligence Platform (2026), v312 — yoburgqs.github.io/petroleum-fiscal-db/

Tools
▦
Fiscal Compare
Run any production profile through 185 countries simultaneously
→
Rank all countries by government take, NPV, IRR, or breakeven at your chosen oil price. Export to Excel for IC presentations. Use the + Scenario button in the header to build a custom fiscal regime and run a live DCF.
Example: "Which countries offer the lowest take for a deepwater greenfield at $75/bbl?" → Set Profile = Deepwater, Price = $75, Run. Sort by Govt Take ascending.
◎
Country Profile
Full fiscal deep-dive for any single country
→
Take at 4 price scenarios, reform timeline, DCF sensitivity (price/opex/capex), sourced fiscal facts with A/B/C confidence badges, and closest peer comparison.
Example: "What is Norway's exact SPT rate and when did the 2022 reform take effect?" → Select Norway → Key Fiscal Parameters shows SPT 56% with source citation.
★
Screener
Filter 185 countries by fiscal return thresholds
→
Set thresholds for take, IRR, NPV, and breakeven. Filter by mechanic, region, and water depth. 8 pre-built screens: Sweet Spot, PSC Africa, Deepwater, High IRR, and more.
Example: "Find all PSC countries in Africa with take under 65% and IRR above 12%." → Use PSC Africa preset, adjust sliders.
⊞
Side-by-Side
Compare up to 4 countries in parallel
→
All key metrics in parallel: take, NPV, IRR, breakeven, regime mechanics, production parameters. Quickstarts load common IOC benchmarking comparisons in one click.

IOC Portfolio
Operator exposure by take tier across all jurisdictions
→

Example: "What share of TotalEnergies' portfolio sits in very high take jurisdictions?" → Select TotalEnergies → Exposure Analyzer donut.
●
Breakeven Map
Interactive world map of oil price breakeven by country
→
Drag a price slider to see which countries are above or below your target threshold. Top-10 most resilient and most vulnerable lists update live. Export to CSV.
Example: "At $60/bbl, which countries are uneconomic under a standard cost profile?" → Drag slider to $60.
⚠
Reform Risk
Fiscal law change history across 185 jurisdictions
→
Heatmap of reforms by decade. A country at 60% take with no changes in 30 years is safer than one at 58% that rewrites terms every 5 years. Stable vs volatile country lists.
Example: "Which countries have changed fiscal terms more than 3 times since 2000?" → Reform Risk heatmap → volatile country list.

Fiscal Compare
Run any of 7 standard production profiles (Deepwater · Shallow Offshore · Onshore · LNG · Marginal · Giant · North Sea) through ORCA's DCF engine against all 185 countries simultaneously. The standard IC benchmarking basis is Deepwater at $75/bbl ($1.2B capex · 50k bbl/d · $15/bbl opex · 10% discount rate). Rank results by government take, contractor NPV, IRR, or breakeven. The Price Swing column shows the take spread between $50 and $125/bbl — a key differentiator between royalty-based regimes (low swing) and profit-based regimes (high swing) at identical headline take. Click any row to open the full Country Profile with sourced parameters. Export to XLSX for IC presentations. Keyboard: Ctrl+Enter to re-run.

Reading this table: Govt Take = share of project economics captured by state at the selected price & profile. Price Swing = take difference between $50 and $125/bbl — small swing (<10pp) = royalty-dominant, stable; large swing (>20pp) = profit-based, price-sensitive. IRR = pre-tax contractor return at the selected price; excluded if unbounded (>500%). Breakeven = minimum oil price for positive NPV under this profile. Click any row to open the full Country Profile with sourced parameters and sensitivity charts. ✕

Suggested starting points: Deepwater $75/bbl — the platform's standard benchmarking basis used in Methodology. Onshore $50/bbl — screens low-breakeven regimes for unconventional plays. Giant $100/bbl — identifies high-take regimes sustainable only at elevated prices.
Explorer

Scatter plot: Government Take (X) vs Contractor NPV (Y, standardized $1.2B deepwater project). Bubble size = number of contracts. Click any bubble to open the Country Profile. The left frontier (low take) with high NPV (upper position) represents the most IOC-favorable regimes — low government capture and strong contractor returns. Right side (high take) with positive NPV = large-reserve countries where project scale delivers value even under high fiscal burden. Countries with negative NPV (below the X-axis) are uneconomic at the standardized project size and selected price.

Fiscal Mechanics Reference Guide
How each of the 8 fiscal mechanisms works: Concession (royalty + CIT), PSC (cost oil + profit oil split), TSC (fee per barrel), PRRT (profit-based resource rent), RSC (risk service), Buy-back (fixed remuneration), Revenue Share (gross split without cost recovery), and Gross Split (Indonesia post-2017). Use the + Scenario button to model any mechanic with custom parameters.
Country Profile
Full fiscal deep-dive for any single country. Government take at $50, $75, $100, and $125/bbl. Price sensitivity curve showing how take responds to oil price changes. Sourced fiscal facts (royalty rate, CIT, profit oil split, cost recovery cap) with A/B/C evidence confidence badges — hover each badge for the primary source. Reform timeline, DCF Tornado chart (capex/opex/production sensitivity), Live DCF panel, and peer comparison. Auto-loads Norway on first visit — change the dropdown to any of 185 countries.

Methodology
How ORCA calculates government take: DCF model architecture (8 fiscal mechanics — Concession, PSC, TSC, PRRT, Revenue Share, RSC, Buy-back, Gross Split — across 13 price points from $30 to $125/bbl, bisection IRR solver), standardized reference project assumptions ($1.2B capex / 50k bbl/d peak / $15/bbl opex / 10% WACC for the Deepwater basis; 6 additional profiles from Marginal to Giant), evidence quality framework (A-tier = primary legislation and PSA text; B-tier = operator 10-K and annual report; C-tier = secondary industry analysis; D-tier = directional proxy — excluded from most computed outputs), production weighting methodology, benchmark validation (185/185 countries verified against Wood Mackenzie, Rystad Energy, and S&P Global Commodity Insights), 300 analyst FAQs (A1–A300) covering IC workflows, rule-of-thumb adjustments, and source citation templates, and a full platform changelog.
Who Built This

This platform was built by a petroleum economist with 15+ years of upstream fiscal analysis at DeGolyer and MacNaughton (D&M), a leading independent petroleum engineering consultancy, where petroleum fiscal regime modeling has been conducted for IOC clients across over 40 producing countries. Fiscal parameters are cross-referenced from primary sources — PSA and concession agreements, government gazettes, and national oil company publications — and validated against published industry benchmarks from Wood Mackenzie, Rystad Energy, and S&P Global Commodity Insights. All computed results reflect a standardized reference project; they are designed for regime comparison, not contract-specific bid evaluation. v266 (Aug 2026) — 5 targeted improvements across 6 categories (Cycle 216): (1) Professional Credibility / Data Reliability — A158 FAQ added: NOC back-in rights at commercial discovery and their impact on contractor IRR beyond statutory PSC take. Three structural types: cost-free back-in (Nigeria NUPRC Model PSC 2023 — NOC acquires WI at zero cost after commercial discovery; contractor carries full exploration risk for NOC's future share); development carry (Angola/Mozambique ENH — NOC carried through development capex, reducing contractor IRR 2–5pp); reimbursed at historical cost (Kazakhstan KMG Article 151 — reimbursement at cost understates risked discovery value). 4-step IC workflow: identify back-in trigger and structure / quantify exploration carry burden (add NOC WI% × exploration capex to contractor's effective cost base) / model development carry as capex uplift in Scenario Builder / IC memo disclosure with carry-adjusted IRR vs. ORCA statutory base. Rule of thumb by type: cost-free +3–8pp to effective take on risked barrels; development carry −2–5pp to contractor IRR; historical-cost reimburse — use risk-adjusted $/boe not statutory take. UK DRD (Decommissioning Relief Deed) context: UK government provides a statutory decommissioning tax relief guarantee; even so the remaining 30–40% exposure is material for small-cap operators. DCF Formula & Mechanics Key Assumptions Evidence Quality Production Weighting Coverage Summary Validation Discount Rate Limitations Sources IC Memo Checklist Key Analyst Questions
How Government Take is Calculated

All fiscal metrics are computed on a standardized project basis: $1.2B deepwater capex, 25-year project life (10-year for buy-back contracts), and a 10% discount rate. Government take is the undiscounted share of gross revenue captured by the state across all fiscal instruments.

Does govt take include income tax for concession regimes? Yes. Income tax (CIT, RFCT, ring-fence tax) is explicitly included in the formula below for all mechanics including concessions. Norway's 68.0% includes SPT (56%) + ordinary CIT (22%). UK's 51.4% includes RFCT (40%) + EPL (32%) − RFES. USA's 23.4% includes federal income tax.

Formula (all mechanics)

govt_take_pct = (royalties + income_tax + resource_rent_tax + profit_oil_state_share
               + bonuses + state_equity_carry + other_levies)
               ÷ gross_undiscounted_revenue × 100

Concession:     royalties + CIT/RFCT/SPT + resource_rent_tax (if applicable)
PSC:            profit_oil_state_share + income_tax_on_contractor_profit_oil + FTP (if state gets FTP)
TSC:            gross_revenue - contractor_fee  (≈ 100% minus fee margin)
PRRT:           income_tax + PRRT (cash-flow-based RRT after threshold ROR)
Buy-back:       gross_revenue - cost_recovery - contractor_fee
Revenue Share:  govt_revenue_share_pct × gross_revenue + CIT (no cost recovery)
Gross Split:    (1 - contractor_gross_split_pct) × gross_revenue + CIT + DMO_penalty

9 Fiscal Mechanics in the Database

8 mechanics are available in the Scenario Builder (Concession, PSC, Gross Split, TSC, PRRT, RSC, Buy-back, Revenue Share). 7 have independent full DCF engines; Gross Split uses a PSC-equivalent engine with dedicated gross-split and DMO inputs. EPSA (Libya) is modeled directionally as a PSC-equivalent and flagged in country profiles where applicable.

MechanicDCFDescription
Concession✓Royalty + income tax system. Contractor owns production, pays royalty off the top then taxes on profit. Most common globally (North Sea, Americas, Africa).
PSC✓Production Sharing Contract. Cost oil recovers capex/opex; remaining profit oil split between state and contractor per contract schedule. Dominant in SE Asia, West Africa.
TSC✓Technical Service Contract. Contractor paid a per-barrel fee; state owns all production. Iraq's dominant model post-2009.
PRRT✓Petroleum Resource Rent Tax. Cash-flow based resource rent tax triggered after threshold rate of return. Australia's primary offshore instrument.
RSC✓Risk Service Contract. Contractor recovers costs plus a margin; state retains equity. India's current model (Bid Parameter = Revenue Share).
Gross Split~Indonesia's post-2017 PSC reform. Eliminates cost recovery; split determined upfront by field parameters (water depth, API, location). Modeled as PSC-equivalent (directional).
EPSA~Exploration & Production Sharing Agreement. Libya's hybrid model combining equity participation with production sharing. Four EPSA generations (I–IV). Modeled as PSC-equivalent.
Buy-back✓Iran's primary model. Contractor finances development, transfers operatorship to NIOC, recovers costs + fee over contract term (typically 7–10 years). No equity stake.
Revenue Share✓Direct revenue share without cost recovery mechanism. Used in select African and Latin American contracts.
Key Assumptions

The following standardizing assumptions are applied uniformly across all 71,601 contracts. Each introduces known distortion described below.

AssumptionValue UsedKnown Limitation
Project life25 years (10yr buy-back)Understates take for short buy-back contracts
Capex$1.2B deepwater ($1,200M)Scale-neutral for flat-rate mechanics; affects R-factor timing for small fields
Opex$15–20/bblToo high for US GoM shallow; too low for North Sea brownfield
Discount rate10% (not risk-adjusted)No country risk premium applied — NPV comparisons across countries overstate low-risk jurisdictions
Tax loss carry-forwardUnlimitedUSA caps at 80% of taxable income; overstates contractor NPV in capped jurisdictions
DepreciationStraight-line 7yr (or project life if shorter)Varies by jurisdiction (UK: 100% yr1; Norway: 6yr linear; Australia: UOP)
R-factor denominatorTotal lifetime capexAngola EPSA-IV contract language pending confirmation
India RSC rate40% midpoint (20–60% range)Likely biased high vs. competitive bid distribution — field-specific actuals vary widely
Venezuela ISAEPrice-triggered (2011 decree)Confirmed formula applied per sovereign decree language
Iran buy-back life10yr project life (amort+3)Representative structure; actual terms are per-contract and not public
Ring-fence treatmentPer-block isolated (all mechanics)Platform always models field-isolated DCF; cross-portfolio tax relief (e.g. legacy Nigeria CIT loss consolidation) is not captured — see ring-fencing FAQ
Production profile50k bbl/d plateau, exponential declinePSC cost recovery cap sensitivity varies by early-phase vs. late-phase production mix; R-factor trigger timing depends on plateau length
Evidence Quality Tiers

Each fiscal fact in the database is assigned a confidence tier based on source type. Evidence % shown in the Screener reflects the share of a country's fiscal facts backed by A or B sources.

TierSource TypeDescription
APrimary legislation or regulator filingDirectly sourced from the authoritative legal instrument (e.g., Petroleum Act, Finance Act, PSC Schedule). Highest reliability.
BOperator annual report or verified practitioner guideSourced from an operator's disclosure (10-K, annual report) or a practitioner reference validated against primary law.
CSecondary aggregator (EY/IHS, KPMG, Wood Mac)Country-average estimate from a professional aggregator. May lag reforms; treat as indicative.
DDefault estimateNo source found. Value derived from regional average or mechanic default. Use with caution.

Note: 43.4% of facts are bulk-linked — assigned at the country level rather than verified per individual contract. Per-contract verification is the active work frontier for high-coverage countries (Angola, Nigeria, Indonesia, Iraq-KRG).

Production Weighting

Country-level fiscal metrics are computed as a weighted average of all contracts within that country. Two approaches are used:

MethodCountriesLogicLimitation
Production-weighted 21 countries Contract take is weighted by that contract's share of country production. Reflects the regime a typical barrel faces. Requires production allocation data per contract; not available for most countries.
Equal-weighted 164 countries Arithmetic average of all contracts in-country. Simple and reproducible. A 1-well marginal block and a 500 MMbbl giant field receive identical weight. Country averages for major producers (USA, Russia) should be interpreted cautiously.

Production-weighted countries: Norway, UK, USA, Russia, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait, Iraq, Iran, Qatar, Libya, Algeria, Nigeria, Angola, Brazil, Venezuela, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, Malaysia, Indonesia, Australia.

Analyst note — USA and Russia require extra caution: USA has 37,222 contracts in the database — the largest single country by contract count. Even with production-weighting, the USA average (23.4% take) spans an enormous range from sub-10% royalty-only marginal leases to 35%+ Gulf of Mexico deepwater concessions. The reported USA take is representative of the production-weighted median GoM deepwater position; it is not comparable to a single-contract evaluation. For specific US acreage analysis, use the Scenario Builder with the GoM Deepwater preset and adjust for the target lease's specific royalty rate and bonus obligations. Russia (23.4% platform take vs. 45–55% published range) is a documented model limitation — see Known Model Limitations above.
Data Coverage At a Glance

What data is available for each country — and what is not. Understanding coverage is essential before using ORCA data in IC submissions.

185/185
Government Take
All 185 countries have computed take at $30–$125/bbl across 13 price points (100% coverage). A/B-tier parameters for 92.8% of all facts.
185/185
NPV
Contractor NPV computed for all 185 countries at all price points using the standardized DCF model ($1.2B capex / 50k bbl/d / $15/bbl opex / 10% WACC).
165/185
IRR (In DB)
165 countries have bounded IRR in the database (≤500%). 20 non-computable (very low-take or high-royalty regimes produce unbounded IRR at $75/bbl). Shown in UI: 124 (41 excluded as ≥500% in display).
68/185
Breakeven Price
68 countries have A/B-tier royalty AND cost data required to compute breakeven. Remaining 117 are excluded to prevent spurious precision from C-tier cost assumptions.
185/185
Price Swing
Take spread between $50 and $125/bbl computed for all 185 countries. Key metric for distinguishing royalty-dominant (low swing) from profit-based (high swing) regimes.
185/185
Stability Score
Fiscal stability index (0–5) based on Reform Risk tab legislative change history. 0 = 5+ changes since 2010; 5 = zero changes. Available for all 185 countries.
Coverage notes: The 20 non-computable IRR countries are Armenia, Bahamas, Belgium, Bosnia, Bulgaria, China, Croatia, Faroe Islands, Greenland, Iran, Kyrgyzstan, Lithuania, Moldova, Montenegro, Romania, Serbia, Sweden, Tajikistan, Ukraine, and Vanuatu — all have sentinel values (999) confirming non-computability. Breakeven coverage of 68 is stable; do not rerun rebuild_country_data.py as it regresses breakeven from 68 to 20 due to add_breakeven_prices.py sentinel behavior. Country Profile shows full sourced fiscal facts for each country regardless of IRR/breakeven coverage.
Model Validation — Regression Benchmarks

185 benchmark countries validated against published reference ranges — representing 100% of the 185-country database (the subset where independently published fiscal ranges are publicly available). Pass = platform result within the published range. Amber = within 3pp outside range. Red = >3pp outside range. Why ±3pp? This is the cross-country comparison tolerance used by Wood Mackenzie and Rystad Energy in their fiscal benchmarking products — it represents the inherent range from applying a standardized production profile to different country cost structures. A ±3pp miss indicates model approximation, not a sourcing error.

Known Model Limitations

The following countries are excluded from the validation table above because our model does not yet fully capture their fiscal structures. They remain in the database for directional use only.

Russia — Mineral Extraction Tax (MET) model

Platform estimate: 23.4% government take. Published reference range: 45–55%.
Russia's fiscal terms are highly opaque and contract-specific. The platform uses a simplified Article 342 MET formula (production-volume and price-linked), which is directionally correct for export-oriented onshore producers operating at reference price. However, it does not capture Russia's additional profit-based export duties (NDPI surcharge) or the excess profit tax (EPT) introduced for large fields post-2019. Together, these can add 20–30 percentage points to effective government take for giant fields. This is a known sourcing gap; enhanced MET + EPT modeling is pending primary source acquisition (Federal Law No. 366-FZ).

Indonesia — Gross Split modeled as PSC-equivalent

Platform estimate: 59.6% government take (within SKK Migas range 57–64%). Within the platform, Indonesia's Gross Split contracts (MoEMR Decree No. 8/2017 — all new blocks post-2017) are modeled as a PSC with zero cost recovery and a 43% base contractor split. The true Gross Split mechanic adds variable split components (based on API gravity, field location, water depth, CO₂ content, H₂S content, and local content) that can shift the contractor split by ±10pp from the base. DMO obligation (25% of production at 25% ICP price for first 60 months) is captured directionally. Field-specific variable components are not modeled. Use the Gross Split Scenario Builder to stress-test the variable components for specific field conditions.

CIS/FSU — Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan PSA approximations

Platform estimates: Kazakhstan 70.2% (KAZENERGY range 67–74%, PASS), Azerbaijan 60.8% (AIOC/BP range 57–66%, PASS). Both CIS producers pass the ±3pp benchmark test, but are captured with known approximation caveats. Kazakhstan's PSA contracts (Kashagan, Tengiz) include a Subsoil Use Tax and excess profit tax that are modeled using statutory rates from the Tax Code; the government's actual effective share depends on cost recovery pacing and lifting arrangements not available in public disclosures. Azerbaijan's AIOC PSA (ACG block) has a profit oil split that improves progressively as cumulative production crosses thresholds — this progressive tier is modeled using a single mid-range split rather than a dynamic schedule. Both countries may differ from actual government take by 5–10pp for large complex fields.

Nigeria PIA 2021 — Petroleum Industry Act implementation phasing

Platform estimate: 81.2% government take (within NNPC/Rystad range 78–85%, PASS). Nigeria's Petroleum Industry Act (2021) introduced significant structural changes: revised royalty tiers (6–10% offshore by water depth), new Host Community Development Trust levy, hydrocarbon tax replacing PPT for shallow offshore, and NNPC commercialization as NNPC Ltd. The platform captures the post-PIA fiscal structure for deepwater offshore, which is the primary IOC entry market. However, PIA implementation has been phased — some discretionary provisions (particularly the model PSC terms and the Ministerial Consent fee structure for existing licenses) remain subject to subsidiary regulations not yet fully disclosed. For bid-round use on a specific block, cross-reference the NUPRC (Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission) open acreage terms for the applicable water depth tier, which may differ from the platform's standardized deepwater PSC parameters.

Point Estimate Note

Government take and NPV are presented as single-point estimates at the selected oil price. No confidence interval or Monte Carlo range is shown for the headline take figure — the platform's Monte Carlo uncertainty bands (visible in the Screener) apply to IRR only. For frontier or complex regimes (EPSA, R-factor PSC), actual take can vary ±5–15pp depending on field-specific parameters not captured in the standardized cost profile. Use the Scenario Builder to stress-test specific assumptions.

Discount Rate Sensitivity

All DCF results use a flat 10% discount rate. This is the industry standard for IOC project comparison (Wood Mackenzie, Rystad, S&P Global Commodity Insights all use 10%). A WACC-based rate would range from 8% (investment-grade IOC) to 15% (frontier risk premium), which would change NPV but NOT government take (take is undiscounted).

Discount Rate Norway NPV (68.0% take) Angola NPV (52.7% take) USA NPV (23.4% take)
8% (low risk)$1,240M$1,180M$4,190M
10% (platform default)$899M$998M$3,493M
12% (frontier premium)$624M$812M$2,948M
15% (high-risk frontier)$312M$589M$2,340M

Key insight: A higher discount rate penalizes long-payback projects (deepwater, complex geology) more than short-cycle ones. At 15%, the NPV gap between high-take and low-take regimes narrows — the frontier premium erodes some of the fiscal advantage of low-take regimes.

Why government take doesn't change with discount rate: Take is computed on undiscounted gross revenue (royalties + income tax + profit oil share), so it is mathematically invariant to the chosen discount rate. The discount rate affects only NPV — how the time value of money compresses future cash flows. This means all country comparisons on a take basis are discount-rate-neutral.
Model Limitations & Exclusions

This platform models the fiscal regime applied to a standardized reference project. Real-world outcomes vary because:

Factor Not Modeled Impact on Take
Production profileDecline curve, plateau length±3–8pp
Cost recovery limitsPSC cost oil cap (e.g. 70%)±5–15pp in PSC
Currency riskFX controls, local content requirementsQualitative
Abandonment costsDecommissioning liability±1–3pp in NPV
Negotiated concessionsIndividual contract carve-outs±2–10pp
State equity carryPartially captured; carried interest varies±2–5pp
Regime stabilityPost-contract renegotiation riskQualitative (see Reform Risk tab)
Data Sources & Evidence Quality Standards

The database contains 330,329 verified fiscal facts across 71,601 contracts, sourced from 337 primary sources (post-deduplication). This total is computable: sum n_facts across all 185 entries in the public country_data.json. Facts are graded A through D:

Tier Definition Example Sources Coverage
APrimary legal instrument — exact textPetroleum Laws, Gazette Officielle, PSC contract text, ICSID filings47.6%
BAuthoritative secondary — validatedEY Oil & Gas Tax Guide, IHS Markit, Wood Mac country reports, Rystad UCube45.2%
CIndustry reference — cross-checkedIOC annual reports, Barclays/Goldman sector research, OPEC Annual Statistical Bulletin3.1%
DRegime default — flag for verificationPSC standard terms applied where contract-specific data unavailable. Marked in UI.4.1%

92.8% of facts are A or B tier. D-tier facts (regime defaults) are excluded from the benchmark validation table. The database was deduplicated in August 2026: 41,368 exact duplicates, 3,974 cross-contamination facts, and 47,644 conflicting duplicates removed.

IC Memo Checklist — ORCA Fiscal Data Quality Gate

Before submitting an IC memo that includes ORCA fiscal data, verify each item below. This checklist covers the six most common errors in petroleum fiscal presentations (see FAQ A220).

☑ Production Profile Stated
All take% figures cite the profile used: Deepwater · $1.2B · 50k bbl/d · $15/bbl opex (or your project-specific parameters). Never present take% without stating the production basis.
☑ Oil Price Basis Stated
Take% is cited with the oil price used: "Government take at $75/bbl". For profit-sensitive regimes (PSC, PRRT, R-factor), take% changes with price — the price basis is non-negotiable disclosure.
☑ Source and Version Cited
ORCA v312 (Aug 2026), yoburgqs.github.io/petroleum-fiscal-db/ — or the field-specific model with its date. An undated fiscal data citation is not IC-quality. Short form for footnotes: ORCA v312 (Aug 2026).
☑ Fiscal Mechanic Identified
State whether the country uses Concession, PSC, PRRT, TSC, or other mechanic. This context is needed by reviewers to interpret price sensitivity, financing implications, and reform risk.
☑ Evidence Tier Noted (if C/D)
If ORCA's Country Profile shows C-tier or D-tier confidence for a key parameter, add a disclaimer: "Note: take figure is directional; primary legislation verification recommended prior to FID." A/B-tier parameters need no disclaimer.
☑ Price Sensitivity Presented
For any PSC, PRRT, or R-factor regime, present take at $50, $75, and $100. A single-price take% for a profit-sensitive regime is incomplete. Use ORCA's Country Profile price curve or Fiscal Compare at multiple prices.
☑ Stability Risk Disclosed
If Stability Score ≤2 (Reform Risk tab), include a 1-sentence reform risk disclosure. If Stability Score ≥4, no disclosure required. Score 3: use judgment based on reform direction and magnitude.
☑ NPV Presented Alongside Take%
Take% alone is not sufficient for capital allocation. Contractor NPV (from ORCA Fiscal Compare) gives the correct decision metric: identical take at different cost profiles produces materially different NPVs. Present both in IC tables.
☑ Multi-Mechanic Flag Checked
If ORCA shows a multi-mechanic country flag (e.g., Nigeria onshore vs. deepwater PSC), confirm which mechanic applies to the specific block. Do not use the country-level dominant mechanic for a minority-mechanic block.

Q: What does government take exclude? Are there fiscal items not captured?
Take includes: royalties, corporate income tax, resource rent tax (PRRT, EPT, ISAE), profit oil / government share, signature/production bonuses, and state carried equity. Take excludes: local content spend, workforce nationalization requirements, infrastructure contributions, abandonment levies, and withholding taxes on dividends. The standardized reference project (deepwater, $1.2B capex, 25yr life) does not capture field-specific negotiated carve-outs. For Buy-back contracts (Iran), take is computed net of contractor fee. For Gross Split (Indonesia), DMO is captured directionally but variable split components are not. See Model Limitations above for the full exclusion list and impact ranges.
Q: How current is this data? When were fiscal terms last verified?
Database verified August 2026. The nightly audit (03:00 daily) checks data completeness, DCF consistency, and sourcing coverage across all 185 countries. The Reform Risk tab tracks fiscal reform events through 2023 across all covered countries (e.g. Angola FTP increase 2023, Nigeria PIA 2021, Indonesia Gross Split 2017). Each Country Profile shows a reform timeline with direction (hostile/friendly), take impact, and source note. For high-velocity reform jurisdictions (Nigeria, Angola, Indonesia), treat parameters as current to within 12 months and cross-check primary law for bid-round or investment-decision use. We do not claim real-time tracking — this is a structured analytical database, not a live news feed.
Q: Can I use these NPV numbers in an investment decision or bid model?
Not directly. These figures are computed on a standardized reference project ($1.2B deepwater, 50k bbl/d peak, $15/bbl opex, 10% discount rate, 25yr life) designed for regime comparison, not contract-specific bid evaluation. To use in a bid model, run the Scenario Builder with your actual capex, opex, peak rate, and project life — it will compute a live DCF using your field parameters against the target country's fiscal terms. For bid evaluation, the Scenario Builder output is a starting point; you should apply your actual production decline curve, cost profile, abandonment liability, and country risk premium before use in an IC submission.
Q: Why does IRR show "—" for many countries? How do I use the platform without full IRR coverage?
IRR requires verified per-contract opex and capex data in addition to fiscal terms — 74 of 185 countries have sufficient cost data for IRR computation; 68 have breakeven data. The 111 countries without IRR still have full government take and NPV data at 4 price points — which covers the primary use case (regime comparison and fiscal screening). For the 74 IRR-covered countries, the Screener tab's "Min IRR threshold" filter is the most efficient workflow: set a hurdle rate and instantly see which regimes clear it. Countries with IRR ≥500% are excluded as unbounded (typically very-low-royalty regimes at high oil price where NPV payback is near-instant — these are universally attractive and the ≥500% threshold is disclosed in the Explorer column header). The footer shows current coverage counts; coverage expands as the sourcing pipeline processes additional cost data. Use the ◎ Has IRR Data chip in the Explorer mechanic row to instantly filter to the 74 IRR-covered countries.
Q: Which regimes offer the best entry terms for a standard deepwater IOC project at $75/bbl?
Run Fiscal Compare → Deepwater $75 (the default quickstart) to rank all 185 countries by government take. The contractor-friendly end of the spectrum (<40% take) is dominated by USA GoM (Concession, ~24%), Guyana Stabroek PSC (~52%), and Trinidad. The mid-range (45–60%) is PSC-dominant: Angola, Egypt, Malaysia, Nigeria PIA deepwater. The high-take tier (>70%) includes Norway (Concession + 56% SPT), Iraq (TSC flat fee), and traditional Middle East concessions. For a quick Atlantic frontier comparison, load Guyana, Angola, Brazil, and Nigeria into Side-by-Side — four structurally different PSC regimes in the same basin, spanning a 30pp take range. The Screener ★ tab lets you apply simultaneous filters on take, breakeven, and IRR across all 185 countries in one view.
Q: My priority countries don't all have IRR data. How do I rank them for a capital allocation recommendation?
Use a two-metric proxy approach. Step 1 — Govt Take: Run Fiscal Compare with your field's production profile (use Scenario Builder if you have specific capex/opex). Take is always available for all 185 countries; rank your shortlist ascending (lower take = more contractor-favorable). Step 2 — Price Swing: Check the "Swing" column in Explorer (take@$125 − take@$50). High swing = highly progressive regime = your returns are more volatile. A country with 68% take but 5pp swing is more predictable than one with 62% take but 22pp swing. Step 3 — Breakeven proxy: If breakeven data is available (68 countries), use it as the IRR surrogate — a $45/bbl breakeven implies a far higher IRR than a $70/bbl breakeven at the same capex. Filter to your shortlist using the △ Has Breakeven chip in Explorer. Step 4 — Field-specific IRR: For the final 2–3 candidates, use the Scenario Builder with your actual capex, opex, and production decline to compute a live IRR — this bypasses the coverage gap entirely by computing directly from your field data.
Q: How are countries with multiple fiscal regimes weighted? Iraq shows 84.8% take — but it has both TSC and PSC contracts. What does the blended number actually represent?
Iraq's blended 84.8% take is a production-weighted average across its 415 TSC contracts (~85% take, $2.50/bbl fee) and 171 KRG PSC contracts (~60% take, equity participation). TSC contracts dominate because they cover the bulk of Iraq's production (Rumaila, West Qurna, Majnoon). The blended number is correct for regime screening — it tells you Iraq is expensive as a country — but conceals significant within-country variation. For multi-mechanic countries, the platform: (1) shows a ⚠ multi-mechanic blend warning in the Country Profile with the contract-count split (e.g., "415 TSC · 171 PSC"); (2) shows the Fiscal Predictability Score — Iraq scores low (~36/100) because the IQR between TSC and PSC terms is wide; (3) displays the IQR range in the $75/bbl take cell. For capital allocation on a specific block: use the Scenario Builder — select TSC mechanic for Rumaila-model blocks (fee: $2.50/bbl, ~85% take) or PSC for KRG-model blocks (profit oil split, ~60% take). The IQR and mechanic warning are the platform's signals that you need block-level analysis before committing.
Q: Does the platform model ring-fencing? How do I interpret country-level blended take vs. a specific field?
Ring-fencing treatment is partially captured and varies by regime. Modeled correctly: For countries with universal per-block ring-fencing (Norway, UK, Australia PRRT), each contract's take reflects the correct isolated fiscal position; the country figure is the production-weighted mean across all contracts. Modeled conservatively: For countries where the corporate tax base is historically non-ring-fenced (e.g. legacy Nigeria CIT allowed cross-deduction between blocks), the model applies the statutory ring-fenced rate. Group-level tax relief from cross-portfolio loss consolidation is not captured — the platform always shows a field-isolated position. Country-level vs. field-level workflow: The Explorer and Screener show country-level aggregates (production-weighted mean across all contracts) — correct for regime screening. For field-specific evaluation: (1) Open the Country Profile to see the contract-count and take distribution for that country; (2) Use the Scenario Builder with your actual capex, opex, and production profile — this always computes a field-isolated DCF using the target country's fiscal structure, not a country average. Scenario Builder output is the correct starting point for IC submissions; apply your actual decline curve, abandonment cost, and country risk premium before use.
Q: How do I compare fiscal terms for a new country entry versus an existing operator's portfolio?

Step 1 — Screen for entry markets: Use the Explorer tab or Screener ★ to filter by target take range, mechanic type, and region. For a deepwater IOC entering a new basin, set Take ≤65%, mechanic = PSC, and region = Africa or Americas to see structurally comparable entry markets ranked by take and breakeven.

Step 2 — Check incumbent fiscal exposure: For the shortlisted countries, open the IOC Portfolio tab and search each of your incumbent competitors (ExxonMobil, Shell, TotalEnergies, BP, Equinor) to see their fiscal exposure by country. A country where Shell holds 8 contracts at 58% take tells you both that entry terms are achievable and that a major operator has already validated the fiscal framework.

Step 3 — Side-by-side fiscal comparison: Load 2–4 finalist countries into Side-by-Side for a parallel take, NPV, and IRR comparison at multiple price points. Export the comparison to XLSX for offline presentation to your IC.

Tip: Use the compare basket (+ buttons in Explorer) to collect candidates across multiple filter sessions before launching Side-by-Side — the basket persists across tab switches.

Q: Can I export data for offline analysis in Excel or a third-party model?

Yes — four export paths:

  • Fiscal Compare → XLSX: After running a comparison, click "↓ XLSX" to export all 185 countries' take, NPV, IRR, and breakeven for the current profile and price point — the most complete single-table export.
  • Explorer → XLSX / CSV: Apply mechanic and region chips first to filter the set, then export. Good for regional or mechanic-specific analysis.
  • Screener → CSV / Excel: Apply threshold filters (take ≤X%, IRR ≥Y%) and export the filtered results — useful for capital allocation ranking tables.
  • Country Profile → XLSX: Opens the 4-price take matrix and full fiscal parameter set for a single country — use for per-country bid model inputs.

API access: The public JSON API at api/v1/countries.json provides machine-readable take, NPV, IRR, breakeven, mechanic, and region for all 185 countries. Use this for integration with Python or R models. Individual country endpoints: api/v1/country/{slug}.json (includes R-factor tier schedules for PSC countries).

Note: All exports reflect the standardized reference project. For field-specific parameters, use the Scenario Builder and note your input assumptions alongside the output.

Q: How current is the data, and how often is it updated?

DB date: 2026-08-15. The platform is updated in continuous improvement cycles, with the fiscal database (country_data.json) updated as new primary sources are processed through the Harvesting pipeline. The nightly audit (03:00 daily) validates data completeness and DCF consistency across all 185 countries — see the footer for last-run status.

What changes between updates: (1) New contracts sourced from operator annual reports, government gazettes, and PSA filings. (2) Fiscal term corrections when secondary sources are superseded by primary legislation. (3) IRR and breakeven coverage expansion — currently 74/185 and 68/185 countries respectively; expanding as capital cost data is compiled.

Stability: Government take figures for the 185 benchmark countries have been stable within ±2pp across the last 6 sourcing cycles (Apr–Aug 2026). Norway, Iraq, Angola, USA, UAE, and Australia have A-tier sourcing locked from primary legislation.

For time-sensitive work: Check the DB date in the footer. If your analysis requires confirmed current-year rates, cross-reference against the primary source cited in the Evidence tooltip for that country.

A12. My capital allocation team needs IRR for every candidate country. How do I handle the 111 countries without IRR data?
Four-step proxy workflow for IRR-incomplete countries:
  1. Stage 1 — Government Take screen: Filter all 185 countries by take ≤ your hurdle threshold. IRR and take are highly correlated at fixed project economics — regimes with take <50% almost universally deliver IRR >15%. Use the Screener's take slider as a fast filter.
  2. Stage 2 — Price swing stress test: Use the Swing (pp) column in Explorer to identify regimes with low take volatility. A country with 45% take at $75 but 60% take at $125 is riskier than one with stable 47% across prices — factor this into your risk-adjusted ranking.
  3. Stage 3 — Breakeven proxy: Use the ◭ Has Breakeven chip to filter to the 68 countries with breakeven data. Breakeven < $55/bbl is a strong proxy for IRR >15% at standard deepwater economics.
  4. Stage 4 — Scenario Builder DCF: For your final 2–3 candidate countries, open the Scenario Builder (header icon), enter country-specific cost assumptions, and compute a full IRR. This converts a data gap into a modeling exercise — which is exactly what an IC memo requires.
Coverage note: IRR requires verified per-contract opex/capex in addition to fiscal terms. The 111 countries without IRR still have full government take and NPV across 4 price points, which is sufficient for regime comparison and first-pass screening. Coverage expands as the sourcing pipeline processes additional cost data.

A14. How do I access fiscal data programmatically for integration with our internal models?
The platform exposes a static JSON API at three endpoints:
  • api/v1/countries.json — full summary for all 185 countries (govt take @4 prices, NPV, IRR, mechanic, region, evidence tier, contract count). Use this for portfolio-wide screening or feeding a country comparison model.
  • api/v1/country/{slug}.json — per-country detail including full fiscal parameters, profit-oil tier schedules, breakeven, Monte Carlo p10/p90, and source_note + evidence_tier per parameter. Slug = country name lowercased with spaces replaced by hyphens (e.g. saudi-arabia, trinidad-and-tobago). Accessible via the API Explorer tab.
  • api/v1/mechanics.json + api/v1/schema.json — mechanic definitions and field schema for parsing downstream.
Recommended integration pattern: fetch countries.json once per session to build a ranked list; call individual country/{slug}.json only for the 5–10 finalist countries where full parameter sets are needed for bid modeling. All endpoints are static (no auth, no rate limit) and cached by GitHub Pages CDN.

XLSX alternative: use Country Profile → Export XLSX for a single-country parameter sheet (includes all four price scenarios + fiscal parameters + source annotations), or Explorer → Excel for the full 185-country filtered table. Both include the same fields as the JSON API in Excel-native format.
A15. I have two candidate countries with similar government take — how do I differentiate using IRR and Breakeven?
Govt Take is a revenue-share metric; it tells you what fraction of gross revenue the government captures, but not the economics of your specific project. Two countries at 55% take can have very different IRRs if their cost structures, royalty bases, or profit-sharing tiers differ. Use this three-step workflow:

Step 1 — Screen by Take (Explorer/Screener). Identify the tier of each country: IF (<45%), Moderate (45–60%), High-Take (60–72%), or State-Dominated (>72%). Two countries at 55% are both Moderate — take alone does not differentiate.

Step 2 — Compare Price Swing. The Swing column (Govt Take @$125 − Take @$50, in pp) tells you how price-responsive the fiscal regime is. A low-swing country (green, <10pp) offers predictable terms at any oil price. A high-swing country (red, >20pp) captures most of your upside in a high-price scenario — important for a project that depends on high-price economics to clear your hurdle rate.

Step 3 — Use IRR and Breakeven for final differentiation. If both countries have IRR data (filter with the ◎ Has IRR Data chip), compare IRR @$75/bbl directly — this accounts for cost structure. If one country lacks IRR data, use Breakeven as a proxy: a lower breakeven means the project is profitable over a wider price range, which approximates a higher IRR. For your final 2–3 candidates, run a field-specific DCF in Scenario Builder with your project's actual capex/opex to get a calibrated IRR for each.

Rule of thumb: Take for headline screening → Swing for price risk → Breakeven for cost efficiency → Scenario Builder IRR for investment decision.
A16. How does the platform model R-factor tiered PSCs, and when should I use the R-factor filter vs. a flat PSC?
An R-factor (recovery factor) is a ratio that triggers progressive profit oil splits as the contractor recoups its investment — typically R = cumulative revenue ÷ cumulative cost. At R<1 the contractor has not recouped capex; at R>1 the government captures an increasing share of profit oil. This is the dominant PSC structure in Africa and the Middle East (Angola, Nigeria, Oman, Algeria, Tunisia, Egypt).

How the platform models R-factor PSCs. The DCF engine uses a production-weighted average profit oil split across the contract's modeled life, calibrated to the mid-tier split (the tier where production is weighted most heavily for the reference project). The platform's IRR column header tooltip notes this limitation explicitly ("arithmetic mean of contract-level IRRs"). The advantage is that it allows direct comparison across 185 countries; the disadvantage is that a project clearing R=1 early generates a different IRR than the model implies.

Use the ◈ R-factor PSC chip in Explorer to filter to the ~23 countries where the platform has verified R-factor tiered contracts. These countries have a more complex fiscal profile than the flat-split figure implies — treat the take figure as a reference band, not a precise estimate.

For investment decisions on R-factor regimes: load the country in Scenario Builder, manually set profit oil split to the mid-tier value (shown in Country Profile parameters), then check sensitivity by re-running with the high tier (R>2 split). The spread between these two runs approximates the take uncertainty from R-factor tiering. Angola Block 17 typically spans 4–8pp across tiers; Nigeria deepwater spans 6–12pp.

Rule of thumb: Use Explorer for screening (the blended take is directionally correct). Use Scenario Builder with explicit tier inputs for any country where R-factor tiering would materially affect your hurdle rate comparison.
A17. When is the government take figure reliable enough to include in a bid recommendation or IC memo?
Use the Evidence badge tier (visible in Country Profile → Fiscal Parameters) as the primary reliability signal. The threshold for a bid recommendation depends on what the take figure will be used for:

Evidence tier A (primary legislation / fiscal code): Use directly in IC memo — cite the specific legislation (e.g. "Petroleum Tax Act §10, Norwegian Offshore Tax — Petroleumsskatteloven"). Treat the figure as authoritative for screening and ranking. Uncertainty is limited to implementation risk, not data quality.

Evidence tier B (operator filing / annual report): Suitable for preliminary IC memo with a one-line caveat ("Sourced from [Operator] 10-K/Annual Report — verify against signed contract before final bid"). Figures are typically accurate but reflect a single operator's interpretation of the regime, not the full contract spectrum.

Evidence tier C (estimated / secondary source): Use for screening only — not for a bid recommendation without independent verification. Flag explicitly: "Take figure is estimated; primary legislation review recommended before advancing to bid stage." Cross-check against the Country Profile price sensitivity curve — if the curve looks anomalous (flat when it should be progressive, or implausibly low), the C-tier source may be stale or wrong.

Evidence tier D (default / no sourcing): Do not include in any recommendation document. This country is in the database for structural completeness but the take figure is a modeled default. Exclude from any ranked shortlist.

Additional checks before a bid recommendation:
  • Confirm the production-weighting flag (Country Profile → Weighting Method). "Equal-weighted" means take is averaged across contracts regardless of output — a single inactive block at atypical terms can distort the figure. Production-weighted figures are more representative of current operating conditions.
  • Check the Price Swing column. A swing >20pp means the regime is highly price-sensitive — small oil price movements produce large government take shifts. This is due diligence risk at the IC level, even if the A/B evidence tier is high.
  • For PSC countries: check if R-factor tiers apply (◈ chip visible in Explorer). If yes, use Scenario Builder to bound the take uncertainty before finalizing your bid economics.
  • For countries with IRR data: the breakeven price is more reliable than the IRR for screening, because breakeven is a direct output of cost structure rather than an annualized return calculation. Compare the breakeven to your project's cost estimate — if they diverge materially, your cost assumptions differ from the platform's reference project.
Rule of thumb: A/B tier take figures are IC-ready with citation. C-tier figures require a verification step. D-tier figures should not appear in external documents.
A18. How do I interpret the Fiscal Reform Risk and Stability Score when comparing regimes?
The Fiscal Predictability Score (0–100, shown in Explorer and Country Profile) combines three signals: reform frequency, reform direction (tightening vs. liberalizing), and IQR (within-country take variation across contract vintages). A higher score means more predictable terms — the government has historically changed rates rarely and within a narrow band.

Score interpretation guide:
  • 80–100 (green): Highly stable. Fewer than 2 reform events per decade, take variation <10pp across vintages. Suitable for long-plateau projects with 15+ year capital commitment (e.g. Norway at 96, UAE at 91).
  • 60–79 (amber): Moderate stability. Some reform activity but terms broadly consistent. Flag for scenario analysis: model a 5pp take increase as a downside case for capital allocation.
  • 40–59 (orange): Elevated reform risk. Multiple reforms in the last decade, often in one direction (tightening). Use Scenario Builder to stress-test take at +10pp; verify that IRR still clears your hurdle at the stressed case.
  • 0–39 (red): High reform risk. Regime has seen material tightening or reversals. Include a reform risk premium in your discount rate (recommended: +150–200bp above base). Do not rely on current take as indicative of terms at project peak production.
Reform Risk tab workflow: Filter by country to see the full reform timeline — direction badges (Tightening / Liberalizing) and rate change columns show what changed and by how much. Cross-reference with the Stability Score: a country with 10 reform events that are all small and bidirectional may score higher than one with 3 large unidirectional tightenings.

Common analyst errors:
  • Treating a current low take as locked-in for a 20-year project. Low take + low Stability Score = the government has historically recaptured upside when prices rise. Nigeria (PIA 2021) and Angola (2020 PSC reform) are recent examples.
  • Ignoring IQR when comparing similar average takes. Iraq average ~84.8% masks TSC vs. PSC block variation of 20+pp — the average is not representative of any single contract.
  • Using reform direction alone without controlling for oil price context. Most 2014–2016 liberalizations were responses to low oil prices; 2021–2023 tightenings tracked the post-COVID price recovery. Check the reform year against the oil price cycle before inferring regime intent.
Rule of thumb: Stability Score <60 adds one required stress-test iteration to any IC submission. Score <40 requires a formal country risk premium in the IRR hurdle.
A19. How do I use NPV and IRR together to evaluate an equity stake in an IOC-operated upstream project?
The platform reports Contractor NPV (the net present value accruing to the IOC after all fiscal deductions) and IRR (the return rate at which that NPV equals zero). For equity stake decisions, use them as a two-part filter:

Step 1 — IRR as the entry gate. Compare IRR to your firm's hurdle rate (typically 12–15% for E&P, higher for frontier acreage). Countries with IRR below your hurdle should be flagged — either negotiate better terms, use a lower-cost profile, or drop. Use the "Has IRR Data" chip in Explorer to filter to the 74 countries with verified IRR.

Step 2 — NPV as the equity-stake calibrator. Once a country clears the IRR hurdle, Contractor NPV tells you the absolute value creation per standard project profile. A 20% equity stake in a $2,000M NPV project creates $400M of value at your working interest. Compare across the shortlist — a higher-take country with a bigger resource base may outperform a low-take country with a marginal structure.

Step 3 — Government NPV as a negotiation anchor. The platform estimates Government NPV = Contractor NPV × (Govt Take%) ÷ (100% − Govt Take%). If Govt NPV is very large relative to Contractor NPV, the government has strong incentive to maintain terms; if it's small, there may be appetite for side-agreements or signature bonuses in exchange for better fiscal terms.

Key calibration: All platform NPV and IRR figures use a standardized production profile (e.g. deepwater: $1.2B capex, 50k bbl/d peak, 8-year plateau). Use the Scenario Builder to re-run with your actual project parameters for equity stake modeling — the standardized figures are directional screeners, not deal inputs.

Rule of thumb for equity sizing: if Contractor NPV ÷ (1 − Govt Take%) ÷ Total Project Value < 1.2×, the fiscal burden is high relative to project economics — increase hurdle rate or reduce working interest to maintain return discipline.
A20. Our team needs to compare finding and development (F&D) cost efficiency across multiple countries. How do I use the platform for cross-border fiscal cost analysis?
Cross-border F&D cost efficiency requires both the fiscal burden (government take) and the economic result (NPV per barrel). Here is the four-step workflow:

Step 1 — Fiscal Compare for a common profile. Run Fiscal Compare using the profile closest to your reference project (e.g. Deepwater $1.2B for a deepwater portfolio comparison, or Onshore $200M for a land portfolio). This ranks all 185 countries by take on the same project basis — a neutral baseline that removes field-size effects.

Step 2 — Export and add your internal F&D cost figures. Export the Fiscal Compare results to XLSX (Export XLSX button appears after running). Add a column for your firm's internal F&D cost estimate per country in the same spreadsheet. Columns already exported: country, mechanic, take@$75, NPV@$75, IRR, breakeven — add your capex/boe and opex/boe alongside these.

Step 3 — Scenario Builder for country-specific adjustments. For the 3–5 finalist countries, run the Scenario Builder with your actual project parameters (matching your internal cost estimates). This yields a country-specific NPV and IRR on a comparable apples-to-apples basis — the Fiscal Compare standardized profile may over- or under-state the regime impact for atypical cost structures.

Step 4 — Price Swing as fiscal risk indicator. After identifying high-NPV candidates, check the Price Swing column in Explorer (take@$125 − take@$50). A high swing (>25pp) means the government's take rises sharply with oil price — your F&D cost efficiency degrades faster than in a low-swing regime. Pair high-swing regimes with a downside price scenario in your sensitivity analysis.

Note: the platform's Contractor NPV is not identical to F&D cost recovery — it is the net present value of the entire project cash flow after fiscal deductions, not a per-barrel cost metric. To convert: Cost recovery breakeven ($/boe) ≈ Capex + PV(Opex) ÷ (Total recoverable boe × (1 − Govt Take%)).
A21. How do I run a price sensitivity analysis across a shortlist of countries to stress-test fiscal outcomes at different oil price assumptions?
Price sensitivity is a core part of any IC-level fiscal comparison. The platform supports two complementary approaches:

Approach 1 — Fiscal Compare across all 4 price points. Run Fiscal Compare at each of the four price scenarios ($50, $75, $100, $125) in sequence. Each run takes under a second. Export each to XLSX — the exports include columns for take, NPV, IRR, and breakeven at the selected price. Stack the four exports in your spreadsheet to create a full price-sensitivity matrix across all 185 countries. Look for countries that move significantly in take rank between $50 and $125 — high-swing regimes (Price Swing >25pp in Explorer) have progressive fiscal structures that hurt contractor economics most when prices rise.

Approach 2 — Scenario Builder for finalist countries. For a shortlist of 3–5 candidates, open the Scenario Builder and select the country preset (Norway, Angola, Iraq, UK, Australia, Guyana, Malaysia, etc.). The DCF inputs default to the country's representative terms. Change the price slider from $50 to $125 in steps — the results update in real time. Save each scenario at each price point to build a comparison table across countries. This approach captures the full DCF waterfall (cost recovery cap, FTP, progressive tiers) rather than a simple take percentage — essential for PSC regimes where cost recovery caps significantly affect contractor cash flow timing at low prices.

Key price-sensitivity signals to look for:
  • Price Swing (Explorer column): take@$125 − take@$50. >25pp = high-swing (progressive); <10pp = low-swing (predictable). Low-swing regimes protect contractor NPV in downturns.
  • Breakeven price: the price floor. Countries with breakeven <$50/bbl remain profitable even in severe downturns. Filter with the "Has Breakeven" chip.
  • NPV crossover: some regimes become NPV-positive only above $70/bbl — visible by running Fiscal Compare at $50 and $75 and comparing ranks. Countries that appear in the top 20 at $75 but not at $50 are price-sensitive entry points.
A22. A country has 95% production coverage but C-tier evidence on most parameters — how do I interpret that combination?
Coverage and evidence tier are orthogonal dimensions. A country can have broad production coverage (most contracts captured) but low evidence confidence (terms sourced from secondary or modeled data), or narrow coverage with very high confidence on the contracts that are present. Neither dimension subsumes the other.

What 95% coverage + C-tier means in practice: The platform has compiled most active contracts for that country (production-weighted), so the aggregate take figure is unlikely to be structurally wrong — you are not missing a major regime. However, the individual fiscal parameters (royalty rate, cost recovery cap, profit oil split) are sourced from secondary cross-references (Wood Mac, Rystad, or equivalent) rather than primary legislation or signed PSA text. The term values are plausible but not primary-verified.

When C-tier coverage-complete data is usable:
  • Screening and ranking: C-tier is sufficient for preliminary country screening (top-20 shortlisting, eliminating outliers). The take figure will be in the right ballpark for most regimes.
  • Portfolio-level comparison: If you are comparing 40 countries and only need relative ranking, C-tier countries can participate. Flag them in your output as "secondary-sourced, ±5pp tolerance."
  • NOT for IC submissions or binding deal terms: If the country is on a finalist shortlist, upgrade the evidence before submission. The source document is identified in the Evidence tooltip — retrieve the primary PSA or legislative text and verify the three or four load-bearing parameters (royalty, cost recovery cap, profit oil split, CIT rate).

Four-step due-diligence workflow for C-tier finalist countries:
  1. Open Country Profile → Evidence section. Note which parameters are C-tier and which document is cited.
  2. Retrieve the cited document (government gazette, operator filing, or Wood Mac country chapter).
  3. Verify the three load-bearing parameters against the primary source. If they match ±2pp, the platform figure is reliable for IC use.
  4. If they diverge by more than 2pp, use the Scenario Builder to re-run the DCF with your corrected parameters and note the override in your memo.

Rule of thumb: coverage tells you what you have; evidence tier tells you how much to trust it. A 95% / C-tier country is usable for screening, requires verification for decision-making.
A23. How should I handle frontier or pre-FID countries in a capital allocation shortlist — where the fiscal regime exists but production and cost data are limited?
Pre-FID countries present a four-part data challenge: (1) Regime uncertainty — fiscal terms may be draft or subject to negotiation; published PSC may not reflect final contract terms. (2) Cost uncertainty — no production history means capex/opex estimates are wide-range; the standardized project profile used by this platform will differ materially from the actual project. (3) Timeline uncertainty — FID delays compress IRR; a 3-year delay on a 25-year project reduces IRR by approximately 15–20% relative (not percentage points). (4) Revenue uncertainty — no decline curve data means plateau length and production profile shape are assumptions, not calibrations.

Three-stage approach for pre-FID countries in a capital allocation shortlist:
  1. Regime scan (Fiscal Compare + Explorer): Use the platform as a regime filter, not a project IRR estimator. Run Fiscal Compare to confirm the country clears a basic government take screen (e.g. <60% take at $75 for a deepwater profile). Countries failing the take screen rarely pass the full economic test — a regime above 65% take at the baseline price leaves insufficient contractor margin for the additional risk premium pre-FID projects require.
  2. Fiscal robustness check (Breakeven proxy): For pre-FID countries without IRR data, use Breakeven as a proxy for fiscal resilience. A breakeven <$65/bbl at the standardized profile signals the regime can absorb meaningful cost overruns and still remain economic. Combined with a take <55%, this is the minimum threshold for competitive pre-FID fiscal terms relative to producing-country alternatives at a $75 scenario. Use the "Has Breakeven" chip in Explorer to identify which pre-FID candidates have breakeven data available.
  3. Scenario Builder stress test (for finalist countries): For any pre-FID country that clears stages 1 and 2, open the Scenario Builder and run the DCF against your company-specific project parameters (your actual capex estimate, expected plateau rate, opex projection). Replace the standardized profile with your company's range. Run at $50/$75/$100 to identify the price below which the project becomes NPV-negative. If that crossover is above $65/bbl, the project requires a sustained high-price environment to be economic — flag for risk committee.

Rule of thumb for pre-FID screening: a frontier country needs a breakeven <$65/bbl AND a take <55% to be competitive with producing-country alternatives at the $75 reference scenario. Below this threshold, the fiscal burden is low enough to absorb pre-FID risk premiums. Above it, compare only if the resource scale (giant field potential) or strategic optionality justifies the additional uncertainty premium.
A24. We have an existing portfolio of blocks across 12 countries. How do I use this platform to assess aggregate fiscal risk exposure and flag which positions are most vulnerable to a sustained low-price environment?
Portfolio-level fiscal risk analysis is a three-layer exercise: (1) Exposure mapping (IOC Portfolio tab): Start on the IOC Portfolio tab — select your operator name to load a prebuilt exposure view showing all countries where your company holds blocks, their fiscal mechanic, government take, and production weight. If your operator isn't in the list, use the Explorer tab with your country list and load them into Side-by-Side for a four-country subset at a time. This gives you the fiscal distribution — the spread between your lowest-take (e.g. USA GoM ~23%) and highest-take (e.g. Iraq TSC ~85%) positions.

(2) Low-price stress test (Fiscal Compare + Breakeven filter): Run Fiscal Compare at $50/bbl — the stress-test price for most IOC planning horizons. Sort by Govt Take (high→low). Positions in the top quartile at $50 are the most exposed to price downside: high take at low prices signals a non-progressive regime that does not reduce the government share as margins compress. Cross-reference with the Breakeven column — any position with a breakeven above $65/bbl at the standardized profile is marginal at $50 and should be reviewed for NPV-negative status under your actual cost structure. Use the Screener's "High Fiscal Risk" preset (take >70% OR breakeven >$70) for a pre-filtered shortlist.

(3) Reform risk overlay (Reform Risk tab): After flagging the highest-exposure positions, go to the Reform Risk tab → "Most Frequently Reformed" and "Most Volatile" panels. Any portfolio country appearing in the top 10 most-reformed list carries a tightening risk premium on top of price risk. The Stability Score (1–5 dots in Explorer) provides a quick rank: positions scoring ≤2 in a high-take regime are the double-jeopardy cases — high current take and high probability of further tightening in the next fiscal cycle.

Aggregation note: This platform provides country-level blended take across all blocks, not block-specific figures. For a portfolio where your actual positions differ significantly from the country median (e.g. you hold a pre-FID frontier block in a country where most contracts are mature concessions), use the Scenario Builder to re-run DCF with your block's specific fiscal terms. Export the Fiscal Compare XLSX (all 185 countries at 4 price points) and filter to your 12 countries — this gives you the full price-sensitivity matrix for cross-portfolio comparison in a single spreadsheet.

Rule of thumb for portfolio fiscal risk: positions scoring >65% take at $50/bbl with Stability Score ≤2 are high-priority for review. Positions scoring <50% take at $50 with Stability Score ≥4 are the core low-risk anchors of your fiscal exposure distribution.
A25. A country has very attractive fiscal terms (low take, high IRR) but the Reform Risk tab shows it has been tightened 4 times since 2010. How do I factor reform risk into a bid recommendation?
Reform risk is the most systematically underweighted variable in first-pass fiscal analysis. A country that looks attractive at current terms can quickly become uneconomic if the fiscal regime tightens by even 5–8pp over the project life — a plausible magnitude given historical patterns. The correct approach is to treat fiscal attractiveness and reform risk as two separate dimensions that must both pass a threshold, not a single blended score.

Step 1 — Separate static attractiveness from reform trajectory. Run Fiscal Compare at $75 to confirm the country's current take rank. Then go to the Reform Risk tab → "Most Frequently Reformed" panel. A country appearing in the top 10 most-reformed with 4+ tightening events since 2010 has a demonstrated pattern of upward take adjustment. Look at the reform direction breakdown: if 3 of 4 events were tightening (not liberalizing), the regime is on a structural upward trajectory, not oscillating around an equilibrium.

Step 2 — Estimate the reform-adjusted take range. In the Explorer, find the country's Price Swing value. A high-swing regime (Swing >25pp) means fiscal progressivity is built in — take automatically rises as prices increase. For a reform-prone country, add a "reform premium" of 3–6pp on top of the current take for planning purposes. Use the Scenario Builder to re-run the DCF with the royalty or CIT rate incremented by 3–6pp — this gives you the NPV at "plausible worst case terms within 5 years." If that scenario still yields a positive NPV at $75, the project has fiscal headroom. If NPV turns negative, the project's economics depend on fiscal terms staying at or below current levels — a weak assumption for a frequently-reformed regime.

Step 3 — Apply the Stability Score in context. The Stability Score (1–5 dots in Explorer) is a quick triage signal: a 5-dot country has had zero reform events since 2010, while a 1-dot country has had 4 or more. However, stability score alone can mislead — some countries have been stable because they were already at high take (no room to tighten), and others have been stable because of a production sharing formula that automatically adjusts take with price (eliminating the political need to legislate). Cross-reference the Stability Score with the mechanic type: a non-progressive Concession regime with a Stability Score of 2 has more tightening risk than an R-factor PSC with a Score of 2 (the PSC already self-adjusts with economics).

Decision framework for the bid recommendation:
  • Current take <55% + Stability ≥4 + Swing <15pp: Fiscal terms are attractive, stable, and non-progressive — a strong positive for the bid recommendation. Flag as "low fiscal risk."
  • Current take <55% + Stability ≤2 + 3+ tightening events: Terms are currently attractive but have demonstrated reform pattern. Model the bid at current terms + 5pp uplift for the IC scenario. Flag as "attractive but reform-exposed — build fiscal flex into contract negotiation." Prioritize stabilization clauses if the PSA terms allow.
  • Current take 55–65% + Stability ≤2: Moderate take with reform history. The combination of already-moderate take + reform risk means the project could quickly become marginal. Require a breakeven <$55/bbl at current terms to retain a sufficient buffer for plausible tightening. If breakeven is $60–70/bbl, the project has little margin for any adverse fiscal change — flag as "fiscal cliff risk."
  • Current take >65%: High current take eliminates the reform premium from the analysis — you are already at the high end, and reform risk becomes catastrophic rather than marginal. A single 5pp tightening at 65% take moves you into the range where most IOC IRR hurdle rates are not met at $75/bbl. A high-take, frequently-reformed country should only appear in a bid recommendation if there is a specific structural justification (e.g., sovereign cost protection clause, unique resource scale, host government buy-in at the MoU level).

Rule of thumb: fiscal attractiveness + reform risk must both pass. A country at <55% take with Stability ≥4 is a fiscal anchor. A country at <55% take with Stability ≤2 is a conditional opportunity — model the 5pp reform scenario and ensure the project still clears your hurdle. Attractive fiscal terms in a volatile regime are a mirage if the field development timeline exceeds the reform cycle.
A26. The platform uses a flat 10% discount rate. Our hurdle rate is 12% for frontier countries and 8% for OECD producers. How should I adjust the NPV comparisons for a mixed-portfolio IC presentation?
The flat 10% discount rate is the industry standard for regime comparison — it keeps take and NPV figures comparable across all 185 countries on a single basis. But for an IC presentation where your portfolio spans both frontier (Nigeria, Angola, Iraq) and OECD (Norway, Australia, Canada), a flat 10% overstates frontier NPV and understates OECD NPV relative to how your investment committee actually evaluates these projects. The correct approach is to use the platform's NPV as a starting point and apply a discount rate adjustment at the IC stage.

Step 1 — Use the Scenario Builder to derive a country-specific NPV. The Scenario Builder lets you input a custom discount rate via the "Discount Rate" field. For each finalist country, run the Scenario Builder with your actual hurdle rate (e.g. 8% for Norway, 12% for Nigeria) and your actual capex, opex, and production profile. The output is a live DCF at your firm's rate — not the platform's standard 10%. The Methodology tab's Discount Rate Sensitivity section (table: Norway/Angola/USA NPVs at 8%, 10%, 12%, 15%) gives you a quick directional sense of how NPV shifts by ±1–3pp on the discount rate.

Step 2 — Understand what changes and what doesn't. Government take is discount-rate-invariant — take is computed on undiscounted gross revenue, so the take ranking (the primary use case of Fiscal Compare) holds regardless of your hurdle rate. What changes is contractor NPV: a higher discount rate compresses NPV more steeply for high-capex long-payback projects (deepwater, LNG) than for short-cycle ones. This means the NPV gap between a 25-year deepwater PSC and a 10-year buy-back contract narrows at 12% vs. 10%. The Govt Take column in Fiscal Compare is always valid for regime comparison; the NPV column requires discount rate alignment for cross-country IC comparison.

Step 3 — Practical IC presentation workflow.
  • First-pass screening: Use Fiscal Compare at 10% flat to rank all candidate countries by take and NPV. This identifies the fiscal frontier (top 20 by contractor NPV) on a level basis.
  • Finalist risk-adjustment: For the top 5–8 candidates, run the Scenario Builder at your firm's risk-adjusted hurdle rate per country. Export each result to the Excel for IC memo. The XLSX includes the Scenario Builder's live DCF output — you can copy this directly into your valuation model.
  • OECD vs. frontier framing: For the IC narrative, separate the comparison into two tiers: Tier 1 (8% OECD, e.g. Norway/Australia) and Tier 2 (12% frontier, e.g. Nigeria/Angola/Iraq). State clearly which discount rate applies to each row. The take column is valid for cross-tier comparison; the NPV column is only cross-comparable within the same tier.

Rule of thumb: a 2pp increase in the discount rate (10% → 12%) reduces contractor NPV by approximately 15–25% for a standard 25-year deepwater project (depending on production profile steepness). A 2pp decrease (10% → 8%) increases NPV by a similar range. For a $1.2B capex project at $75/bbl, this translates to roughly $90–250M NPV swing — material enough to flip a marginal project's IC recommendation. Always disclose the discount rate used in any NPV figure in an IC document.
A27. The Swing (pp) column in Explorer shows some countries at <5pp and others at >30pp. How do I use Price Swing in a fiscal risk decision — when should I prefer a low-swing regime over a high-IRR high-swing one?
Price Swing (pp) measures fiscal price-responsiveness: it is the difference in government take at $125/bbl versus $50/bbl. A high-swing country captures a larger share of your oil price upside — the fiscal terms are progressive. A low-swing country keeps take near-constant across the price cycle — the regime is neutral or regressive. The right choice depends on your price view and the project's payback structure.

Understanding the Swing signal by tier:
  • <10pp Swing (green — neutral/regressive): Concession-dominant regimes with flat royalty + CIT and no R-factor adjustment. Examples: USA (GOM) ~6pp, Canada ~8pp, Ireland ~5pp. Contractor captures most of the price upside; government take stays predictable. Best for projects that depend on $75+ oil to clear hurdles — high-price scenarios stay contractor-friendly.
  • 10–20pp Swing (amber — moderately progressive): PSC with cost recovery caps or mild R-factor tiers. Examples: Angola ~14pp, Malaysia ~16pp, Brazil ~12pp. Government captures moderate upside. These regimes are typical for large IOC portfolio countries where fiscal predictability and entry terms are both acceptable.
  • >20pp Swing (red — highly progressive): PRRT (Australia ~34pp), Norwegian Windfall Tax (~28pp), or strong R-factor PSCs. Government captures most of the oil price upside above the base case. At $125/bbl the contractor's incremental economics erode rapidly. These regimes work best for projects with very low breakevens — strong base-case economics that clear hurdles even when high-price scenarios are government-captured.

Decision framework — low-swing vs. high-swing:
  • Prefer low-swing when: Your project's IRR is marginal at $75/bbl and depends on a $100+ scenario for IC approval. High-swing regimes erode the high-price scenario that makes the project viable. Also prefer low-swing for short-cycle assets (3–5yr payback) where fiscal predictability across the project life matters more than base-case take level.
  • Prefer high-swing when: Your project has robust base-case economics (breakeven <$50, IRR >20% at $75) and you are primarily comparing entry terms rather than stress-testing a marginal project. High-swing regimes often pair with lower base-case take — the government trades current-price take for price-upside participation. If you expect a sustained $75–85 environment, a high-swing regime at 55% take may outperform a low-swing regime at 48% take on a $125 upside basis.
  • Watch for Swing + Reform interaction: A high-swing regime that also has a high Stability Score (≥4) is the best-case combination — the fiscal terms are progressive but stable. A high-swing regime with Stability ≤2 is the worst case: take is price-responsive AND subject to reform, meaning both the base and the upside can be eroded simultaneously by a policy change. Use the Reform Risk tab to overlay swing and stability before finalizing a country ranking.

Rule of thumb: Swing is a risk distribution metric, not a quality metric. A 30pp swing is not inherently better or worse than a 5pp swing — it determines who captures the oil price lottery. Use IRR and Breakeven to assess economic quality; use Swing to assess how project economics are distributed across price scenarios.
A28. When I compare an ORCA take figure with a published Wood Mackenzie or Rystad number for the same country, they sometimes differ by 5–10pp. Why does this happen, and how should I reconcile the difference?
Differences between ORCA and commercial databases in the 5–10pp range are expected and reflect four well-understood structural differences, not data errors:

1. Reference project assumption mismatch. ORCA applies a single standardized production profile to every country (e.g. Deepwater: $1.2B capex, 50k bbl/d, $15/bbl opex). Wood Mackenzie and Rystad calibrate each country to that country's actual production cost structure — a deepwater well in Angola costs more to operate than one in the Gulf of Mexico. If your reference project parameters differ from the platform's, use the Scenario Builder with your actual capex/opex to obtain a ORCA result comparable to a field-specific third-party estimate.

2. Price scenario difference. Always confirm which oil price the third-party number assumes.
