  • Fully state-dominated with limited IOC access: Kuwait (no PSC/concession open to IOCs; KIEAE/EY take reflects historical terms only), Iran (IPC terms for IOCs post-sanctions — sanctions resolution required for entry), Saudi Arabia HSEP (ongoing bid rounds but small acreage relative to Aramco's core). For these countries, the take figure is directionally valid for scenario planning but the realistic IOC entry vehicle requires checking the most recent bid round terms directly from the national regulator.
Workflow for IC submissions on mixed-access countries:
  1. Check the multi-mechanic blend warning in the Country Profile — the ⚠ flag appears when a country has contracts of materially different mechanics (e.g. Iraq TSC + KRG PSC). Read the contract-count breakdown to understand what fraction of the database take figure reflects your target entry vehicle.
  2. Select the relevant mechanic in the Scenario Builder. Do not use the country-level blended figure for a bid model — select the mechanic that matches your block type and recompute take at your project parameters.
  3. Cross-check against the most recent bid round disclosure. For Saudi HSEP, UAE ADNOC concessions, and Iraq KRG bid rounds, the current terms may differ from the platform's database vintage. Cite both: "Platform take: X% (ORCA v274, standardized basis); Current bid round disclosure: Y% (source: [national regulator])."
  4. Apply the FAQ A64 counterparty quality overlay. In mixed-access countries, Stability Score reflects the overall reform history of the fiscal regime — but IOC-accessible block terms may have additional contractual stabilization (ADNOC typically guarantees 30-year concession terms). Note this asymmetry in your IC disclosure.
Rule of thumb: if a country's take figure surprises you (unusually high or low relative to the basin), check the contract-count split in the Country Profile before using the figure in a bid model. Saudi 87.3% and Kuwait 92.4% are correct for HSEP/KIEAE IOC-accessible terms — not representative of the national average economics that Aramco/KNPC operate at.
A66. Two countries show nearly identical government take at $75/bbl, but one is a Concession and the other is a PSC. Does the fiscal mechanic affect how I should use these figures in a bid model?
Yes — identical headline take at a single reference price ($75/bbl) can mask materially different economics at other prices, different capex levels, and different timeline sensitivities. The mechanic drives three structural differences that matter for bid models:

1. Price-sensitivity (Swing): Concessions with a royalty-dominated structure collect a fixed percentage of gross revenue regardless of profitability — this creates a high-take, low-swing profile. PSCs with a cost recovery cap and profit oil split effectively defer government take to the post-recovery period, which compresses take at low prices (cost recovery eats most of the revenue) and increases take at high prices. The platform's Price Swing metric (take at $125/bbl minus take at $50/bbl) is the fastest way to diagnose this: a Swing >20pp typically signals a profit-based mechanic (PSC, PRRT) that will have materially different economics at off-reference prices. Two countries showing 58% take at $75/bbl may show 52% vs. 64% at $50/bbl if one is a concession and the other a PSC — a 12pp spread on the same headline.

2. Breakeven price sensitivity: Under a PSC with a cost recovery cap, a high-capex project may fail to recover costs before the cost cap is hit — extending the breakeven price relative to a concession where the royalty is gross-revenue-based and does not compound the cost problem. For the platform's standardized $1.2B deepwater project, a 50% cost recovery cap (Indonesia/Philippines range) typically adds $5–12/bbl to breakeven vs. a royalty-only concession with the same headline take. Check the Breakeven Map tab and Country Profile cost_recovery_limit field before using a PSC take figure for go/no-go decisions.

3. Cash flow timing: Concession royalties accrue from first production; PSC profit oil splits only begin after cost recovery — which may be 3–6 years post-startup for a $1.2B deepwater project at $75/bbl. The result is that a concession with 55% take and a PSC with 55% take at a single reference price may have NPV differences of $50–150M on a $1.2B project, solely due to payment timing. This is the primary reason the platform reports NPV separately from take: NPV at $75/bbl already reflects the discount rate effect of timing differences between mechanics.

Workflow for IC submissions comparing mechanics:
  1. Start with the Fiscal Compare tab. Run both countries and read Price Swing alongside take. If Swing differs by >10pp between the two, the reference price comparison is misleading — note this explicitly in your IC memo.
  2. Run the Scenario Builder separately for each mechanic. Select Concession for the first country and PSC for the second. Compare IRR — not take — as your primary bid-ranking metric. IRR already discounts the payment timing difference that the take percentage ignores.
  3. Apply a price stress test. Run both countries at $50/bbl and $100/bbl using the Scenario Builder. If the PSC country shows a wider IRR swing than the Concession country, this is a feature (PSCs protect contractor take at low prices via cost recovery) or a risk (PSCs generate higher government take at high prices) depending on your price view.
  4. Disclose the mechanic type in the IC memo. "Country A (Concession, royalty 12% + CIT 30%, take 57% at $75/bbl, Swing 8pp, IRR 14.2% at $75/bbl standardized)" vs. "Country B (PSC, 60% cost recovery cap, 65/35 profit split, CIT 25%, take 57% at $75/bbl, Swing 19pp, IRR 13.1% at $75/bbl standardized — lower IRR despite identical take due to cost recovery timing)."
Rule of thumb: for a $1.2B project, a 10pp Swing difference between two same-take countries translates to roughly $80–150M NPV difference at $50/bbl and a 1.5–3pp IRR difference. Never rank bid targets by take alone when mechanics differ — use IRR from the Scenario Builder as the equalizing metric.
A67. How do I interpret government take figures for countries with production-sharing contracts that include a Domestic Market Obligation (DMO) — and does DMO materially change the effective take for an IOC?
A Domestic Market Obligation (DMO) requires the contractor to supply a fixed percentage of production to the domestic market — typically at a subsidized domestic price well below international export netback. DMO is a common feature of PSCs in Indonesia, Malaysia, Egypt, Iraq (gas), and several West African regimes, and it creates a structurally important wedge between the platform's government take figure and the IOC's effective realized economics. Understanding how DMO operates is essential before citing the platform's take in an IC submission for any DMO-active regime.

How DMO works — three structural mechanics:
  1. DMO with cost recovery waiver (Indonesia Gross Split, Indonesia classic PSC 2002): Contractor must supply 25% of production to Pertamina/BPH Migas at domestic price (~$35–45/bbl in 2023, vs. $75–80 Brent) for the first 60 months of production; in exchange, contractor receives an additional cost recovery tranche offsetting the price discount. The platform's Indonesia take figure is calibrated to the post-DMO profit oil split — but the domestic price discount for the first 5 years of production is not fully captured. For a 50,000 bbl/d project, the first-60-months DMO obligation at $35/bbl vs. $75 export price costs the contractor approximately $110–150M NPV — equivalent to ~1.5–2.5pp effective IRR reduction. Use the Scenario Builder: reduce average realized price by 9% (25% of production × $40 discount at a 70/30 export/domestic split) and compare IRR against the headline take figure.
  2. DMO without offset (Egypt EGPC, Malaysia Petronas): Contractor supplies 10–15% of gas/oil production at domestic controlled price with no cost recovery offset. In Egypt, the gas domestic price ($2.65/MMBtu) is materially below Brent-linked export netback ($7–9/MMBtu); the platform's Egypt gas PSC take captures the production split but not the price discount on the DMO tranche. For Egypt gas PSCs, add a price adjustment factor of (1 − DMO% × domestic/export price ratio) to the Scenario Builder's realized price to correctly model effective contractor economics.
  3. DMO at arm's-length market price (Malaysia Petronas GPSA, some PNG LNG terms): Contractor supplies 20–25% of production at a regulated domestic market price set at 80–90% of export netback. This is the least punitive structure — the effective take penalty is 2–5pp vs. full export realization. The platform's Malaysia and PNG take figures are calibrated to include this structure directionally.
Workflow for IC submissions in DMO-active regimes:
  1. Check the Country Profile DMO field. The domestic_market_obligation_pct field is populated for Indonesia, Malaysia, Egypt (gas), Iraq (gas), and Papua New Guinea. If non-zero, a DMO is active and the platform's take figure understates effective government capture of contractor revenue.
  2. Compute the effective price discount in Scenario Builder. Set realized price = Brent × (1 − DMO% × (1 − domestic_price/export_price)). For Indonesia classic PSC: 0.75 × Brent + 0.25 × $40 domestic ≈ Brent × 0.87 at $75 Brent. Run IRR at this effective price and disclose the DMO adjustment in your IC memo.
  3. Check DMO duration. Indonesia's 60-month DMO window is the most common structure — it is time-limited and therefore most penalizing for short-plateau or fast-declining fields where the DMO obligation coincides with peak production years. For a slow-ramp or late-plateau project, the DMO impact is smaller as a share of total project revenue.
  4. Disclose the DMO in IC memo language. Standard IC language: "Government take per ORCA v274 (Aug 2026): X% at $75/bbl standardized Deepwater profile. Effective contractor realized price adjusted for DMO obligation: $[price]/bbl (DMO [pct]% at domestic price $[domestic]/bbl for [duration] months). DMO-adjusted IRR: [adjusted IRR]% vs. pre-DMO platform IRR: [unadjusted IRR]%."
Rule of thumb: for Indonesia (25% DMO at ~$35–45 domestic, 60-month window), the DMO reduces effective contractor IRR by 1.5–2.5pp on a standard deepwater project. For Egypt gas PSCs (10–15% DMO at $2.65/MMBtu domestic vs. $7–9/MMBtu export), the effective penalty is 2–4pp IRR reduction over project life. For Malaysia at 80–90% domestic/export parity, the DMO impact is <1pp and is typically omitted from IC memo headline adjustments. Always disclose the DMO structure in any IC submission involving Indonesia, Egypt gas, or Malaysia PSC benchmarking.
A68. What does the Price Swing metric mean, and how should I use it to compare fiscal regimes across different oil price environments?
Price Swing = government take at $100/bbl minus government take at $50/bbl. It measures how much the government's fiscal share increases as the oil price rises — a structural property of the regime, not a cyclical observation. High Swing means the government captures a disproportionate share of price upside; low Swing means the IOC retains more upside at high prices.
  • Low Swing (0–8pp), e.g. UAE 2.1pp, Saudi Arabia 2.8pp: Concession regimes with fixed or capped royalties and stable CIT rates. The IOC retains nearly all price upside above the baseline. Attractive for high-price scenario modeling, but note that these low-Swing states typically have high base-case take (UAE 73.4%, Saudi 87.3%) — the upside retention occurs within a high-take envelope.
  • Moderate Swing (8–18pp), e.g. Norway 12.1pp, UK 9.4pp, Australia 11.3pp: SPT/PRRT/windfall-profit mechanisms activate at higher prices, capturing incremental revenue above a threshold. These regimes are calibrated to allow IOC returns at $60–70/bbl while shifting surplus above ~$80/bbl to the state. Modeling note: the $75/bbl platform default sits in the linear range; always run Scenario Builder at both $60 and $100 to see where the SPT kink point is.
  • High Swing (18–30pp), e.g. Nigeria PSC 24.3pp, Angola PSC 21.8pp, Algeria 26.1pp: R-factor PSCs and price-triggered royalty steps dominate. The government take ratchets sharply as price rises through tier thresholds. In a $100/bbl environment these regimes can consume 75–85% of revenues; in a $50/bbl environment the same contract may yield 55–65% take. IC evaluation must model the full price distribution, not point estimates.
  • Very High Swing (>30pp), e.g. Venezuela 38.4pp, Libya 35.2pp: Hybrid mechanisms with both price-triggered royalty escalation and profit-share ratchets. These regimes are typically directional-only benchmarks — the platform captures the fiscal architecture but the investment environment is sanctioned or commercially inaccessible.
4-step IC workflow for Price Swing analysis:
  1. Open Fiscal Compare → select target countries → click Price Swing sort to rank by Swing descending. Identify countries in the same take tier at $75/bbl that diverge sharply in Swing — these are the highest-analytical-value comparisons.
  2. For each country pair of interest, run Scenario Builder at $50, $75, and $100 with your project parameters. The Swing-implied take change (×your revenue assumption) is the dollar value of price risk borne by the IOC.
  3. Interpret Swing in the context of base-case take: a 20pp Swing on a 40% base-case regime means the IOC's net share falls from 60% to 40% at $100 — still positive. The same 20pp Swing on a 65% base-case regime means IOC net share falls from 35% to 15% — potentially sub-economic at high prices without cost-recovery protections.
  4. IC memo language: "Fiscal regime [Country] exhibits a [X]pp Price Swing (government take at $100/bbl minus $50/bbl), versus peer [Country B] at [Y]pp. At our base-case $75/bbl the take differential is [Z]pp. Sensitivity to a $100/bbl scenario adds [$ amount] in government fiscal burden relative to $75/bbl, using the platform's Scenario Builder at $1.2B capex/$15/bbl opex reference project."
Rule of thumb: Swing <10pp = concession-dominant regime; Swing 10–20pp = hybrid/SPT regime; Swing >20pp = aggressive R-factor PSC or multi-mechanism regime. Use Swing alongside Breakeven (downside protection) and base-case take (government claim) for the three-metric fiscal characterization required for any IC memo country comparison.
A69. How do fiscal ring-fencing rules affect the cost recovery pool across a multi-block portfolio — and how does the platform handle ring-fencing in its DCF model?
Ring-fencing is a fiscal boundary rule that determines whether costs from one contract area can offset revenue from another. It is one of the most analytically important but least-discussed aspects of upstream fiscal design — a seemingly identical government take figure can represent very different contractor economics depending on whether the regime is ring-fenced at the license level, field level, or company level.
  • License-level ring-fence (strictest): Each exploration/production license is treated as a separate cost recovery pool. Costs from Block A cannot offset revenue from Block B, even within the same PSC framework. Impact: a portfolio of 5 licenses cannot pool exploration write-offs against producing block revenue until each license individually passes cost recovery. Typical jurisdictions: Nigeria (OPL/OML boundary ring-fence), Angola (block-specific EPSA ring-fence), Libya (EPSA IV per-block). In these regimes, exploration portfolio diversification increases fiscal risk by creating multiple simultaneous cost recovery queues.
  • Company-level ring-fence (most permissive): All license costs and revenues across a jurisdiction pool together. Exploration capex from Block A can be recovered against Block B production revenue in the same fiscal year. Impact: reduces effective cost recovery timing risk for active explorers. Typical jurisdictions: UK (petroleum ring-fence encompasses all UKCS production), Norway (SPT/CIT computed at company level across all NCS licenses), Australia (PRRT per-project but exploration pooling available under Exploration Expenditure Credit).
  • Field-level ring-fence (intermediate): Costs pool at the individual field/discovery unit, not the license. Development capex and production revenue for a single field are isolated; appraisal costs may span multiple blocks. Typical jurisdictions: USA Gulf of Mexico (per-lease royalty, combined development unit allowed), Malaysia (Petroleum Agreement per-field development area).
  • Carry-forward without ring-fence breach: Most PSC regimes allow unrecovered cost oil to carry forward at cost (no interest) within the same block, but do not allow cross-block netting. The platform's DCF model uses license-level ring-fencing as the default — costs are recovered from the single reference project's revenue only. This is the most common institutional assumption for standardized fiscal comparison (Wood Mac, Rystad, and S&P Global Commodity Insights all use per-contract ring-fencing for their standardized fiscal metrics).
Platform treatment and IC workflow:
  1. Check the ring-fence field in Country Profile. Export Country Profile XLSX → the ring_fence_level parameter shows the documented ring-fencing rule for the primary contract type in that country. Tier A/B entries cite the specific legislative clause (e.g. Nigeria PPTA Section 19 license ring-fence, Norway Petroleum Taxation Act Section 3d company consolidation).
  2. For single-block evaluation (standard IC use): the platform's per-contract DCF is correct as-is — the reference project has one cost pool. Use take, IRR, and NPV as presented.
  3. For multi-block portfolio evaluation: the fiscal benefit of company-level ring-fencing (UK/Norway) or exploration cost pooling (Australia) is NOT captured in the standard platform take figure. Run Scenario Builder twice — once at a single-project scale, once with lower effective capex per block (reflecting the exploration write-off benefit). The difference in IRR approximates the portfolio ring-fence benefit.
  4. IC memo language: "Government take for [Country] is [X]% at $75/bbl (ORCA v274, standardized Deepwater profile, per-contract ring-fence assumption). [Country] operates a [license/company/field]-level ring-fence; for a [single-block/multi-block] portfolio this [does / does not] create cross-subsidization potential. Adjusted portfolio-level take assuming [describe pooling] is estimated at [Y]% — see Appendix [F] for Scenario Builder ring-fence sensitivity."
Rule of thumb: License-level ring-fencing (Nigeria/Angola/Libya) increases effective fiscal burden by 2–5pp IRR for explorers with discovery drag on undeveloped blocks; company-level ring-fencing (UK/Norway/Australia) adds 1–3pp IRR benefit for active explorers relative to the per-block standard. This gap is analytically significant for portfolio-wide capital allocation decisions — always disclose ring-fence assumption when comparing UK/Norway vs. Sub-Saharan Africa concession IRRs in the same IC table.
A70. What is an R-factor in a Production Sharing Contract, and how does ORCA model it when a PSC has multiple R-factor tiers?
The R-factor (revenue factor or recovery ratio) is a contractual mechanism in PSCs that links the government's profit oil share to how much revenue the contractor has already received relative to their cumulative investment. It is the primary progressive mechanism in Nigerian, Angolan, and Algerian PSC regimes — and understanding it is essential for modeling cash flow timing differences between PSC variants.

Definition: R = cumulative contractor revenue ÷ cumulative contractor costs. When R < 1, the contractor has not yet recovered their investment — they remain in the low-government-take tier (high contractor profit oil, e.g. 55/45 government/contractor split). When R = 1, the contractor has exactly recovered costs. As R rises above 1, the government's profit oil share ratchets upward through pre-set tiers. A PSC might specify:
  • R < 1.5: Profit oil 55/45 (govt/contractor) — pre-recovery tier
  • 1.5 ≤ R < 2.0: Profit oil 65/35 — mid-recovery tier
  • R ≥ 2.0: Profit oil 75/25 — post-recovery tier
The contractor crosses each threshold as cumulative production revenue accumulates relative to their sunk capital. The key insight: R-factor is a retrospective measure — it depends on what has already been produced and at what price, not on the current production rate alone. A high-price environment accelerates R, pushing the contractor into the high-government-take tier sooner. A low-price environment keeps R below 1 longer, protecting contractor returns.

How ORCA models R-factor PSCs. The platform uses a mid-tier R-factor approximation: for each country, the DCF model applies a single blended profit oil split that represents the expected production-weighted average across the R-factor schedule, given the standardized reference project profile ($1.2B capex / 50k bbl/d peak / $15/bbl opex). At $75/bbl Deepwater, the reference project typically crosses R=1 in year 3–4 and reaches R=1.5 in year 6–7. The platform's reported take reflects the weighted-average government share across all R-factor tiers over the full project life — not the lowest or highest tier alone. This is disclosed in the Evidence tooltip for R-factor PSC countries (Nigeria, Angola, Algeria, Algeria, Congo, DRC).

IC workflow for R-factor PSCs:
  1. Check the Country Profile for R-factor tier schedule. The API endpoint api/v1/country/{slug}.json includes the full tier schedule (thresholds and splits) for PSC countries. R-factor sensitivity is most material for Nigeria (OPL/OML blocks), Angola (EPSA IV blocks), and Algeria (Sonatrach JV PSC blocks).
  2. Model R-factor sensitivity in Scenario Builder. High-capex projects (>$2B) stay in the pre-recovery tier longer — the platform's mid-tier approximation understates contractor take for high-cost developments. Low-capex brownfield projects may rapidly cross R=2, overstating contractor take in the platform vs. the actual blended outcome. Use the Scenario Builder at your actual capex to see the NPV impact.
  3. Apply an IC adjustment for oil price sensitivity. At $100/bbl, R crosses each threshold 20–30% faster than at $75/bbl, compressing contractor profit oil for a larger share of the project life. The platform's Price Swing metric (take@$100 − take@$50) is the fastest proxy for R-factor sensitivity: a Swing >20pp signals a regime where price acceleration dramatically shifts R-factor tier crossings. Nigeria PSC Swing ≈24pp is a direct consequence of R-factor acceleration at high prices.
  4. IC memo language: "Government take for [Country] PSC is [X]% at $75/bbl (ORCA v274, standardized profile, R-factor mid-tier approximation — actual take varies from [low tier]% to [high tier]% depending on R-factor tier achieved over project life). At $100/bbl, take is [Y]% (R-factor acceleration adds [Z]pp vs. $75/bbl reference). See Scenario Builder sensitivity at actual project capex ($[W]M) in Appendix G."
Rule of thumb: For a $1.2B reference project in a Nigeria OML PSC, the R-factor mid-tier approximation is within 3pp of a full dynamic R-factor schedule at $75/bbl. At $50/bbl, the project may not cross R=1.5, making the low tier dominant — take 5–8pp lower than the platform figure. At $100/bbl, the project crosses R=2.0 in year 5–6, making the high tier dominant — take 5–8pp higher. Always present R-factor PSC take as a range ($50/$75/$100 scenario) rather than a point estimate for IC submissions in Nigeria, Angola, or Algeria.
A71. How do I use the IOC Portfolio tab to assess my company's fiscal exposure by region — and what does the peer comparison chart tell me?
The IOC Portfolio tab is designed for one specific use case: instantly answering "where is [IOC] exposed to high-take regimes, and how does that exposure compare to peer operators?" It is not a full portfolio model — it maps operator-country relationships from a curated IOC_DATA set against the platform's fiscal database, producing a take-tiered breakdown of the operator's geographic footprint.

Step 1 — Select an operator. Click one of the quick-select buttons (ExxonMobil, Shell, TotalEnergies, BP, Equinor, Chevron, Eni) or type a company name in the search box. The tab immediately renders: (a) a donut chart showing the operator's country count by take tier (IOC-friendly <40%, Mid 40–55%, High 55–70%, State-heavy >70%); (b) a portfolio summary table listing each country, the operator's take exposure, and a link to the Country Profile; (c) a peer comparison bar chart showing the operator's portfolio average take vs. a composite peer group average.

What the peer comparison chart tells you. The bar chart compares the selected operator's portfolio-average government take at $75/bbl (production-weighted across their active countries) vs. the peer group average (the 6 other major IOCs in the quick-select set). A bar showing the operator >3pp above the peer average means their geographic footprint is skewed toward higher-take regimes; below the peer average means they have a higher-than-average proportion of low-take exposure (e.g. USA GoM, Guyana, or UAE concessions). This is the fastest single-metric answer to "are we in expensive countries relative to our peers?"

How to use this for capital allocation pre-screening:
  1. Identify your operator's take tier concentration. A donut with >40% in the State-heavy tier (>70% take) signals a portfolio skewed toward integrated NOC partnerships, service contracts (Iraq TSC), or frontier concessions with limited upside at high prices. This is not necessarily bad — it depends on acreage quality — but it sets the fiscal context for any new entry decision.
  2. Use the peer comparison to identify relative fiscal positioning. If your operator is 5pp above peer average take, any new entry should prioritize low-take regimes (<45%) to bring the portfolio average down. If you're already below peer average, fiscal diversification is less urgent — acreage quality and IRR may be more constraining.
  3. Cross-reference with the Country Profile for each high-take country in your portfolio. Click any country in the portfolio table to open its Country Profile — you'll see the full fiscal breakdown, reform history, and Stability Score. High-take countries with Stability ≥4 (Norway, Qatar, UAE) are acceptable; high-take countries with Stability ≤2 (Russia, Nigeria pre-2023, Venezuela) represent fiscal risk exposure worth flagging in IC materials.
  4. Export portfolio summary to XLSX. The "↓ XLSX" button in the IOC Portfolio tab exports the full country-level table including take tier, Stability Score, and NPV — suitable for attaching to an IC memo as the fiscal exposure annex.
Limitation: IOC_DATA reflects publicly reported operator positions. The platform's IOC data is derived from annual reports, operator disclosures, and industry databases. It reflects approximate country-level positions, not individual block take or equity working interest percentage. A country shown in ExxonMobil's portfolio may reflect a minority position in one block (e.g. 2% WI in a 185-country database) or a dominant operatorship (25% WI in Stabroek Block). Use the Country Profile and Side-by-Side for field-level due diligence on specific positions.

Rule of thumb: Use the IOC Portfolio tab as a pre-screening tool for competitive intelligence: "TotalEnergies operates in 18 countries with avg take 61% at $75/bbl, 2pp above peer average, with 28% of positions in the State-heavy tier — concentrated in Africa and Middle East. Our target new entry in Guyana (52% take, IOC-friendly) would reduce TotalEnergies' portfolio average take by ~1pp if weighted equally to existing positions." This framing turns a fiscal database exercise into a portfolio-strategy narrative for IC presentations.
A72. Two countries show the same mechanic and nearly identical government take at $75/bbl — which additional fiscal signals should I prioritize when screening for a capital allocation decision?
Government take at a single reference price is a useful entry-level filter, but it is an insufficient basis for distinguishing between two fiscally similar regimes. When take is within 3pp (the standard Wood Mackenzie/Rystad benchmark tolerance), the decision shifts to four secondary signals available directly in this platform:

1. Price Swing (fiscal leverage). The Fiscal Compare table shows Price Swing — the difference in government take between $50/bbl and $125/bbl. Two countries with identical take at $75/bbl can have Swing values differing by 15–20pp. A PSC with a cost recovery cap will show high Swing (take rises sharply as profit oil increases at higher prices); a flat-royalty concession will show low Swing (take barely changes with price). IC rule of thumb: Swing <10pp = low fiscal leverage (predictable in stress), Swing >20pp = high fiscal leverage (tax burden accelerates in a $100+ environment). Prefer low-Swing regimes when oil price outlook is uncertain.

2. IRR at $75/bbl. The Screener tab and Fiscal Compare table both show IRR. Two regimes with identical 55% take can show IRR differences of 3–5pp due to timing differences in cash flow — PSCs delay cost recovery behind profit oil splits; concessions collect royalties from Day 1. A higher IRR at the same take level indicates faster capital return, which is directly relevant to investment payback thresholds. Note: IRR is available for 74 of 185 countries — if your target country lacks an IRR figure, use Breakeven as a proxy (lower Breakeven = faster initial return).

3. Breakeven price. The Breakeven Map and Country Profile both show the price at which a standardized project achieves zero NPV. Two countries with identical take at $75/bbl can have Breakevens differing by $15–20/bbl depending on fiscal front-loading (royalties on gross revenue reduce NPV faster than CIT on net profit). IC rule of thumb: Breakeven <$55/bbl = resilient to energy transition downside; Breakeven >$75/bbl = exposed in a prolonged low-price environment. When two regimes show identical take, prefer the lower-Breakeven country for long-horizon capital (15+ year projects).

4. Stability Score + Reform Risk. Even identical fiscal economics are not equivalent if one regime has a history of unilateral renegotiation. Check the Reform Risk tab and Country Profile Stability Score (0–5 scale) for both countries. A Stability Score of 4–5 (≤1 reform event in 15 years) commands a fiscal premium that is not reflected in the take figure — and should be disclosed in any IC memo comparing stable vs. reform-volatile regimes at similar take levels. IC rule of thumb: a 2+ point Stability Score gap justifies a 2–4pp IRR premium to the lower-stability regime even at identical take.

Recommended 4-step tiebreaker workflow:
  1. Fiscal Compare: confirm both countries are within 3pp take at your target price. If outside 3pp, take is the differentiator — stop here.
  2. Check Price Swing: sort by Swing column in Fiscal Compare results. The lower-Swing regime has more predictable fiscal exposure. For a $75/bbl base case with meaningful downside risk to $50/bbl, prefer the lower-Swing option.
  3. Check Breakeven and IRR: open both Country Profiles. Compare Breakeven (resilience signal) and IRR if available. A 3pp IRR advantage or $10/bbl Breakeven advantage is material for most IC thresholds.
  4. Check Stability Score: if Stability Scores differ by ≥2 points, include a reform risk note in your IC memo and apply a qualitative IRR haircut to the lower-stability regime.
Rule of thumb: When take is within 3pp, the ranking should be: (1) lower Swing → more predictable; (2) lower Breakeven → more resilient; (3) higher IRR → faster payback; (4) higher Stability Score → lower reform risk. A regime that ranks better on all four secondary signals is structurally superior even at identical headline take — and that argument should be made explicitly in the IC memo rather than relying on take alone.
A73. A country has a contractual stabilization clause but also scores 2 out of 5 on Reform Risk. How do I reconcile these conflicting signals in an IC memo?
A contractual stabilization clause and a low Reform Risk (Stability) score are measuring different things — they are not in conflict, but they operate at different layers of fiscal risk. Understanding the distinction is essential for accurate IC memo disclosure.

What a stabilization clause protects: A stabilization clause is a contract-level protection — it binds the host government to the fiscal terms in a specific PSC, concession, or TSC for the life of that contract. It does not bind the government for new contracts, does not prevent off-contract levies (WHT, export duties, emergency fees), and is only as enforceable as the country's arbitration framework (ICSID, UNCITRAL, ICC). Three structural types exist: (1) full freezing clause — entire tax regime frozen at contract date; (2) equilibrium/economic stabilization — government must compensate for any fiscal change that reduces the contractor's economic position; (3) intangibility clause — weakest form, acknowledges fiscal certainty without providing enforcement. See also FAQ A40 for detailed mechanics by country.

What Reform Risk (Stability Score) measures: The platform's Reform Risk tab and Stability Score (0–5 scale) measure historical reform frequency — how many times the country's statutory fiscal regime has changed in the past 15 years. A score of 2/5 (≥4 reform events in 15 years) signals a government with a demonstrated willingness to amend laws unilaterally. This is a legislative risk signal, not a contract-specific protection assessment.

Why both can be true simultaneously: A country can have both a contractual stabilization clause (protecting your specific block) and a high reform frequency (exposing all future contracts, off-contract levies, and the enforceability environment itself). High reform frequency countries (Stability Score 2/5) often enact reforms precisely by challenging existing stabilization clauses — Angola 2020 FTP reform, Kazakhstan 2004 resource rent revisions, Nigeria PIA 2021 transition provisions all renegotiated or bypassed stabilization protections for existing PSC holders. The stabilization clause is a legal assertion; its enforceability depends on the same institutional environment the Reform Risk score is flagging as unstable.

Recommended IC memo reconciliation — 4-step framework:
  1. Identify the clause type. A full freezing clause (Angola pre-2004, Kazakhstan PSA 1994) is materially stronger than an equilibrium clause or intangibility clause. Check the Country Profile source notes — where the platform has A/B tier sourcing for the relevant block, the clause type is often indicated in operator filings or the production-sharing agreement itself. Disclose: "Block X is subject to a [type] stabilization clause under [legislation/article]."
  2. Check the arbitration record. A low Stability Score (2/5) in a country with a strong ICSID arbitration enforcement record (Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, Angola post-2023) is less alarming than the same score in a country with a history of ignoring ICSID awards (Bolivia 2012, Ecuador 2022 Andes Petroleum renegotiation). If you have access to ICSID/ICC award databases, note in the IC memo whether the country has satisfied or challenged prior arbitral awards.
  3. Stress-test off-contract levies. Run Scenario Builder at $50, $75, and $100/bbl for the block profile. Note the effective take at each price. Off-contract levies — export duties, excess profit charges, environmental fees — are typically not covered by PSC-level stabilization. Use the Price Swing column in Fiscal Compare to identify price-sensitive upside exposure that may attract off-contract windfall measures even if the core PSC terms are stabilized.
  4. Disclose both signals explicitly in the IC memo. Do not net them against each other. The correct framing: "Block X has a [clause type] stabilization clause that covers the core royalty/profit oil/CIT structure (estimated effective take: [X]% at $75/bbl; ORCA v274). However, the country's Reform Risk Stability Score is 2/5, indicating 4+ fiscal law amendments in the past 15 years. Off-contract levies and export duties are not stabilized. The blended risk position reflects contractual protection for identified fiscal parameters alongside structural reform risk for the broader fiscal environment. Recommend legal counsel review of arbitration enforceability prior to FID."
Rule of thumb: A stabilization clause reduces but does not eliminate reform risk. A Stability Score of 2/5 with a strong freezing clause = moderate risk (comparable to a Stability Score of 3/5 without stabilization). A Stability Score of 2/5 with only an intangibility clause = high risk — treat fiscal terms as subject to change over a 10–15 year project life and apply a 2–3pp IRR haircut in the base case.
A74. A country shows a single take figure but I know it operates different fiscal terms for onshore vs. offshore acreage. How does the platform handle dual-zone regimes, and how should I adjust for zone-specific analysis?
Dual-zone regimes — where a government applies materially different royalty rates, tax rates, or cost recovery terms by acreage type (onshore vs. offshore, shallow vs. deepwater, conventional vs. unconventional) — are common among mid-tier and OECD producers. The platform handles them in two ways depending on data availability.

How ORCA handles dual-zone regimes:
Single majority mechanic (most countries): Where one zone dominates production (e.g., Angola offshore dominates, Libya onshore dominates), the platform's take figure reflects the dominant-zone fiscal terms. The Country Profile Evidence badge will show source citations referencing the dominant contract type (e.g., "deepwater PSC"). The minority zone is not separately modeled unless it has materially different fiscal terms that would shift the result by more than 3pp at $75/bbl.

Zone-weighted average (selected countries): For a handful of countries where both zones are IOC-material (Mexico, Libya, Kazakhstan, Canada, Italy), the platform uses a production-weighted average of onshore and offshore effective take. This is disclosed in the Country Profile source notes for those countries.

Country examples where zone distinction matters for IOC decisions:
  • Norway: All terms apply uniformly onshore/offshore (no Norwegian onshore production). Platform figure is purely Norwegian Continental Shelf. No zone adjustment needed.
  • Brazil: Pre-salt PSC (55–65% take, Petrobras 30% mandatory WI) vs. post-salt concession (30–40% take, competitive bidding). Platform figure approximates the pre-salt PSC tier which dominates new IOC investment. If evaluating sub-salt concession legacy blocks, apply a 15–20pp downward take adjustment from the platform figure.
  • Mexico: Shallow water and onshore farmout contracts (35–45% government take) vs. deepwater production sharing contracts (55–65% take). Platform reflects a blended average; for specific license type, use Scenario Builder with the correct mechanic selection (Concession for onshore/shallow, PSC for deepwater).
  • India: NELP-era PSC (55–70% take) applies to most IOC-accessible blocks; OALP exploration contracts (40–55% take) apply to new bid rounds from 2017. Platform reflects NELP basis; OALP screening requires 10–15pp downward adjustment.
Recommended IC memo workflow — 4-step zone adjustment:
  1. Identify the acreage type. Is the target block offshore deepwater, shallow, or onshore? Check the Country Profile source note — it specifies which acreage type the platform's take figure represents. If your target block is the minority type, flag the discrepancy.
  2. Check royalty structure by zone. Many countries have lower royalty offshore (exploration incentive) and higher onshore (established production). A 5% offshore vs. 12.5% onshore differential translates to roughly 4–10pp effective take difference depending on price. If the Country Profile shows royalty data, you can compute the adjustment directly.
  3. Use Scenario Builder for the target zone. For the countries above where the platform figure is zone-weighted, use Scenario Builder with the correct mechanic (Concession vs. PSC) and adjust the royalty input to the zone-specific rate. This produces a zone-adjusted IRR directly comparable to peer countries without the dual-zone distortion.
  4. Disclose zone basis in the IC memo. The correct framing: "Platform take of [X]% represents [onshore/offshore/blended] fiscal terms for [Country] (ORCA v274, standardized profile). Target block [Block Name] is [zone type] — zone-adjusted effective take estimated at [Y]% using zone-specific royalty of [Z]% (source: [regulator publication]) with other parameters held constant."
Rule of thumb: For countries with a single dominant acreage type (Norway, Angola, Nigeria, UAE, Guyana — all offshore-dominated), the platform figure is directly applicable. For countries with material dual-zone production (Brazil, Mexico, Libya, Kazakhstan, Indonesia), verify the target block zone before using the headline take in an IC submission. A 5pp royalty difference between zones = 4–8pp effective take difference at $75/bbl in a concession regime; 2–5pp in a PSC regime (cost recovery buffering reduces royalty sensitivity).
A75. A country on my shortlist shows "—" for IRR. How should I screen and rank it when IRR data is unavailable, and what can I use as a substitute for IC work?
IRR is available for 124 of 185 countries (67% coverage; values ≥500% excluded as unbounded returns — e.g. very-low-royalty regimes at high oil price where payback is near-instant). The remaining 61 countries are either excluded as unbounded (41 countries with IRR ≥500%) or lack sufficient cost-structure data (20 countries) (verified opex and capital cost benchmarks) to close the DCF at a defensible precision. A "—" in the IRR column is not a data error — it is an explicit flag that the platform does not have confident cost data to support a DCF result. This matters for IC work: a fabricated IRR number is worse than an acknowledged gap.

Why IRR is missing for a country:
  • No verified opex/capex benchmark: The DCF requires country-specific lifting cost ($/bbl) and capital intensity ($/bbl/d). For frontier and undeveloped basins (e.g., Somalia, Eritrea, Togo), no operator has disclosed project economics in sufficient detail to anchor these inputs.
  • Pre-FID acreage with no production history: Countries with purely exploratory acreage and no producing fields cannot support a credible reference project cost assumption — the cost uncertainty exceeds the fiscal signal.
  • Directional take only: Countries marked "PASS directional" in the benchmark validation have take figures sourced from published regime terms, but costs are directional estimates. These countries have Govt Take and NPV but not IRR.
Screening workflow when IRR is unavailable — 3-step approach:
  1. Use Govt Take as the primary screen. Govt Take (185/185 coverage) is the most reliable signal for regime comparison. Sort Fiscal Compare by Govt Take. Countries with IRR unavailable can still be ranked relative to their peers on fiscal burden — a 45% take regime with no IRR is demonstrably lower-burden than a 70% take regime with IRR, regardless of costs.
  2. Apply the regional peer IRR proxy (FAQ A12). Identify 2–3 regional peer countries with available IRR and similar fiscal mechanics. The proxy IRR for your target country = peer IRR ± adjustment for the take differential. Rule of thumb: 1pp take difference ≈ 0.3–0.5pp IRR difference at $75/bbl in a concession regime; 0.2–0.3pp in a PSC regime. Disclose the proxy basis in your IC appendix.
  3. Use the Scenario Builder with analyst-supplied costs. If your team has a cost estimate for the target basin (from seismic vendor reports, peer company disclosures, or Wood Mac/Rystad frontier cost databases), enter those assumptions directly in the Scenario Builder. This produces a project-specific IRR you can cite — disclose your cost assumptions and the source. This approach is more defensible for IC than a proxy, provided the cost inputs are sourced.
IC memo language for IRR-unavailable countries:
"IRR for [Country] is not available in the ORCA platform (v250) due to insufficient verified cost benchmarks for this acreage. Govt Take of [X]% at $75/bbl places [Country] in the [low/mid/high] quartile of the [mechanic] universe. Regional peer proxy IRR estimated at [Y]% based on [Peer A] ([Z]% IRR, [W]pp lower take) and [Peer B] ([Z2]% IRR, [W2]pp higher take). Scenario Builder IRR modeled at $[capex]M capex / [peak rate] bbl/d / $[opex]/bbl opex = [SB IRR]% (inputs sourced from [your source])."

Rule of thumb: A country with Govt Take <45% and no IRR can typically be assumed competitive with regional peers on returns — the fiscal burden is low enough that reasonable cost variations rarely flip the ranking. For high-take frontier countries (take >60%, IRR unavailable), the cost uncertainty matters more: a $5/bbl opex swing can change IRR by 2–4pp. In that case, run Scenario Builder sensitivity explicitly at ±$5/bbl opex before including the country in an IC shortlist.
A76. My target country had a major fiscal reform in the past 1–2 years. How current are the platform’s fiscal parameters, and how should I account for reform risk in my IC analysis?

Platform currency: ORCA fiscal parameters reflect terms as of August 2026, cross-referenced from primary legislation, government gazette amendments, and NOC publications. For countries with active reform histories (Stability Score ≤3), parameters may lag gazette publication by 3–9 months for complex multi-law amendments. The Evidence badge (A/B/C) on the Country Profile tab indicates source tier and approximate data age.

Four-step IC workflow for recently-reformed countries:

  1. Check the Reform History tab. Filter by country and sort by most-recent event. Look for events dated 2024–2026 tagged as “Royalty rate change,” “Fiscal law amendment,” or “New petroleum code.” If 2+ events appear in the past 24 months, the fiscal structure may have changed since ORCA’s last verified update.
  2. Cross-check with the Evidence badge. Country Profile tab → evidence header. If Evidence A is <50% for the core fiscal parameters (royalty, profit-oil split, CIT), the platform is relying on third-party estimates rather than primary law texts. In reform environments, this gap widens. Treat the platform figure as directional and note the limitation in your IC memo.
  3. Run a Scenario Builder sensitivity. If the reform introduced a new royalty tier or profit-oil split, model the pre-reform and post-reform parameters in Scenario Builder side-by-side. A typical reform magnitude for developing producers is ±5–15pp take. Map this to IRR impact: each 10pp take increase reduces IRR by approximately 1.5–3pp at the standardized Deepwater profile.
  4. Disclose reform uncertainty in the IC memo. If the reform is dated within 18 months of the IC meeting and primary law text has not been independently obtained, the following disclosure is required: “Government take of [X]% at $75/bbl reflects ORCA platform parameters (v250, Aug 2026). [Country] enacted [reform name] in [month/year] (per ORCA Reform History tab); amended fiscal parameters have not been independently verified from primary gazette text as of IC date. Directional take adjustment of [Y]pp applied per Scenario Builder sensitivity — see Appendix [D] for pre/post-reform IRR comparison.”

Countries with notable 2024–2026 reform activity (per ORCA Reform History): UK (EPL modifications Aug 2024 + windfall tax step-down trajectory); Mozambique (LNG tax holiday extensions for Coral Sul FLNG); Ghana (fiscal amendment Petroleum Revenue Management Act 2024); Indonesia (Gross Split regulation update 2025); Ecuador (hydrocarbon law reform 2025). These countries warrant an explicit pre/post-reform sensitivity in any IC submission dated 2025–2026.

Rule of thumb: Stability Score ≤2 + Reform History event within 18 months = treat ORCA take as directional (±8pp uncertainty band). Stability Score 3 + event 12–24 months ago = verify one primary source before citing. Stability Score ≥4 = platform parameters are likely current (stable legislative environment, infrequent amendments).

A77. How do local content requirements affect the effective contractor economics, and does the platform’s government take figure include mandatory local spend obligations?

Platform scope: ORCA’s government take figure reflects statutory and contractual fiscal flows — royalties, profit oil, income tax, resource rent taxes, and state equity dividends. Local content requirements (LCR) are not included in the take figure because they are contractual cost obligations imposed on the contractor, not fiscal transfers to the government treasury. They reduce effective contractor IRR without appearing in the fiscal regime’s take arithmetic.

Three LCR cost channels to quantify for IC purposes:

  1. Local goods and services premium. Mandatory local procurement (typically 30–70% of goods value in Nigeria, Angola, Brazil, Indonesia Gross Split TKDN) increases effective operating cost by 8–15% above international market rates. For a $15/bbl opex structure with 40% mandatory local services, the effective cost premium is ~0.8–1.5pp IRR at standardized Deepwater reference project scale.
  2. Local workforce and training levies. Many PSC/concession frameworks mandate training levies ($500K–$2M/year per block) and local hiring quotas (40–80% of non-specialist positions). Rule of thumb: for a 10-year field development, training levies represent 0.3–0.8pp IRR impact — material for small fields, immaterial for large-scale LNG.
  3. Community development and technology transfer funds. Some post-2015 PSC frameworks (Nigeria, Mozambique LNG amendments) require community development fund (CDF) contributions of 0.5–2% of gross revenue — effectively an off-balance-sheet royalty equivalent. Add these to royalty when computing total government share for IC purposes.

Four-step IC adjustment workflow:

  1. Identify LCR tier. High-LCR jurisdictions (Nigeria, Angola, Brazil, Indonesia): 10–20% effective opex premium. Medium-LCR (Ghana, Mozambique, Kenya, Tanzania): 5–10%. Low-LCR (Ireland, Norway, Canada, USA GoM): de minimis (<1%).
  2. Apply opex uplift in Scenario Builder. Increase the opex input by the estimated LCR premium. For Nigeria deepwater ($18/bbl standard opex), a 12% premium adds ~$2.2/bbl — run at $20/bbl for an LCR-adjusted IRR comparison against low-LCR jurisdictions.
  3. Add CDF as royalty equivalent. If the jurisdiction requires a CDF contribution of X% of gross revenue, add X% to the royalty input in Scenario Builder. A 1% CDF requirement reduces contractor IRR by ~0.3pp at Deepwater reference scale.
  4. Disclose in the IC memo. Standard language: “Platform government take of [X]% reflects statutory fiscal flows only. LCR-adjusted effective contractor cost: opex increased [Y]% to reflect mandatory local services premium (per [Country] [Act/Decree]). LCR-adjusted IRR: [Z]% vs. unadjusted [Z+Δ]% — see Appendix E for LCR sensitivity range.”

Rule of thumb: For mature-LCR jurisdictions (Nigeria, Angola, Brazil, Indonesia), add 5–12% to opex before cross-country IRR ranking. For frontier jurisdictions with aspirational LCR targets (Ethiopia, Uganda, Tanzania), model 2–5% opex premium as a sensitivity rather than base case. For OECD producers (Norway, Canada, USA GoM, UK), LCR cost impact is de minimis.

A78. How do carbon pricing schemes and CCUS obligations affect upstream petroleum economics, and how should an IC analyst adjust government take comparisons for carbon cost exposure?

Platform scope: ORCA’s government take figure reflects statutory and contractual fiscal flows only — royalties, profit oil/gas, income taxes, and resource rent taxes. Carbon pricing obligations are not included in the take figure because they are cost obligations that accrue to regulatory compliance accounts, not fiscal transfers that appear in the petroleum fiscal contract. They reduce effective contractor IRR without changing the fiscal contract’s take arithmetic.

Three carbon cost exposure categories for upstream IC analysis:

  1. Explicit carbon price (ETS or carbon tax). Jurisdictions with legislated carbon pricing applied to upstream operations: Norway (~$84/tCO² carbon tax + EU ETS ~€60/tCO² = effective $150+/tCO²); UK (UK ETS ~£40/tCO²); Canada (CAD 80/tCO² federal backstop); Australia (Safeguard Mechanism baselines). For a deepwater field emitting 25 kg CO²/bbl, Norway carbon cost adds ~$3.75/bbl to opex. Rule of thumb: at $80/tCO², each 10 kg CO²/bbl of upstream emissions intensity reduces IRR by ~0.3–0.5pp at reference project scale.
  2. Flaring penalties and methane levies. Regulatory flaring prohibitions with economic penalties: Nigeria NUPRC flaring penalties ($3.50/Mcf 2024 rate, rising annually); US GoM methane waste rule ($15/Mcf above threshold). Flaring-intensive onshore operations (West Africa, Russia directional) face a persistent $0.50–$2.00/bbl operational cost invisible in the statutory take figure. For IC field benchmarking: always note whether the target asset is flaring-limited or associated gas-stranded.
  3. CCUS contractual obligations. Post-2020 PSC/concession amendments in some jurisdictions mandate carbon capture and storage as a license condition: Norway Longship CCS (Equinor Northern Lights project, $50–$70/tCO² storage cost benchmark); UAE CCUS requirement for large offshore developments (ADNOC Al-Reyadah, $30–$40/tCO²); emerging CCUS language in post-2022 Ghana/Kenya blocks. These are capex items that do not appear in government take but substantially reduce NPV of high-emission assets.

Four-step carbon-adjusted IC workflow:

  1. Identify jurisdiction carbon tier. Flag carbon pricing tier: Tier A (explicit ETS/carbon tax >$50/tCO²: Norway, UK, Canada); Tier B (methane/flaring penalties: USA GoM, Nigeria, Algeria); Tier C (nascent/aspirational: most Sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia); Tier D (no carbon pricing: Gulf states, most MENA).
  2. Estimate upstream emissions intensity. Offshore deepwater: 15–30 kg CO²/bbl (low venting/flaring). Onshore conventional: 25–60 kg CO²/bbl. Gas-dominant fields: add methane leakage conversion. Adjust for field-specific flaring rate if operator data is available.
  3. Apply carbon opex uplift in Scenario Builder. Convert annual carbon cost to $/bbl and add to opex input. Example: Norway deepwater ($149/tCO² combined) x 25 kg CO²/bbl = $3.73/bbl carbon adder → increase opex from $15/bbl to $18.75/bbl for carbon-adjusted IRR. Compare against Gulf state (Tier D, $0 carbon adder) on same base IRR for transition-scenario portfolio ranking.
  4. Disclose in IC memo. Standard language: “Platform government take of [X]% reflects statutory fiscal flows. Carbon exposure: Tier [A/B/C/D]. Carbon-adjusted opex: [Y] $/bbl (including [Z] $/bbl carbon cost at [$W/tCO²] and [E] kg CO²/bbl upstream intensity). Carbon-adjusted IRR: [Z]% vs. statutory [Z+Δ]% — see Appendix F for $50/$100/$150/tCO² sensitivity.”

Rule of thumb: Norway and UK are Tier A (high carbon cost, material IRR impact: $2–$5/bbl adder for deepwater). USA GoM and Nigeria are Tier B (moderate: $0.50–$2/bbl for flaring-intensive operations). Gulf states (UAE, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait) are Tier D — zero explicit carbon cost today, but Scope 1 reporting requirements are tightening through ADNOC and Saudi Aramco ESG frameworks. Use Fiscal Compare Custom tab to rank same-price-scenario IRRs, then manually apply carbon tier adder for a full energy-transition-aware portfolio screen.

A79. A country on my shortlist requires mandatory state equity participation (e.g., the NOC holds a 15–25% carried or paid interest in all upstream licenses). Does ORCA's government take figure include the value of the NOC's equity stake — and how do I correctly model contractor economics at a specific working interest?

How ORCA handles NOC equity: ORCA’s government take figure is inclusive of the NOC equity return — it represents the government’s total fiscal and equity share of project economics at the standardized reference project. Specifically: (1) Royalties and profit oil/tax flows are modeled per statute; (2) The NOC’s carried or paid equity share generates a dividend stream that is treated as part of government revenue in the take calculation. The contractor’s share is therefore the residual after all statutory fiscal flows AND the NOC’s equity dividend are removed.

Why this matters for IC analysis: If ORCA shows a country at 62% take and the NOC holds 20% equity, the contractor’s 80% working interest receives approximately 38% of gross project value — but this 38% is already net of the NOC’s equity dividend. A common error is to double-count the NOC equity: treating it as a separate deduction from the contractor’s share when ORCA’s take already reflects it.

4-step IC adjustment workflow for partial working interest:

  1. Read ORCA’s take at face value. The Govt Take @$75 figure (e.g., 62%) represents the government’s combined fiscal + equity share. Contractor’s share = 1 − 0.62 = 38% of standardized project value.
  2. Scale to your working interest. If your company holds 40% of the contractor’s share (e.g., in a joint venture where a third-party IOC holds the remaining 60%), your net economics = 0.40 × 38% = 15.2% of gross project value. Use Scenario Builder Contractor NPV × 0.40 to get your equity-share NPV.
  3. Distinguish carried vs. paid NOC equity. Carried NOC interest (exploration costs borne by IOC; NOC back-in at FID or first production) creates a front-loaded IOC cost burden not captured in ORCA’s statutory take. Add exploration cost recovery uplift: typically 1.2–1.5× exploration capex for the carried portion as an effective IRR reduction. Paid NOC equity (NOC funds its pro-rata share from first license) creates no IOC distortion — ORCA’s take is accurate as-is.
  4. IC memo disclosure language: “Fiscal terms: ORCA government take [X]% @$75/bbl (Deepwater/Concession), inclusive of [NOC name] [Y]% equity participation. Contractor (100% WI basis): NPV $[Z]M, IRR [W]%. Company net at [Q]% WI: NPV $[Z×Q]M. NOC carry adjustment: [carried/paid — see footnote]. Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026).”

Rule of thumb by NOC equity tier: 0% NOC equity (e.g., USA GoM) — ORCA take = pure fiscal take, contractor = 1 − take. 10–15% carried NOC (e.g., Senegal, Namibia) — add 0.3–0.6pp IRR reduction for carry cost. 20–25% paid NOC (e.g., Angola SONANGOL, Nigeria NNPC) — ORCA take already fully captures NOC dividend; no additional adjustment needed. 30%+ paid NOC (e.g., Malaysia PETRONAS, Kazakhstan KMG) — verify whether the NOC’s full equity participation is in the statutory take figure (source: Evidence badge A/B confidence level).

Platform note: Countries where NOC carry creates a material exploration-cost uplift are flagged in source notes (Evidence tier B countries with NOC-carry disclosure). Use the Country Profile → “Key Fiscal Parameters” section to check the state_participation field and carry terms.

A80. I need to compare the fiscal burden of two PSC countries where one uses a cost recovery cap of 60% and the other uses 80%. How material is this difference for contractor economics, and how do I model it in the Scenario Builder?

Cost recovery cap mechanics: The cost recovery cap defines the maximum share of gross production revenue the contractor can ring-fence each period to recover capex and opex. A 60% cap means that even if costs in a given year exceed 60% of gross revenue, the contractor can only recover 60% — the excess is “cost carried forward” to future periods. An 80% cap allows faster capex recovery, which materially improves early-phase IRR through the time value of money effect.

How material is the 60% vs. 80% gap? At ORCA’s standardized reference project ($1.2B capex / 50k bbl/d / $15/bbl opex at $75/bbl), the 80% cap adds approximately 1.5–3.0pp contractor IRR vs. a 60% cap, depending on the profit oil split and price environment. The gap widens significantly in low-price environments ($50/bbl): at $50/bbl, faster cost recovery under an 80% cap provides a ~3–5pp IRR advantage vs. 60% cap because the contractor recovers costs before profit oil sharing erodes returns. In high-price environments ($100/bbl), the gap narrows to ~0.5–1.5pp because cost recovery completes quickly under both cap levels.

4-step Scenario Builder modelling workflow:

  1. Check the cost_recovery_cap field in Country Profile. Navigate to Country Profile → “Fiscal Parameters” for each country. Compare cost_recovery_cap values directly. If both countries show the same profit oil split but different caps, the cap difference is the primary IRR driver.
  2. Run Scenario Builder at $50/bbl for both countries. Select each country’s PSC preset (or configure manually). Run at $50/bbl, 20-year project life. Record IRR and Contractor NPV. The spread at $50/bbl reveals the cap’s full protective value: a 60% cap country will show meaningfully lower IRR at low prices because cost recovery spills into years 5–8 rather than completing in years 2–4.
  3. Assess opex-to-capex ratio sensitivity. The cap matters most for capex-heavy, early-production-rate projects. For an onshore low-cost project ($300M capex / 20k bbl/d), a 60% cap may not bind — costs recover quickly at any cap level. For a deepwater project ($1.2B+ capex / 50k bbl/d), the cap is binding for years 1–4 and the 80% vs. 60% spread is maximized. Use the Scenario Builder capex slider to test your specific project geometry.
  4. IC memo disclosure language: “Country A (60% CR cap): Contractor IRR [X]% @$75/bbl, [Y]% @$50/bbl. Country B (80% CR cap): Contractor IRR [W]% @$75/bbl, [Z]% @$50/bbl. Differential attributable primarily to cost recovery cap: [X−W]pp @$75, [Y−Z]pp @$50. Source: ORCA v274 Scenario Builder (Aug 2026), $1.2B capex / 50k bbl/d / $15/bbl opex basis.”

Rule of thumb by cost recovery cap tier:

  • 50% cap (Nigeria legacy JDAs, Malaysia vintage blocks): Highest carry-forward risk; most punitive in low-price cycles. ~2–4pp IRR penalty vs. 80% cap.
  • 60% cap (Angola, DRC, standard West Africa PSC): Moderate carry-forward. ~1.5–3pp IRR discount vs. 80% cap at $75/bbl.
  • 80% cap (Guyana Stabroek, Namibia frontier blocks, modern incentive PSCs): Near-full early recovery; IRR closest to pure NPV-maximizing structure.
  • 100% / No cap (Indonesia Gross Split — no cost recovery layer; USA GoM — royalty/tax only): Cost recovery concept absent; contractor bears full cost risk, receives full revenue net of royalty.
A81. My target country levies a signature bonus at the time of contract award. Does ORCA's government take figure include the signature bonus — and how should I adjust my IRR model to account for upfront government payments?

Short answer: No — ORCA's government take does not include signature bonuses. ORCA's take metric reflects recurring fiscal obligations (royalty, profit oil/tax share, state equity returns) applied to the standardized reference production profile. Signature bonuses, training fees, social development contributions, and community benefit obligations are upfront lump-sum payments that ORCA does not model because they depend on the specific bid round, block attractiveness, and competitive tension — not on the fiscal code architecture. Their magnitude can range from negligible (<$5M for a frontier block with no prior drilling) to commercially significant ($500M–$2B+ in highly competitive deepwater bid rounds in Brazil, Nigeria, and UAE/ADNOC).

Types of upfront government payments:

  • Signature bonus: Paid at contract execution. Fully expensed or amortized depending on jurisdiction; in most PSC regimes, signature bonuses are not cost-recoverable (Nigeria, Angola, Indonesia, Malaysia — check country-specific terms). Non-recoverable bonuses directly reduce contractor NPV and IRR.
  • Training fees / capacity building: Annual levy (commonly $100K–$2M/yr) for host government human capacity development. Small individual amount; material over a 20-year license life ($2–40M). Typically not cost-recoverable.
  • Social contribution / community benefit obligation: Infrastructure or social development funds mandated at contract execution or first oil. Angola's Local Development Fund, Nigeria's NEDP levy, Uganda's SDP. Treated as a recoverable capital cost in some regimes; non-recoverable in others.
  • Relinquishment fees and area rental: Annual per-km² fee on acreage held. Lower in magnitude (<$1M/yr for standard blocks) but impacts pre-production cash flow.

4-step IC adjustment workflow:

  1. Check the country's bid round history for disclosed bonus payments. National oil company announcements, bid round results, and annual reports from active operators (e.g., TotalEnergies, Shell, Equinor) disclose signature bonuses for reference blocks. Use the ORCA Country Profile Evidence badge — Tier A/B sources often include bid round transaction data from Wood Mac or Rystad that discloses disclosed bonus ranges.
  2. Model the bonus as a Year-0 cost in the Scenario Builder. Navigate to Scenario Builder → Advanced. Add the estimated bonus as an additional Year-0 capex item (or use the "additional Year-0 cost" input if available). This reduces contractor NPV by the bonus amount and reduces IRR by approximately 0.5–2.5pp depending on project size. For ORCA's standard $1.2B capex reference project: a $100M bonus reduces contractor IRR by ~0.8pp; a $500M bonus reduces IRR by ~3.2pp.
  3. Assess cost recoverability. In PSC regimes where signature bonuses are cost-recoverable (uncommon but present in some jurisdictions — check the contract), the IRR impact is partially offset by future cost oil recovery. The non-recoverable portion is the effective economic cost. Rule of thumb: assume non-recoverable unless the specific contract text confirms otherwise.
  4. IC memo disclosure language: "ORCA government take of [X]% at $75/bbl (v250, standardized Deepwater profile) excludes the signature bonus paid at contract execution. Estimated bonus for [Country] bid round based on [source]: $[Y]M (non-recoverable under [PSC/concession] terms). Bonus-adjusted contractor IRR: [W]% (vs. pre-bonus [Z]%). Bonus as % of total project capex: [Y/1,200]%. See Appendix [G] for bonus sensitivity: $50M / $100M / $250M / $500M bonus scenarios."

Rule of thumb by country tier:

  • Mature/competitive basins (Nigeria deepwater, Brazil pre-salt, UAE/ADNOC): Bonuses $200M–$2B+. Material — always model explicitly. IRR impact 2–8pp.
  • Mid-tier producers (Angola, Ghana, Tanzania LNG, Mozambique): Bonuses $20M–$200M for frontier/nearshore blocks. Moderate impact 0.5–2pp IRR.
  • Frontier/pre-FID (most ORCA-benchmarked frontier countries): Bonuses typically <$10M and competitive tension-driven. Negligible IRR impact; model conservatively at $5M.
  • Concession regimes (most OECD jurisdictions — Norway, UK, Canada): No competitive signature bonus; work programme commitments substitute. Bonus adjustment not applicable.
A82. My target country has both active concession (royalty-tax) contracts and PSC contracts operating simultaneously. ORCA shows one take figure — which regime does it represent, and how do I handle the dual-regime environment in an IC memo?

Short answer: ORCA reports the dominant mechanic by contract count. Countries like Malaysia, Egypt, India, Brunei, and Indonesia have both concession and PSC contracts active simultaneously — often reflecting a historical transition from one regime to another, or differentiated terms by block vintage, water depth, or field size. ORCA's country-level take figure reflects the fiscal mechanic that covers the majority of in-country contracts in the database. The Regime Explorer tab shows the full contract-type distribution for every country.

Why dual-regime countries exist:

  • Historical transition: Many countries shifted from concession to PSC in the 1970s–1980s (Egypt, Algeria, India, Indonesia) but legacy concession contracts remain active until expiry. The "old" and "new" regimes coexist.
  • Depth/vintage differentiation: Malaysia and Brunei apply PSCs to deepwater and frontier blocks while maintaining concession terms (Production Sharing Contracts and Service Agreements) for mature shallow-water fields. Egypt applies two distinct regimes: EGPC standard PSC for oil blocks vs. EGAS framework for gas developments (different cost recovery caps and profit-split tiers).
  • Field-size bifurcation: India's NELP (New Exploration Licensing Policy) PSC and the older Nomination regime (ONGC/OIL royalty-tax blocks) coexist; new acreage since OALP/HELP uses a revenue-sharing variant, creating three simultaneous mechanics.
  • Sub-national jurisdiction overlap: The USA has federal GoM PSC-equivalent terms, state onshore royalty-tax regimes, and tribal land fiscal structures all simultaneously active — ORCA reports the federal GoM as the representative.

4-step IC workflow for dual-regime countries:

  1. Check the Regime Explorer for contract-type distribution. Navigate to Regime Explorer → filter by Country. The mechanic breakdown (e.g., "Malaysia: 67% PSC / 33% Concession by contract count") tells you which ORCA take figure is dominant and which regime your specific target block likely falls under. Check the Country Profile Evidence badge for regime notes.
  2. Identify your target block's regime from the contract note. The Fiscal Compare and Country Profile tabs show the take figure and mechanic for the selected country. If the dominant regime does not match your target block, use the Fiscal Compare "Custom" view to run a Scenario Builder comparison: set the mechanic to match your block's actual regime (Concession or PSC), adjust the cost recovery cap and profit-split from country-specific contract terms, and compute a project-specific take.
  3. Use the Fiscal Compare side-by-side to benchmark both regimes. If your IC decision involves comparing two contracts in the same country (one concession, one PSC), run both as separate Fiscal Compare entries with the correct mechanic parameters. The take differential for the same country under different mechanics can be material — typically 5–15pp difference for PSC vs. concession in the same jurisdiction (Egypt oil PSC ~62% vs. EGPC concession legacy ~44%).
  4. IC memo disclosure: "ORCA country take of [X]% at $75/bbl (v250, [Mechanic] regime) reflects the dominant [PSC/Concession] contract architecture for [Country] by contract count ([N]% of in-country contracts). Target block [Block Name] operates under the [Concession/PSC] regime — project-specific take computed at [Y]% using Scenario Builder with [mechanic-specific parameters]. Government take comparison adjusted for regime type: [Country] [PSC] peer set vs. [Country] [Concession] peer set analyzed separately."

Rule of thumb by dual-regime prevalence:

  • PSC-dominant countries with legacy concession (Egypt, Indonesia, India): ORCA reports PSC take. Concession take for legacy fields is typically 8–18pp lower. If your block is a legacy concession, adjust down from ORCA's PSC take using the Regime Explorer concession take data.
  • Concession-dominant countries with PSC for deepwater/frontier (Malaysia, Brunei, UK): ORCA reports the dominant/majority mechanic. Deepwater PSC blocks in these countries typically carry 5–12pp higher take than the shallow-water concession. If your block is deepwater, use Fiscal Compare Custom with PSC mechanics and the specific profit-split tier for the block vintage.
  • Countries undergoing active regime transition (Kenya: PSA→PRRT discussion; Mexico: CNH concession + migrated PSCs): ORCA reflects the current dominant mechanic. Flag the transitional context in IC memos — fiscal take may shift 3–10pp if the new regime is adopted for your block.
A83. Our team is evaluating a farm-in to acquire working interest in an exploration block. The vendor's DCF shows a positive NPV. How do I adjust ORCA's government take figures to reflect the farm-in transaction structure, and how does the farm-in premium affect the IC?

Short answer: A farm-in does not change the fiscal regime — it changes cost basis and carried period for the acquiring party. ORCA's government take figure is correct and unchanged by working interest; what changes is your entry cost and your share of project costs and revenues. The farm-in premium — the consideration paid to the vendor — is a Year-0 outflow that replaces or supplements a portion of the exploration carry. Model it as a bonus payment in Scenario Builder.

Why the vendor's DCF may differ from ORCA's take:

  • Sunk costs vs. forward costs: The vendor's DCF likely includes pre-farm-in exploration costs (seismic, wells, licensing) that you are partially reimbursing. Your IC should model only forward costs from close, plus the farm-in premium — not the vendor's historical spend.
  • Carry provisions: Some farm-ins include a carried interest through exploration (the farmee drills one or more wells and the farmor's share is carried — costs paid by farmee, recovered from production). For PSC-structured blocks, carried exploration costs are a cost-oil item and affect cost recovery timing. For concession blocks, the carry reduces your effective exploration cost but not the statutory take.
  • Working interest vs. net revenue interest: In many PSC jurisdictions, the government take is computed at the gross level before WI allocation. Your WI-proportional take share equals the gross take — WI does not dilute the government's percentage, only your share of the residual.
  • Ring-fencing: If the farmed-in block is ring-fenced at the license level (Nigeria, Angola, Libya), cost recovery and profit sharing cannot be pooled across blocks. Model the farmed-in block as a standalone DCF with its own cost pool — do not net against other blocks in the same country.

4-step farm-in IC workflow using ORCA:

  1. Regime Explorer: confirm mechanic and ring-fencing. Open the target country in Regime Explorer, check the fiscal mechanic (Concession/PSC/RSC) and the ring_fence_type field. License-level ring-fencing (Nigeria/Angola/Libya) = standalone DCF mandatory. Company-level (Norway/UK) = cost pooling allowed.
  2. Scenario Builder: set WI-adjusted inputs. Scale all cost inputs by your WI%: capex × WI%, opex × WI%, production × WI%. Add the farm-in premium as an additional Year-0 cost item (outside the production profile). For carry provisions: model carried exploration capex at zero cost to you for the carried wells; begin cost recovery from first production per the block agreement.
  3. IRR comparison: project IRR vs. farm-in IRR. Run the base case at 100% WI to confirm ORCA's government take is consistent with your model. Then re-run at your WI% with farm-in premium included. The difference between the two IRRs is the farm-in cost premium dilution — should not exceed 3–5pp on a well-priced deal.
  4. IC memo: disclose farm-in structure and carry. State the WI acquired, the farm-in premium (absolute and as % of estimated exploration cost), the carried interest provision (if any), and which DCF inputs are forward costs vs. carry. Cite ORCA government take figure and note that take is WI-invariant per the statutory fiscal regime.

Rule of thumb by regime type:

  • Concession block farm-in (Nigeria/Angola/Libya/USA GoM): Farm-in premium is pure Year-0 outflow. IRR sensitivity is primarily through entry cost. A fair-valued farm-in premium should be roughly equivalent to the cost of drilling one exploration well — above that, the farmee is paying for optionality and exploration risk reduction that may not be recoverable in the DCF.
  • PSC block farm-in with carry (Indonesia/Malaysia/Egypt): Carried exploration costs reduce farmee's early outflow but are recovered from cost oil over the production period — treat as deferred cost recovery, not a subsidy. IRR improvement from carry is 1–3pp depending on carry depth and cost recovery cap.
  • Multi-block farm-in (portfolio transaction): Model each block separately if ring-fencing is license-level. Aggregate only for portfolio IRR and NPV reporting in the IC memo cover page — individual block economics must stand on their own per A37 IC memo workflow.

IC memo language template: "The [WI]% working interest acquired via farm-in is modeled on a forward-cost basis from [close date]. Farm-in consideration of $[X]M is included as a Year-0 cost item. Government take of [Y]% reflects the [Concession/PSC] fiscal regime per ORCA v274 (yoburgqs.github.io/petroleum-fiscal-db); take is working-interest-invariant. [If applicable: A [Z]-well exploration carry is included; cost recovery of carried wells begins at first production per the [block name] PSC terms, modeled as cost oil recovery from Year [N].]"

Source: Recommended Action. Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026).

A84. We are evaluating two gas-weighted countries where ORCA shows similar government take to an oil-weighted benchmark. How do I adjust the platform's figures for gas-linked contracts, and how does gas price uncertainty affect the IC?

Short answer: ORCA's DCF uses a Brent crude basis. For gas-weighted countries, the statutory fiscal structure is correct, but effective take depends on the gas price linkage — LNG netback, hub price, or domestic reference price — not Brent. Adjust using Scenario Builder with a gas-equivalent revenue input.

The three gas price linkage structures and their IC implications:

  • LNG netback pricing (Australia PRRT, Mozambique/Tanzania PSA, Papua New Guinea PSC): Revenue is the LNG cargo price minus liquefaction cost and shipping. At JKM (Japan-Korea Marker) $12–16/MMBtu, the oil-equivalent revenue is approximately $70–94/bbl — similar to the $75/bbl ORCA reference price. However, netback-linked contracts expose the contractor to LNG price volatility independently of oil prices, and liquefaction costs ($3–5/MMBtu) are a first-mover deduction that reduces effective revenue. PRRT and Australia in particular are more sensitive to netback deduction timing than to statutory rate changes.
  • Hub-linked pricing (US GoM, North Sea UK/Norway, Netherlands): Gas sold at Henry Hub ($2–4/MMBtu US average), TTF (European gas hub), or NBP. At $3/MMBtu Henry Hub, the oil-equivalent revenue is approximately $18/bbl — roughly one-quarter the ORCA reference price. Statutory take at $75/bbl oil dramatically overstates effective fiscal burden on gas-weighted US onshore or Gulf Coast contracts. For UKCS and Norway North Sea where gas can reach TTF-linked prices of $10–15/MMBtu, oil-equivalent revenue is $60–90/bbl — much closer to the oil reference.
  • Domestic reference price (Indonesia DMO, Egypt GSA, domestic supply obligations): Gas sold at below-market domestic reference prices under Domestic Market Obligations (DMO). Indonesia's DMO sets domestic gas at 25% of export LNG price — effectively $3–5/MMBtu for domestic supply volumes. DMO provisions reduce effective contractor revenue on the DMO-committed portion (typically 25% of production). This is a revenue haircut, not a fiscal take increase, but the effective government take rises because the contractor's net revenue on DMO volumes is much lower (see FAQ A67 on DMO mechanics).

4-step gas adjustment workflow using ORCA:

  1. Identify the gas price linkage mechanism. Check the Country Profile source note for the gas pricing structure. LNG-linked: use JKM or TTF basis in Scenario Builder.
