Hub-linked (Henry Hub): use $3/MMBtu × 6 = $18/bbl oil-equivalent as a low-price stress case. Domestic DMO: reduce revenue on the DMO proportion (typically 25% of volumes at 25–35% of export price).
  2. Run Scenario Builder at gas-equivalent oil price. For LNG-linked contracts at JKM $13/MMBtu: set oil price to approximately $78/bbl (close to the standard $75 reference — LNG netback is near-equivalent to Brent). For Henry Hub-linked at $3/MMBtu: set oil price to $18/bbl and observe IRR — this reveals fiscal burden at low gas price stress. Compare IRR at $75 vs. $18 to quantify the Price Swing equivalent for a gas-price shock.
  3. Apply DMO revenue haircut if applicable. For Indonesia-type DMO contracts: reduce peak production rate by 25% (DMO volumes) and set corresponding revenue at 25% of the hub price. Run Scenario Builder twice — once at full export price, once blending 75% export + 25% DMO price. The difference is the DMO take equivalent (typically 3–7pp effective government take increase for pure gas fields).
  4. IC memo: disclose gas price basis and DMO adjustment. State the gas pricing linkage, the reference price used (JKM/TTF/HH), the DMO provision if applicable, and that ORCA's statutory take figure is confirmed correct but effective take varies with gas price relative to oil. Cite the gas price scenario used in Scenario Builder alongside the standard $75/bbl oil reference case.

Rule of thumb by gas price linkage:

  • LNG-linked (JKM/TTF basis): ORCA take figures are broadly valid at current LNG prices ($12–16/MMBtu = $70–94/bbl oil-equivalent). Use as-is with a note that gas price risk is distinct from Brent crude risk. Key countries: Australia, Mozambique, Tanzania, Papua New Guinea, Qatar, Malaysia (MLNG).
  • Hub-linked (Henry Hub): ORCA take at $75/bbl overstates effective fiscal burden on US gas-weighted plays at Henry Hub $3/MMBtu (oil-equivalent ~$18/bbl). Run the $50/bbl stress case as a proxy for the HH gas price scenario — fiscal burden at $50/bbl is directionally representative of a US gas-price environment. Key countries: USA onshore shale gas basins.
  • DMO-constrained (Indonesia/Egypt/domestic obligation): Add 3–7pp to ORCA's statutory take for the effective DMO burden. Use FAQ A67 for the country-specific DMO mechanics. Key countries: Indonesia (SKK Migas 25% DMO), Egypt (EGPC domestic supply), Malaysia (Petronas domestic gas pricing).

IC memo language template: "Government take of [Y]% for [Country] reflects the statutory [PSC/Concession] fiscal regime per ORCA v274 (yoburgqs.github.io/petroleum-fiscal-db) at a $75/bbl Brent-equivalent reference price. This project is gas-weighted with revenues linked to [JKM/TTF/Henry Hub]. At [gas price basis] of $[X]/MMBtu (oil-equivalent approximately $[Z]/bbl), the effective take is modeled at [adjusted take]% using ORCA Scenario Builder with a $[Z]/bbl price input. [If DMO applicable: A 25% DMO commitment at $[domestic price]/MMBtu reduces the blended contractor revenue by approximately [N]pp effective take.] Gas price uncertainty is treated as a separate risk factor from Brent crude price risk in the sensitivity table."

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). See also FAQ A52 (gas/LNG price adjustment overview), FAQ A67 (DMO mechanics), FAQ A56 ($50/bbl energy-transition stress test).

A85. Two of my IC candidate countries include a PSC provision allowing the NOC to acquire a 15–25% carried interest after a commercial discovery is declared. ORCA shows one government take figure per country — does the back-in option affect this figure, and how do I model it in the IC?

Short answer: ORCA's government take reflects the statutory fiscal structure (royalty, profit oil, CIT) and includes paid NOC equity as a cost center — but it does NOT capture the contingent economic value of a free-carry back-in option, because that option transfers all exploration risk to the contractor and is exercised only after the NOC has waited for discovery confirmation. The back-in dilutes effective contractor IRR beyond the statutory take figure and must be modeled explicitly in any IC memo.

The three back-in structures and their IC implications:

  • Free-carry back-in at exploration cost (most common — Kenya EPSA 20%, Ghana GNPC 10%, Uganda PEPD 15%, Indonesia Pertamina 10%): The NOC acquires equity post-discovery by reimbursing the contractor's sunk exploration cost at a nominal rate — no interest, no time-value compensation. The contractor bears 100% of exploration risk; if successful, the NOC "backs in" at book cost and shares production upside. The statutory fiscal regime (royalty + profit oil + CIT) is unchanged, but the contractor's working interest drops from the pre-discovery level (typically 85–100%) to the post-back-in level (typically 70–85%). Economic impact: the NOC appropriates a share of the exploration premium — the value above exploration cost that the block acquires on discovery. For a $150M exploration program with a 15% free-carry back-in: the contractor effectively gifts the NOC a proportional share of the discovery NPV net of exploration cost.
  • Back-in at fair market value (paying back-in — Malaysia PETRONAS 15%, some Francophone Africa): The NOC acquires equity at a negotiated discovery FMV — a commercial transaction. The contractor is compensated at the resource value, not just exploration cost. IRR dilution is minimal if the FMV is reflective of the discovery upside (FMV buy-in resembles a farm-out at discovery, not a free ride). Check Country Profile evidence for FMV vs. cost-basis language in the relevant Petroleum Law or model contract.
  • Development carry-through (Nigeria NNPC Block carry — NOC carried through exploration AND development): The NOC is carried through both phases, repaying its cost oil share from production revenue under the cost recovery mechanism. This is a development-phase financing arrangement for the NOC — the contractor funds both exploration and NOC's development capital, recovering via cost oil. IRR dilution is more severe than a discovery-only back-in because the contractor's capital at risk includes the NOC's development share. Model as an additional pre-payout cost oil deduction. See FAQ A32 for state equity carried vs. paying WI mechanics.

4-step back-in modeling workflow using ORCA:

  1. Identify the back-in structure from the Country Profile source note. Check for the back_in_right, noc_equity_option, or equivalent parameter in the source evidence. Look for whether the back-in is cost-basis (reimbursement), FMV (paying), or development carry. If the back-in is well-documented in the primary PSC/concession agreement, the Evidence badge will cite the specific clause. If not present, check Fiscal Compare → Country Profile → source_note field for the relevant contract terms.
  2. Model the working interest step-down explicitly. For a 15% free-carry back-in: run Scenario Builder at 85% WI (post-discovery contractor share), with the full exploration cost ($150M typical for a deepwater well program) allocated to the contractor in Year 0–3. The NOC contributes $0 during exploration, then acquires 15% of production revenue net of royalty and profit oil. IRR at 85% WI will be approximately 1.5–3.5pp lower than the 100% WI statutory-take basis shown in ORCA, depending on discovery size and production profile.
  3. Quantify the exploration carry economic cost. Rule of thumb: each 5pp of free-carry back-in on a deepwater discovery costs the contractor approximately 0.5–1.2pp IRR (at the ORCA reference project scale: $1.2B development capex / 50k bbl/d). For smaller discoveries (<50 MMbbl), the IRR dilution per 5pp back-in rises to 1.5–2.5pp because the exploration cost is a larger fraction of total NPV. For giant fields (>500 MMbbl), the back-in cost is modest per unit of production — the NOC captures a larger absolute NPV but the contractor's IRR falls less severely because the discovery NPV dominates the exploration cost.
  4. Disclose the back-in in the IC memo as a separate line item. The statutory take figure from ORCA is correct for the fiscal regime but does not capture the back-in's equity dilution effect. IC memo must state the back-in structure, the basis (cost vs. FMV), and the adjusted post-back-in contractor IRR from Scenario Builder. See IC memo language template below.

Rule of thumb by country (free-carry, cost-basis back-in unless noted):

  • Kenya (NOCK EPSA 20% back-in at exploration cost, deepwater and onshore): ~1.5–3pp IRR dilution on a midsize discovery ($200–500M NPV range). Use Scenario Builder at 80% WI with $100–200M exploration cost as Year-0 expense. East Africa deepwater context: Rystad/NOCK benchmarks support take 55.3% pre-back-in, effective ~60% post-back-in on the 20% carry.
  • Ghana (GNPC 10% back-in at cost + 10% carried through exploration, deepwater): ~0.5–1.5pp IRR dilution on Jubilee/TEN-scale discoveries. GNPC's back-in is partially free-carry (10%) partially contributing (additional 5% at FMV in some blocks). Check block-specific terms — Jubilee-era terms differ from post-2016 Petroleum Commission blocks.
  • Uganda (PEPD 15% back-in at cost, Albertine Rift PSCs): ~1–2pp IRR dilution. Notable: Uganda also imposes a Capital Gains Tax on back-in transfers (10% of deemed gain) — an additional fiscal cost not captured in statutory take. Check Country Profile for CGT note.
  • Indonesia (SKK Migas 10% back-in at cost, Gross Split PSC): ~0.5–1.2pp IRR dilution at Pertamina's standard back-in terms. Gross Split PSC eliminates cost recovery — the 10% back-in is a pure equity share with no separate cost-recovery mechanism post-back-in. Pertamina participates as a full working interest partner from first production.
  • Nigeria (NNPC 60% PSC equity, development carry): This is not a back-in option but a statutory NOC participation structure. NNPC is carried through both exploration and development; the contractor funds 100% upfront and recovers via cost oil. See FAQ A32 for full mechanics. IRR dilution is embedded in the ORCA government take figure for Nigeria PSCs.

IC memo language template: "Government take of [X]% at $75/bbl (ORCA v274, standardized Deepwater profile) reflects the statutory [PSC/concession] fiscal regime for [Country] — royalty [R]%, cost recovery cap [CR]%, profit oil [Y]%, CIT [Z]%. [Country]'s fiscal framework includes a [%] NOC back-in right exercisable after commercial discovery at [exploration cost reimbursement / fair market value / development carry]. This back-in is not captured in the ORCA statutory take figure. Working interest reduces from [operator WI]% at exploration to [post-BI WI]% post-discovery; pre-discovery exploration cost of $[X]M is borne 100% by the contractor. ORCA Scenario Builder run at [post-BI WI]% WI with $[X]M Year-0 exploration cost yields contractor IRR of [Y]% @$75/bbl, vs. [Z]% on a statutory-take-only basis. Back-in equivalent take uplift: approximately [+N]pp effective government take over project life. See Appendix [G] for back-in sensitivity (10% / 15% / 20% back-in scenarios)."

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). See also FAQ A32 (state equity carried vs. paying WI), FAQ A39 (JV working interest treatment), FAQ A83 (farm-in/farm-out fiscal modeling). Country-specific back-in rates: NOCK Kenya Petroleum Act 2019 Section 72; GNPC Ghana Petroleum Act 1983 as amended; SKK Migas Indonesia Government Regulation 53/2017 Gross Split; Uganda Petroleum (Exploration, Development and Production) Act 2013 Section 51.

A86. ORCA's IRR figures for two of our shortlist countries differ from our in-house DCF by 2–4pp despite matching statutory take percentages. Our model uses jurisdiction-specific depreciation schedules (UK: 100% Year-1 capital allowance; Norway: 6-year linear; Australia: unit-of-production). How does ORCA model depreciation, and how do we reconcile the IRR gap?

Short answer: ORCA uses a standardized 7-year straight-line depreciation for all countries and mechanics — this is a deliberate simplification to enable consistent cross-country comparison. Jurisdiction-specific schedules (accelerated first-year allowances, unit-of-production, uplift deductions) create real IRR differences vs. ORCA's figures. The delta is predictable and adjustable using Scenario Builder's annual cost input.

ORCA's depreciation baseline (all mechanics except Norway SPT): Capital expenditure is depreciated using straight-line amortization over 7 years (or project life if shorter than 7 years). This applies uniformly across all 185 countries unless a mechanic-specific treatment overrides it (Norway SPT uplift is handled as a separate deduction; see FAQ A38). The platform's Methodology tab → Model Parameters table documents this assumption. The 7-year schedule represents a mid-point between aggressive accelerated schedules (UK, Australia) and conservative long-life schedules (some Asian concessions at 10–12 years).

The three most common jurisdiction-specific depreciation schedules and their IRR impact vs. ORCA:

  • UK — 100% first-year capital allowance (Ring Fence Expenditure Supplement / RFES): All development capex is deductible in Year 1 against Ring Fence CIT and Energy Profits Levy. This front-loads the tax shield dramatically vs. ORCA's 7-year straight-line. Impact: UK IRR in ORCA will typically be understated by 1.5–3pp for development-phase projects because the actual UK tax shield is more valuable (higher NPV of deductions) than the ORCA 7-year spread. For a $1.2B capex project: ~$170M/year vs. $1.2B in Year 1 — at 56% effective tax rate, the NPV of the UK accelerated deduction is approximately $70–120M higher, translating to ~1.5–3pp IRR uplift.
  • Norway — 6-year linear depreciation + 17.69% investment uplift: ORCA's Norway take reflects the SPT uplift deduction (documented in the JS engine). The standard depreciation is 6-year linear (vs. ORCA's 7-year). For a 15-year project, the 1-year difference is modest: approximately 0.3–0.8pp IRR delta attributable to the depreciation schedule alone. The more significant Norway-specific gap is the RFES tax refund on exploration costs (78% refund rate makes exploration NPV-neutral for the Norwegian state — ORCA captures this via take calculation but does not model the exploration refund as a separate cash inflow). Net IRR gap vs. ORCA: typically <1pp if the SPT uplift is correctly applied.
  • Australia (PRRT) — Unit-of-Production (UOP) method: PRRT augmented depreciation uses a UOP method tied to proved reserves, which front-loads deductions in high-production years (early in project life). For a standard Deepwater profile (50k bbl/d plateau with exponential decline), UOP deductions are weighted to Years 1–5 vs. ORCA's flat 7-year spread. Impact on IRR: typically +0.8–2pp uplift from the front-loaded UOP schedule at $75/bbl. However, Australia's PRRT exclusion amount (8.5% + long-term bond rate = ~12% uplift) more than offsets this — ORCA's Australia take may slightly overstate the contractor's IRR because the effective PRRT threshold is high. The net PRRT IRR gap is often within 1pp of ORCA if the starting basis is the same.

4-step workflow to reconcile the IRR gap using ORCA:

  1. Confirm the statutory take matches. Use the Country Profile tab to verify ORCA's take parameters match your in-house model (royalty rate, CIT rate, PRRT/SPT rate, profit oil split). If take percentages differ by more than 1pp, the root cause is fiscal parameter input — not depreciation. Fix the parameter mismatch before investigating depreciation timing.
  2. Isolate the depreciation contribution. In your in-house model, run the same project under 7-year straight-line depreciation (matching ORCA). If the IRR gap closes to <0.5pp, depreciation timing is confirmed as the primary driver. If a gap remains under identical depreciation, check discount rate basis (ORCA: 10%, unadjusted; no country risk premium) and production profile calibration.
  3. Adjust using Scenario Builder annual cost inputs. ORCA's Scenario Builder allows annual capex timing via the Custom Profile input. To model accelerated depreciation, front-load the capex deduction in the custom annual cost schedule: for UK 100% Year-1, enter the full $1.2B as Year-1 capex with $0 in subsequent years. The engine will apply the CIT deduction in Year 1, producing an IRR closer to the UK-actual outcome. This is an approximation (the Scenario Builder does not have an explicit depreciation schedule override), but it captures most of the tax shield timing effect.
  4. Disclose the depreciation basis in the IC memo. IC memos should specify which depreciation schedule was used. If presenting ORCA figures, note "ORCA 7-year straight-line depreciation, standardized"; if presenting jurisdiction-specific figures, note the schedule and source (e.g., "UK Finance Act 2023 Section 12, 100% Year-1 RFES"). Never compare ORCA figures to in-house figures without reconciling the depreciation basis — a 2–3pp IRR gap from depreciation alone can change a project's IC-readiness tier.

Rule of thumb for depreciation-driven IRR uplift vs. ORCA (at $75/bbl, $1.2B capex, 15yr project):

  • UK accelerated: +1.5–3pp IRR vs. ORCA (100% Year-1 RFES front-loads tax shield)
  • Australia PRRT UOP: +0.8–2pp IRR vs. ORCA (production-weighted deductions in high-flow years)
  • Norway 6yr linear: <1pp IRR vs. ORCA (near-identical to 7yr; SPT uplift more material than depreciation timing)
  • Indonesia Gross Split: no depreciation deduction (cost recovery eliminated; ORCA and actual IRR align on depreciation — no timing gap)
  • 10–12yr long-life schedules (some Asian concessions): −0.5–1.5pp IRR vs. ORCA (slower depreciation reduces NPV of tax shield vs. ORCA 7yr)

IC memo language template: "IRR for [Country] computed using ORCA v274 (Aug 2026), standardized 7-year straight-line depreciation of development capex. [Country]'s actual fiscal code uses [jurisdiction schedule: e.g., 100% Year-1 capital allowance / 6yr linear / unit-of-production]. Jurisdiction-specific depreciation adjustment: +[X]pp IRR (source: [Finance Act / Tax Code reference]). Adjusted IRR: [ORCA IRR + adjustment]% @$75/bbl. ORCA Scenario Builder run at jurisdiction schedule approximation (front-loaded capex timing) yields [SB IRR]% — see Appendix [H] for depreciation sensitivity comparison."

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). ORCA Model Parameters table (Methodology tab) documents the 7-year straight-line baseline. UK depreciation: Finance Act 2023, Section 12 (RFES / Ring Fence Expenditure Supplement). Norway depreciation: Norwegian Petroleum Tax Act Section 3b (6-year linear + Section 5 uplift). Australia PRRT depreciation: PRRT Act 1987, Section 22 (augmented bond rate deduction + UOP). See also FAQ A38 (PRRT vs. SPT methodology), FAQ A41 (IRR DCF model specification), FAQ A59 (cross-project-type capital allocation).

A87. ORCA's IRR figures are computed at a flat 10% discount rate with no country risk premium. Our IC committee requires a risk-adjusted hurdle for international upstream investments. How do I layer in a political risk adjustment, and how does this interact with ORCA's Reform Risk Stability Score?

Short answer: ORCA uses a standardized 10% discount rate with zero country risk premium (CRP) — this ensures cross-country IRR comparability without embedding analyst-specific risk views. Applying a CRP is the analyst's responsibility. ORCA's Reform Risk Stability Score provides the ordinal signal; CRP magnitude requires external inputs (EMBI+ spreads, political risk insurance, or internal credit models).

Why ORCA uses a flat 10% rate: Consistent with Wood Mackenzie and Rystad benchmarking methodology (both use 8–12% depending on peer set). A single rate across all 185 countries ensures cross-regime IRR comparisons isolate the fiscal variable — if the UAE (87.6% take) and Guyana (52.3% take) were discounted at different risk-adjusted rates, the IRR gap would confound fiscal regime differences with risk-premium differences. The CRP layer belongs in the IC memo, not in the benchmark computation. (See FAQ A41 for full DCF model specification.)

Three methods to apply a country risk premium on top of ORCA's IRR:

  • Method 1 — Hurdle rate uplift (most common): Add the CRP to your required return. Example: Nigeria Scenario Builder shows IRR 16% / CRP 4pp (Stability Score 2/5) ⇒ risk-adjusted hurdle = 14%. Project clears if ORCA IRR ≥ 14%. Cleanest IC disclosure: fiscal result (ORCA IRR at 10%) and risk overlay (CRP assumption) are explicit and separately auditable.
  • Method 2 — NPV discount: Apply risk factor to Scenario Builder NPV: Risk-Adjusted NPV = ORCA NPV × (1 − risk_factor). Typical factors: 5–10% OECD/investment-grade EM; 15–25% frontier; 30–50% high-risk frontier (Stability ≤ 1). Transparent in IC but harder to reconcile with IRR hurdles.
  • Method 3 — Breakeven uplift (discount-rate-independent): Add a risk buffer to Breakeven: if Breakeven = $42/bbl and your country risk buffer = $6/bbl (~3pp IRR on mid-size project), require Breakeven < $36/bbl. Avoids discount rate sensitivity; robust when comparing concession vs. PSC regimes with different cash flow timing.

Stability Score → CRP tier mapping (rule of thumb):

  • Score 5 (OECD/Norway/UAE — zero reform events): CRP +0pp.
  • Score 4 (Brazil/Malaysia/Colombia — 1 event): CRP +1pp ⇒ adjusted hurdle 11%.
  • Score 3 (Ghana/Tanzania/Peru — 2 events): CRP +2pp ⇒ adjusted hurdle 12%.
  • Score 2 (Nigeria/Angola/Ecuador — 3–4 events): CRP +3–4pp ⇒ adjusted hurdle 13–14%.
  • Score 1 (Libya/Venezuela/Myanmar — 5+ events): CRP +5–7pp ⇒ adjusted hurdle 15–17%.

4-step IC workflow:

  1. Run Scenario Builder at project-specific inputs. Record the base IRR at 10% / 0% CRP.
  2. Read the Stability Score from Explorer or Country Profile. Map to CRP tier above, or use internal sovereign credit model (EMBI+ spread, Moody's/S&P, PRI quote). For large capital commitments, use a formal CRP from a recognized source.
  3. Apply hurdle uplift for the IC table. Disclose: “ORCA IRR of [X]% at 10% / 0% CRP. Country risk premium [Y]pp per [source]. Risk-adjusted hurdle [Z]%. Project [clears / does not clear].”
  4. Cross-check with Breakeven uplift. If IRR clears but Breakeven fails after risk buffer, flag in IC — typically signals high-take + thin IRR margin where a modest CRP destroys value. High-take + high-risk is the most common IC rejection pattern in international upstream.

IC memo language template: “Government take benchmarked via ORCA v274 (Aug 2026), standardized reference profile ($1.2B capex / 50k bbl/d Deepwater / $15/bbl opex / 10% discount rate / 0% CRP). Base IRR: [X]% @$75/bbl. Country risk premium [Y]pp per [EMBI+/internal model/Stability Score tier]. Risk-adjusted hurdle: [Z]%. ORCA Scenario Builder at project inputs: base IRR [A]% (see Appendix [H]).”

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). Model Parameters (Methodology tab) documents the 10% baseline. See also FAQ A41 (IRR DCF model specification), FAQ A63 (Breakeven + IRR composite viability screen), FAQ A29 (enforcement integrity due diligence), FAQ A12 (IRR proxy workflow for IRR-unavailable countries).

A88. Our IC committee requires a capex overrun sensitivity table (base / +25% / +50%) for all international upstream investments. ORCA's reference project uses a fixed $1.2B capex. How do I model cost overrun scenarios in the Scenario Builder, and which fiscal regime types are most resilient to capex overruns?

Short answer: Enter overrun capex directly in Scenario Builder's Capital Expenditure field. PSCs with high cost recovery caps (≥60% CR) cushion overruns by accelerating cost oil recovery — the additional capex is partially recovered before profit oil split, reducing the effective fiscal penalty. Concessions and royalty-first regimes provide no such cushion: every dollar of overrun is subject to royalties from the first barrel.

Why fiscal regime type determines overrun resilience: In a PSC with 60% cost recovery cap, an extra $300M capex overrun generates additional cost oil that the contractor recovers before the profit oil split is applied. The government absorbs a share of the overrun indirectly (via delayed profit oil). In a concession, the government collects royalty on gross revenue regardless of cost — every barrel produced faces the same royalty rate whether costs are $1.2B or $1.8B. This structural difference means capex overruns hurt concession economics disproportionately vs. high-CR-cap PSCs.

Rule of thumb for IC sensitivity table (IRR impact by regime type):

  • High-CR-cap PSC (80% cap — Guyana, Ghana deepwater): +25% capex (→ $1.5B) ⇒ −2–3pp IRR; +50% capex (→ $1.8B) ⇒ −4–5pp IRR. Partially buffered by cost oil recovery acceleration.
  • Mid-CR-cap PSC (60% cap — Angola, Nigeria deepwater): +25% capex ⇒ −3–4pp IRR; +50% capex ⇒ −5–7pp IRR. Moderate buffer; at high overruns the CR cap becomes a binding constraint.
  • Concession — low royalty (5–10% — Norway, UK, Australia): +25% capex ⇒ −3–4pp IRR; +50% capex ⇒ −6–8pp IRR. No cost recovery buffer; full royalty on overrun production from first barrel.
  • Concession — high royalty (>15% — Iraq TSC, Indonesia Gross Split): +25% capex ⇒ −4–6pp IRR; +50% capex ⇒ −8–12pp IRR. Highest overrun sensitivity — royalty drains revenue before any cost recovery.

4-step IC workflow:

  1. Run Scenario Builder at base inputs. Use project-specific capex / opex / peak rate (or ORCA reference $1.2B / $15/bbl / 50k bbl/d Deepwater). Record base IRR at $75/bbl.
  2. Re-run at +25% capex overrun. Multiply your base capex by 1.25 and enter in the Capital Expenditure field. Keep all other inputs constant. Record the overrun IRR.
  3. Re-run at +50% capex overrun. Multiply by 1.50. Record the high-overrun IRR. This is the IC committee's stress case.
  4. Export each Scenario Builder result. Use XLSX export for each scenario; combine into a single IC appendix table: Scenario / Capex ($M) / IRR (%) / Δ vs. Base (pp). Flag if the +50% case breaches your IC hurdle rate — this typically triggers a contingency escrow or phased-FID recommendation.

IC memo language template: “Capex overrun sensitivity per ORCA Scenario Builder v250 (Aug 2026), [Mechanic] regime, $75/bbl reference price: Base $[X]M ⇒ IRR [A]%; Overrun +25% $[Y]M ⇒ IRR [B]% (−[A−B]pp); Overrun +50% $[Z]M ⇒ IRR [C]% (−[A−C]pp). [Country] [PSC/Concession] structure provides [high/moderate/limited] cost recovery buffer for capex overruns — PSC cost oil recovery cap of [X]% partially offsets the overrun prior to profit oil split. All scenarios use project-specific inputs; see Appendix [I] for full Scenario Builder inputs.”

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). See also FAQ A41 (IRR DCF model specification), FAQ A86 (depreciation and capital allowance timing), FAQ A63 (Breakeven + IRR composite viability screen), FAQ A56 ($50/bbl energy-transition stress test).

A89. My IC committee requires a data currency statement in all fiscal memos: "This data was current as of [date] — material changes since that date have been identified as follows: [...]." How do I assess ORCA's data vintage and identify potential post-vintage regime changes?

Short answer: ORCA's fiscal parameters reflect benchmark publications dated 2023–2025 (EY, Wood Mac, Rystad, IHS Markit), validated against primary government and contract sources through August 2026. For IC disclosure, treat parameters as current to approximately H1 2025 for published benchmark sources, with platform updates through August 2026 for reform events captured in the Reform History tab. Always check the Evidence badge (Country Profile) and Reform History tab for post-vintage changes before IC submission.

Why the publication lag matters: Professional fiscal databases close their data year in Q4 and publish updated guides in Q1–Q2 of the following year. The EY Oil & Gas Tax Guide 2024 reflects regimes as of approximately September 2023. ORCA benchmark validation cites these publication dates — parameters sourced from "EY 2024" are effectively current to late 2023. For most stable jurisdictions (Stability Score 4–5), this lag is immaterial because the fiscal framework has not changed. For volatile jurisdictions (Score 1–2), 12–18 months is long enough for a meaningful regime amendment.

Rule of thumb for IC data currency assessment by Stability Score tier:

  • Score 5 (0–1 reforms in 15 years — Norway, UK, Australia, USA): Framework stable. No additional verification needed beyond standard ORCA cite. Data currency risk: minimal.
  • Score 4 (2–3 reforms — Brazil, Malaysia, Kazakhstan): Check Reform History tab for events since 2023. If none found: data current. If found: assess whether amendment is captured in ORCA parameters (compare ORCA's source date to reform enactment date).
  • Score 3 (4–6 reforms — Nigeria, Indonesia, Angola): Check Reform History for 2024–2025 events. If found: run Scenario Builder sensitivity at ±5pp take to bound the IC uncertainty. Disclose the sensitivity range in the IC memo.
  • Score 1–2 (7+ reforms — Bolivia, Venezuela, Argentina, Chad): High data-currency risk. Verify current terms against country petroleum authority website or recent IOC press releases before IC submission. Use ORCA take as directional floor/ceiling only; disclose pending primary verification.

4-step IC data currency workflow:

  1. Check Evidence badge in Country Profile. “A” (primary source: PSA/government gazette) = highest currency confidence. “B” (secondary benchmark: EY/Wood Mac/Rystad) = current to publication vintage. “C” (directional/IHS Markit stub) = treat as indicative; verify before IC.
  2. Check Reform History tab. Filter to target country. Look for reform events dated 2024–2025. If the most recent reform predates the ORCA benchmark source date: no adjustment needed. If it postdates: cross-reference the ORCA Reform History description against the country petroleum authority’s press releases or official gazette.
  3. If post-vintage reforms found: model Scenario Builder. Run at the ORCA take as a base case (pre-reform) and at your estimated post-reform take (derived from gazette/press release). Disclose the pre/post-reform IRR range in the IC memo appendix. This bounds the fiscal uncertainty without requiring a full primary-source verification if IC timeline is tight.
  4. Draft data currency disclosure. If no post-vintage reforms found: one-sentence disclosure. If reforms found but bounded: three-sentence disclosure with appendix reference. If reforms unverified and high-impact: flag as a FID condition requiring independent legal/fiscal verification before commitment.

IC memo language template: “Fiscal parameters for [Country] sourced from ORCA Petroleum Fiscal Intelligence Platform v250 (Aug 2026). Primary benchmark source: [EY Oil & Gas Tax Guide [year] / Wood Mac [year] / Rystad [year]] — effective data cut-off approximately [H1/H2 YYYY]. ORCA Reform History tab: [N] fiscal reform events in the past 5 years (most recent: [description, date]). [Choose one: (a) No material regime changes identified between benchmark cut-off and IC submission date — data is suitable for IC use. (b) Reform event identified: [description] enacted [date]. Scenario Builder sensitivity at pre/post-reform take estimates: IRR [X]% (pre) to [Y]% (post) — see Appendix [Z]. (c) Post-vintage reform unverified — independent fiscal counsel verification required prior to FID commitment.] Evidence badge: [A/B/C]. Citation: ORCA v274, yoburgqs.github.io/petroleum-fiscal-db/.”

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). See also FAQ A13 (three-tier source verification workflow), FAQ A17 (IC-readiness tier guidance by country tier), FAQ A51 (Reform Risk workflow), FAQ A76 (recently-reformed fiscal regime IC workflow), FAQ A73 (stabilization clause vs. Reform Risk Stability Score), FAQ A87 (country risk premium adjustment).

A90. My project has a 25k bbl/d peak rate and $600M capex — roughly half ORCA's reference project. How material are the scale effects on government take, and how do I calibrate the platform's benchmark take figure for my actual project parameters?

Short answer: Scale effects on government take are 0–8pp for most regimes and mechanically predictable. The Scenario Builder is the correct calibration tool — enter your actual capex, opex, and peak rate to compute a project-specific take directly. The reference project (50k bbl/d / $1.2B capex / $15/bbl opex) is a calibration anchor for cross-regime ranking, not a constraint on what you can model. Scale matters most for sliding-scale royalty concessions and PSCs where the cost recovery pool is proportionally large relative to revenue.

Why scale affects take — the four fiscal mechanics that are non-linear with project size:

  • Sliding-scale royalties (volume-linked): Royalty rates that step up with production rate (e.g., 5% at <5k bbl/d → 15% at >50k bbl/d) penalize large projects disproportionately. A 25k bbl/d project may stay in the 5–10% royalty tier where the platform's reference project at 50k sits in the 10–15% tier. Scale benefit: 3–8pp lower take for small projects in volume-linked royalty regimes. Countries: USA GoM (OCS royalty rate schedule), Brazil (ANP royalty 5–15% by volume), Norway (not applicable — flat royalty discontinued). Check the Country Profile's royalty_rate field and source note for tier thresholds.
  • PSC cost recovery dynamics (capex-to-revenue ratio): In a high-cost-recovery-cap PSC (e.g., 80% cap), a smaller project with $600M capex at $75/bbl and 25k bbl/d generates ~$685M/yr gross revenue. The cost recovery phase ends in year 1–2 (capex recovered almost immediately). Compared to the reference project ($1.2B capex / $1,370M/yr revenue) which also exits cost recovery in year 1–2, the dynamics are similar — scale has modest impact when both projects recover capex within the first 2 years. The exception is ultra-low-rate frontier projects where revenue barely covers the cost recovery cap, extending the capex recovery phase and suppressing profit oil to the government. Rule of thumb: scale matters most when rate <10k bbl/d (revenue insufficient to clear cost recovery cap quickly).
  • Specific/volumetric levies (per-barrel fees): Surface fees, area fees, and training levies are often fixed per barrel regardless of rate. On a 25k bbl/d project, a $0.50/bbl training levy represents a higher share of revenue than on a 50k bbl/d project. Impact is typically <1pp IRR — immaterial unless the project is marginal. See FAQ A57 for government take exclusions that fall outside ORCA's statutory take computation.
  • R-factor thresholds (PSC profit oil split): R-factor = cumulative contractor receipts / cumulative contractor expenditure. A smaller project ($600M capex) at the same production rate reaches R=1.0 faster than the reference project ($1.2B capex), crossing into less-favorable profit oil split tiers earlier. This means a smaller project experiences higher-tier government take sooner than the platform's weighted-average R-factor trajectory implies. Net effect: smaller projects in R-factor regimes may see 1–4pp higher effective take than the platform's reference. See FAQ A47 for R-factor mechanics and threshold identification.

Mechanics where scale has minimal effect (near-zero adjustment needed):

  • Flat-rate royalty concessions (UK, Norway, most Gulf concessions): A fixed 12.5% royalty is 12.5% regardless of rate. No scale adjustment needed for royalty line. RFCT (UK) and PRRT (Australia) are profit-based — their rates are insensitive to project scale; what matters is profitability level, not volume. Scale effect: 0–1pp.
  • Revenue-share contracts (TSC / EPSA IV-type): Revenue share is a straight percentage of gross revenue; scale does not alter the effective take. Countries: Libya EPSA IV, some Middle East TSCs. Scale effect: 0pp.
  • CIT-only regimes (lower royalty jurisdictions): Corporate income tax is purely profit-driven; project scale affects the tax base proportionally. Scale effect: 0–2pp (from overhead allocation differences).

4-step project-scale calibration workflow:

  1. Identify the mechanic type for your target country. Open Country Profile → mechanic field. Concession with sliding-scale royalty: proceed to Step 2. PSC: check cost_recovery_cap and profit_oil_tier_schedule fields for R-factor sensitivity. Revenue share / flat royalty: platform take is approximately correct at your scale; minor adjustment only.
  2. Run Scenario Builder with your actual project parameters. Input: capex = $600M, opex = $8–12/bbl (onshore) or $15–20/bbl (offshore small field), peak rate = 25k bbl/d, plateau duration = your profile. The Scenario Builder DCF engine uses your inputs directly — it does not approximate from the reference project. The IRR and NPV outputs are your project-specific take, not the benchmark take.
  3. Compare Scenario Builder output to Country Profile take. If the spread is <3pp: scale is immaterial; use the platform take for IC benchmarking and note the reference project basis. If the spread is 3–8pp: use the Scenario Builder IRR for your project and note the scale-adjusted basis in the IC memo. If the spread is >8pp: check for sliding-scale royalty tier differences or R-factor acceleration — one of these is likely the driver.
  4. Draft IC memo disclosure. "Government take benchmarked against ORCA reference project (50k bbl/d / $1.2B capex): [X]%. Project-specific take modeled in ORCA Scenario Builder (25k bbl/d / $600M capex / $[Y]/bbl opex): [Z]%. Scale adjustment: [+/−N]pp, driven by [sliding-scale royalty tier / R-factor acceleration / cost recovery timing]. Scenario Builder inputs and full DCF output available in Appendix [N]."

Rule of thumb by mechanic and scale:

  • Flat royalty concession (UK, Gulf, most Middle East): <2pp scale adjustment regardless of project size. Platform take is directly usable for IC benchmarking.
  • Sliding-scale royalty concession (USA GoM, Brazil, Russia): 3–8pp lower take for small projects (<30k bbl/d) vs. reference. Run Scenario Builder; lower royalty tier is a material benefit for small fields.
  • Standard PSC (60–80% CR cap, flat profit oil split): 0–3pp scale adjustment. Most impact comes from profit oil split timing. Scenario Builder captures this precisely.
  • R-factor PSC (Nigeria, Guyana, Iraq-KRG): 1–4pp higher effective take for small projects (faster R-factor threshold crossing). Scenario Builder R-factor trajectory applies your capex directly.
  • PRRT / SPT (Australia, Norway): 0–2pp. These are profit-based; scale changes the absolute tax amounts but not the effective rate on a proportional basis.

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). See also FAQ A41 (IRR DCF model specification — reference project parameters), FAQ A47 (R-factor mechanics), FAQ A42 (cost recovery cap sensitivity), FAQ A57 (government take exclusions — surface fees and training levies), FAQ A88 (capex overrun sensitivity), FAQ A60 (gas vs. oil fiscal adjustments for non-reference products).

A91. Our IC committee needs a single “blended portfolio take” figure across our 5-country shortlist. How do I compute a production-weighted average government take from ORCA data, and how should I disclose this metric in a capital allocation memo?

Short answer: ORCA supports portfolio-level blended take through a 3-step workflow — Fiscal Compare for the ranked table, XLSX export for production-weighting in your model, and explicit IC disclosure of the weighting methodology. The blended take is a summary metric, not a substitute for per-country analysis; use it alongside IRR dispersion and Swing range to characterize portfolio fiscal risk.

Why production-weighted average take — what it captures and what it misses:

  • What it captures: Portfolio-level government take weighted by each country’s share of projected production (bbl/d or MMboe) gives the IC committee a single fiscal efficiency metric for the overall investment program. It is analogous to a weighted-average cost of capital for fiscal burden — countries with larger allocations dominate the portfolio take, which is the correct economic weighting. A portfolio that is 60% Norway / 40% Nigeria has a materially different fiscal profile than the simple average suggests.
  • What it misses: Blended take collapses IRR dispersion, mechanic-type diversity, and price-sensitivity differences into a single number. A portfolio with 50% in a flat-royalty concession (low Price Swing) and 50% in an R-factor PSC (high Price Swing) may show identical blended take at $75/bbl but diverge sharply at $50 or $100. Always present blended take alongside IRR range and Price Swing range as the three-metric portfolio characterization.

3-step portfolio blended take workflow:

  1. Run Fiscal Compare for all shortlisted countries. Open Fiscal Compare → add all 5 countries to the basket → select a common price and profile (Deepwater $75/bbl is the standard IC reference) → click Run. The results table shows Govt Take, NPV, IRR, Breakeven, and Price Swing for each country at a common basis. This is the IC-ready regime comparison table.
  2. Export to XLSX and add your production allocation weights. Click “⇓ Excel” to download the Fiscal Compare results. Add a column for your projected production allocation (bbl/d or gross MMboe over project life) for each country. Compute blended take as: Σ(Country Take × Country Production) / Σ(Country Production). Example: Norway 48% take × 40k bbl/d + Nigeria 68% take × 20k bbl/d + Guyana 52% take × 15k bbl/d + UAE 89% take × 10k bbl/d + Australia 57% take × 15k bbl/d ÷ 100k total = 59.7% blended portfolio take. If production weights are not finalized, use equal weighting with a note — sensitivity to weighting assumption should be in the IC appendix.
  3. Present portfolio metrics as a three-metric block in the IC memo. The correct IC portfolio fiscal summary: (a) Blended weighted-average take: [X]% at $75/bbl Deepwater reference; (b) IRR range across portfolio countries: [low]% to [high]%; (c) Price Swing range: [low]pp to [high]pp (portfolio fiscal risk indicator — a wide range signals that the portfolio’s fiscal burden diverges significantly across price scenarios). Present all three — a single blended take without dispersion metrics understates the IC committee’s exposure.

Disclosure conventions for IC memos:

  • Disclose the weighting basis explicitly. “Blended portfolio government take of [X]% weighted by projected gross production allocation (bbl/d): [Country A] [N1]% / [Country B] [N2]% / …. All country takes sourced from ORCA Petroleum Fiscal Intelligence Platform v250 (Aug 2026), standardized Deepwater profile ($1.2B capex / 50k bbl/d / $15/bbl opex / $75/bbl). Per-country take and IRR in Appendix [A]; Scenario Builder project-specific sensitivities in Appendix [B].”
  • Flag unequal Evidence badge quality. If one country in the portfolio has a C-rated evidence badge (directional only), its take may carry a ±4–6pp uncertainty vs. ±1–2pp for A-rated countries. Disclose this asymmetry: “[Country X] take is directional (Evidence badge C) — blended portfolio take carries ±[Y]pp uncertainty attributable to [Country X] weighting of [N]%.”
  • Note the price sensitivity of the blended figure. Run the same Fiscal Compare at $50/bbl and $100/bbl and recompute the blended take. If the blended take range is >10pp across the $50–$100 corridor, include the blended Price Swing as a separate disclosure: “Blended portfolio take ranges from [low]% at $50/bbl to [high]% at $100/bbl (blended Price Swing: [range]pp), driven primarily by [mechanic type] exposure in [Country].”

Rule of thumb — portfolio blended take interpretation:

  • <50% blended take: Portfolio skewed toward low-royalty concessions or frontier PSCs with deep cost recovery. High IRR potential at mid-cycle prices; exposure to royalty uplift at high price scenarios is limited. Typical for OECD + frontier portfolio mix.
  • 50–65% blended take: Mid-range portfolio consistent with a mix of standard PSCs, Gulf concessions, and Atlantic margin producers. This is the IOC industry average range. IRR in the 12–18% band at $75/bbl for a well-structured portfolio.
  • >65% blended take: Portfolio weighted toward high-government-take regimes (West Africa deepwater PSCs, OPEC Gulf concessions, resource-rent-tax jurisdictions). Lower mid-cycle IRR but potentially lower Price Swing — the government absorbs a larger share of price upside. Requires explicit IC justification for strategic rationale (resource access, reserve replacement, NOC relationship).

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). See also FAQ A37 (IC capital allocation memo workflow — full 5-step process), FAQ A59 (cross-project-type capital allocation), FAQ A56 ($50/bbl energy-transition stress test), FAQ A87 (country risk premium adjustment), FAQ A17 (IC-readiness tiers by evidence badge).

A92. I’m evaluating a farm-in to acquire a 30% working interest in an existing PSC block. The vendor is quoting an effective government take of 58% at deal sanction. How do I use ORCA to validate this figure, compare it to a greenfield entry alternative, and present the farm-in fiscal quality in an IC memo?

Short answer: ORCA computes lifecycle government take from first production on a fresh-entry basis. A farm-in at an existing block typically shows 3–10pp higher effective take than ORCA’s standardized figure, because the cost recovery pool is partially exhausted and any R-factor thresholds may already have been triggered. Use ORCA’s standardized take as the greenfield comparator, then apply a mature-block adjustment based on the remaining cost pool to validate the vendor’s quoted figure.

Why vendor-quoted take often differs from ORCA’s standardized figure:

  • Cost pool exhaustion: ORCA models a full cost recovery phase from Day 1. In a mature PSC block, a substantial share of the original cost pool has already been recovered by the operating partner. The incoming farm-in partner inherits a smaller remaining pool — meaning the project enters profit-oil sharing sooner, which increases the government’s share of remaining revenues. A block that is 5+ years past FID may have exhausted 60–80% of its cost recovery capacity.
  • R-factor tier acceleration: In R-factor PSCs (Angola, Nigeria OPL, Azerbaijan ACG-type), cumulative revenues may already have exceeded early-tier thresholds, placing the block in a higher government profit-oil tier than ORCA’s standardized computation assumes. Ask the vendor: “What is the current R-factor, and which profit-oil tier applies today?” If the R-factor has crossed 1.5 or 2.0, effective take may be 5–10pp above ORCA’s standardized mid-tier approximation.
  • Entry cost is not government take, but it loads the IRR: The acquisition premium (bonus, signature payment, WI purchase price) does not affect headline government take, but it directly loads the WI’s IRR. A 58% take regime can yield a 10% IRR on a greenfield basis and only 7% IRR after paying a $250M acquisition premium for a 30% WI. The take figure and the acquisition economics are two separate assessments — both belong in the IC memo.

4-step farm-in validation workflow:

  1. Run Country Profile for the target country. Open Country Profile → select the PSC country → record the fiscal mechanic, profit-oil split structure, cost recovery cap, and Evidence badge rating. This confirms the contractual regime type and ORCA’s data quality for this jurisdiction. A B- or C-rated Evidence badge means the vendor’s quoted take cannot be validated to the same precision as an A-rated country.
  2. Run Fiscal Compare to establish the greenfield baseline. Add the target country to Fiscal Compare at $75/bbl Deepwater reference. Record: Govt Take (greenfield new-entry), IRR, Breakeven, and Price Swing. This is your “what would I get on a greenfield basis in this jurisdiction?” comparator — the floor of valuation logic for a farm-in bid.
  3. Apply a mature-block adjustment to estimate farm-in effective take. Use the following rule of thumb adjusted by block age: (a) Block in active cost recovery (<3 years past FID): WI effective take ≈ ORCA take ±2pp — minimal adjustment needed, most cost pool intact. (b) Block in mid-life profit-oil phase (3–8 years past FID): WI effective take ≈ ORCA take + 3–6pp — cost pool significantly eroded, profit-oil mechanics dominate. (c) Late-life block (>8 years past FID): WI effective take ≈ ORCA take + 5–10pp — cost pool nearly exhausted, nearly all revenues flow to profit-oil split. If you have the vendor’s data room access, request the “remaining unrecovered cost pool” — this single figure allows a precise adjustment rather than the rule-of-thumb range.
  4. Run Scenario Builder at your WI’s actual economics. Open Scenario Builder → set capex to your acquisition cost + WI share of ongoing development ($[entry premium] + $[WI development capex]) → set opex to your WI share of operating costs → set production to your WI share of gross plateau rate. The resulting IRR is your WI-adjusted IRR. Compare this to the Fiscal Compare greenfield IRR: the IRR delta is the all-in economic cost of the farm-in premium relative to a hypothetical greenfield entry in the same jurisdiction.

IC memo framing — greenfield vs. WI acquisition comparison:

  • Present as a two-column table. The correct IC structure: | Metric | Greenfield (ORCA Reference) | WI Acquisition (Farm-In) | Delta |. Rows: Fiscal mechanic; ORCA standardized take at $75/bbl; Estimated WI effective take (adjusted); Entry capex ($M, 100% WI); Time to first production (years); Project IRR at $75/bbl; IRR delta (greenfield → WI); Key assumption. This table lets the IC committee see both the fiscal quality of the jurisdiction and the premium cost of the acquisition route.
  • IC memo language template: “Government take for [Country] PSC benchmarked at [X]% (ORCA v274, standardized Deepwater profile, new-entry basis). Farm-in effective take estimated at [X+Y]% due to [cost pool at approximately [%] exhaustion / R-factor at [N] triggering [tier] profit-oil split]. WI acquisition IRR estimated at [Z]% on a [30]% WI basis, incorporating $[acquisition premium]M entry cost and $[ongoing capex]M WI development contribution (ORCA Scenario Builder v250, $75/bbl, [peak rate] bbl/d WI share, $[opex]/bbl). Compares to greenfield ORCA reference IRR of [W]% in the same jurisdiction. Farm-in premium reflects [strategic rationale: reserve replacement / acreage position / operator alignment / appraisal risk reduction].”

Rule of thumb — farm-in fiscal attractiveness by cost pool status:

  • Early entry (<3 years past FID): Effective take ≈ ORCA standardized ±2pp. IRR delta vs. greenfield is almost entirely driven by entry premium and geological risk reduction (not fiscal). Farm-in competes on a near-equivalent fiscal basis to organic exploration — entry premium must be justified by reserve certainty or operational control.
  • Mid-life entry (3–8 years): Effective take ≈ ORCA + 3–6pp. Fiscal penalty is material but usually offset by eliminated exploration and FID risk. The key IC question is whether the IRR is still >10% (or company hurdle) after the take uplift. PSC blocks with low profit-oil splits (45/55 contractor-favorable) tolerate this better than high-government-split PSCs.
  • Late-life entry (>8 years): Effective take ≈ ORCA + 5–10pp. The fiscal case is usually challenged — only compelling if production is long-plateau (reservoir-driven), if the acquisition price reflects a steep discount, or if the strategic rationale (operational control, block consolidation) outweighs the fiscal penalty. ORCA’s IRR figure should not be used as-is for late-life blocks — always use Scenario Builder with a truncated production profile.

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). See also FAQ A37 (IC capital allocation memo workflow — full 5-step process), FAQ A70 (R-factor PSC mechanics and tier structure), FAQ A59 (cross-project-type capital allocation), FAQ A63 (carry structure and working interest mechanics), FAQ A90 (project-scale calibration), FAQ A91 (portfolio blended take).

A93. ORCA shows a Price Swing figure for each country. What exactly does it measure, how do I interpret it for IC analysis, and what swing threshold should trigger a flag in a capital allocation recommendation?

Short answer: Price Swing measures the percentage-point change in government take between $50/bbl and $100/bbl using the platform’s standardized reference project. A high swing means the regime is structurally progressive — the government captures a larger share of contractor upside at high prices. For IC analysis, Swing >20pp signals a regime where your $75/bbl base-case IRR substantially overstates contractor returns in a $50/bbl downside scenario. Swing <8pp signals a flat regime where the contractor bears price risk symmetrically.

What Price Swing measures: Swing = Govt Take @$100/bbl − Govt Take @$50/bbl (both computed on the same standardized reference project). A 25pp swing means that at $50/bbl the government takes 50% and at $100/bbl the government takes 75% — the government’s share rises 25pp as the price doubles. Progressive regimes are often designed this way deliberately (R-factor PSCs, PRRT, sliding-scale royalties). The question for IC analysis is whether the base-case IRR is being computed at the correct price and whether the price sensitivity is adequately disclosed.

What drives high vs. low Price Swing:

  • High Swing (>20pp) — progressive regimes: R-factor PSCs (Angola, Nigeria OPL, Azerbaijan ACG-type) where profit-oil tiers accelerate at higher cumulative receipts; PRRT/resource rent tax regimes (Australia, Papua New Guinea) where the RRT threshold activates above a return hurdle; sliding-scale royalties (USA GoM, Canada, Norway SPT). These regimes capture commodity upside for the state — the contractor participates in price upside at a declining share.
  • Low Swing (<8pp) — flat/neutral regimes: Simple royalty-plus-CIT concessions with flat rate royalty and a standard CIT rate (many African onshore concessions, Central/Eastern European concessions, small frontier producers). In these regimes, the government share is largely fixed regardless of price. The contractor captures most of the price upside (and downside).
  • Moderate Swing (8–20pp) — mildly progressive: Standard PSCs without R-factor (flat profit-oil split), mild sliding-scale royalties, or concessions with windfall provisions. These regimes offer a middle path — meaningful contractor upside participation without the extreme fiscal drag of PRRT or R-factor regimes at $100+/bbl.

4-step IC workflow using Price Swing:

  1. Run Fiscal Compare at $75/bbl and note the Swing column. Flag any country with Swing >20pp for step 2. Countries with Swing <8pp pass through without adjustment — the $75/bbl take figure is representative across a wide price range.
  2. For high-Swing countries (>20pp): run Fiscal Compare at $50/bbl to stress-test the downside. A country that ranks 8th at $75/bbl may rank 20th at $50/bbl if it has high Swing. Use the Fiscal Compare 4-Price Export (XLSX) to see the full ranking at $50, $75, $100, and $125 simultaneously — the quickest way to identify which countries’ IC rankings are price-deck-dependent.
  3. Use Scenario Builder to isolate the Swing driver. Select the high-Swing country in Scenario Builder → run at $50/bbl and $100/bbl → compare IRRs. A 10% IRR at $75 that drops to 4% at $50 and rises to 18% at $100 signals a regime with high price beta — volatile but potentially lucrative at high oil prices.
  4. Disclose Swing explicitly in the IC memo. Standard language: “Government take of [X]% at $75/bbl (ORCA v274, standardized Deepwater profile). Price Swing of [Y]pp indicates a [progressive/flat/mildly progressive] fiscal regime: take ranges from [X-Y/2]% at $50/bbl to [X+Y/2]% at $100/bbl. Base-case IRR of [Z]% at $75/bbl declines to [Z-N]% at $50/bbl per Scenario Builder sensitivity. Contractor economics are [strongly/modestly/minimally] exposed to oil price risk relative to a flat-royalty benchmark.”

Rule of thumb — Swing thresholds for IC flagging:

  • Swing <8pp (flat): No IC adjustment required. The $75/bbl take figure is representative across $50–$100/bbl. Examples: Central/Eastern European concessions (Estonia 29.7%, Lithuania 28.4%). The contractor bears price risk symmetrically.
  • Swing 8–20pp (moderate): Disclose the range in the IC memo. Run the $50/bbl downside in Scenario Builder. The ranking shift at $50 vs. $75 is typically 2–5 positions in a 10-country shortlist — meaningful but not disqualifying. Examples: standard West Africa PSC (Angola 52.7% at $75, ~65% at $100).
  • Swing >20pp (highly progressive): Flag explicitly. Re-run Fiscal Compare at $50/bbl. Present both the $75 and $50 rankings in the IC appendix. High-Swing regimes (Australia PRRT, Norway SPT, USA GoM sliding royalty) require separate downside scenario analysis. At $50/bbl, a highly progressive regime can see IRR fall by 5–10pp relative to the $75 base case — enough to flip a marginal IC decision.
  • Swing >30pp (extreme): The $75/bbl take figure is unreliable as a sole IC metric. Present as a range: “Government take: [X]% at $50/bbl to [X+30]% at $100/bbl.” Consider whether the contractor has sufficient price upside under the regime to justify FID risk. Common in PRRT-heavy regimes at high-production-cost fields.

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). See also FAQ A36 (energy transition fiscal risk — Swing as transition signal), FAQ A43 (windfall profit tax modeling), FAQ A47 (R-factor mechanics and price sensitivity amplification), FAQ A56 ($50/bbl demand-shock stress test), FAQ A72 (4-signal tiebreaker: Price Swing/IRR/Breakeven/Stability Score).

A94. My target country uses a sliding-scale royalty tied to production rate (e.g., 5% below 5,000 bbl/d, 10% at 5,000–20,000 bbl/d, 15% above 20,000 bbl/d). ORCA’s reference project is 50,000 bbl/d. How do I determine which royalty tier applies to my project, and how do I model production-decline-driven tier migration in an IC submission?

Short answer: ORCA computes government take on a 50,000 bbl/d peak-rate reference project and typically captures the top royalty tier. If your project peaks below a tier threshold, ORCA will overstate effective royalty take — and therefore overstate government take. The correction is two steps: (1) identify which tier your peak production falls in, and (2) model a production-weighted average royalty across the project life in Scenario Builder, since production decline migrates a project through lower tiers in later years. The net adjustment is typically −2–8pp effective take for smaller fields, depending on the scale of the tier discount and the production profile.

Why this matters for IC analysis: Sliding-scale royalties are explicitly designed to incentivize smaller or higher-cost fields by applying lower rates at lower production. At 50,000 bbl/d, ORCA’s reference project hits the top-tier royalty in most jurisdictions. A 10,000 bbl/d satellite development may qualify for a tier that is 5–10pp lower, meaningfully improving contractor economics. If you use ORCA’s take figure without adjustment, your IC IRR will be understated — sometimes enough to flip a marginal investment recommendation.

Where sliding-scale royalties appear most often:

  • USA Gulf of Mexico (BOEM): Tiered royalty by water depth and production volume. Deepwater royalty suspension volumes (RSV) exempt the first N MMBoe from royalty entirely. Projects below the RSV threshold have effective royalty rate of 0% until exhausted.
  • Canada (Alberta, SAGD and conventional): Alberta’s sliding-scale royalty is price- and production-linked, ranging from ~5% at low production/price to 40% at high production/price. The effective rate for a 5,000 bbl/d SAGD operation at $75/bbl can be 15–20pp lower than a 50,000 bbl/d conventional heavy oil project.
  • Norway (production-linked sliding scale): Norway’s 78% marginal rate is not a production-sliding scale, but the investment tax credit (uplift) and the full deductibility of exploration costs effectively create a size-differential outcome. Smaller Norwegian fields benefit disproportionately from the uplift mechanism.
  • Malaysia (Petronas PSC tiers): Profit oil split in Malaysia PSCs uses a tiered R-factor that accelerates as the ratio of cumulative revenues to cumulative costs rises. Higher-production fields hit higher R-factor tiers faster, increasing the government share.
  • Australia (PRRT threshold): PRRT activates only after a project achieves a threshold rate of return. Smaller projects take longer to cross the PRRT threshold, so effective PRRT take over project life is lower than for a high-production, fast-payback project. ORCA captures this correctly for the 50,000 bbl/d reference but may overstate PRRT for smaller fields at lower production plateau rates.

4-step IC workflow for sliding-scale royalty adjustment:

  1. Identify the applicable royalty tier for your project’s peak production rate. In Regime Explorer, navigate to the target country and note the royalty rate and any footnotes indicating a tiered structure. If the Regime Explorer shows a single royalty rate (e.g., “12.5%”), check the Country Profile source notes (Evidence badge) to determine if this is a flat rate or a representative rate from a tiered schedule. Primary sources (production licenses, national oil law, regulator publications) will specify tier breakpoints.
  2. Compute the production-weighted average royalty across the project life. A simplified approach: if your project produces 15,000 bbl/d for 3 years (Tier 2: 10%) and then declines below 5,000 bbl/d for 7 years (Tier 1: 5%), the production-weighted royalty is approximately ‘[(15k×3×10%) + (5k×7×5%)] / [(15k×3) + (5k×7)]’ = 7.8%. Compare to the ORCA 50k reference which would apply 15% (Tier 3), overstating royalty by 7.2pp.
  3. Model the adjustment in Scenario Builder. In ORCA Scenario Builder, enter your project’s actual peak rate and profile. Note that Scenario Builder applies the DCF engine with ORCA’s stored royalty rate (which is the Tier 3 rate for the 50k reference project). To model the lower-tier rate: enter your capex and opex at actual project scale, then compare IRR results against a manual adjustment: reduce the government take by the delta between your weighted-average royalty and ORCA’s stored rate, expressed as a percentage-point reduction in total take. Alternatively, if the country’s royalty schedule is a flat percentage of revenue, the royalty impact on IRR is approximately ‘(ORCA rate − actual rate) × Oil Price × Production Volume / Total Project Value’ — typically 0.5–1.5pp IRR per 5pp royalty reduction.
  4. Disclose the tier basis explicitly in the IC memo. The correct IC framing (see template below) names the applicable tier, the ORCA reference-project assumption, and the adjustment made. Do not simply use the ORCA take figure without disclosure if your project peak rate falls below the reference project’s tier threshold.

Rule of thumb — royalty tier adjustment magnitude by project scale:

  • Project >35,000 bbl/d peak: ORCA reference-project tier is likely applicable. Effective royalty delta <2pp. Use ORCA figure with no adjustment required. Disclose: “Project peak rate consistent with ORCA 50k bbl/d reference; top royalty tier applicable throughout plateau.”
  • Project 10,000–35,000 bbl/d peak: Project may straddle tier boundaries. Production-weighted average royalty likely 2–5pp below ORCA reference rate. Run Scenario Builder at actual peak rate. Disclose tier basis.
  • Project <10,000 bbl/d peak (small field / satellite / incremental): Project likely qualifies for Tier 1 or 2 royalty throughout most of its life. Delta from ORCA reference may be 5–10pp effective royalty reduction. ORCA take figure requires explicit tier adjustment. Do not use without disclosure.
  • Royalty-free thresholds (USA GoM RSV, UK marginal field relief, some frontier incentive programs): First-N-barrel royalty suspensions are not captured in ORCA’s standard take figure. The effective royalty for a project qualifying for RSV/marginal relief may be 0% for the first several years, reducing lifetime effective take by 5–15pp depending on field size relative to the threshold volume.

IC memo language template: “Government take of [X]% for [Country] reflects ORCA v274 (Aug 2026) standardized reference project (50,000 bbl/d peak Deepwater, $1.2B capex, $15/bbl opex). [Country]’s royalty schedule is production-tiered: [Tier 1: Y% at <[N1] bbl/d / Tier 2: Z% at [N1]–[N2] bbl/d / Tier 3: W% at >[N2] bbl/d]. This project peaks at [peak rate] bbl/d and is expected to remain in [Tier 1/2] throughout plateau, with production-weighted average royalty estimated at [adjusted rate]% over project life (vs. ORCA reference rate of [W]%). Adjusted effective government take: approximately [X − delta]%, or [delta]pp below ORCA benchmark. IRR adjusted upward by approximately [IRR delta]pp from ORCA Scenario Builder result of [SB IRR]% to [adjusted IRR]% at actual project scale. See Appendix [J] for full production-tier royalty schedule and annual royalty calculation.”

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). See also FAQ A90 (project-scale calibration for smaller fields), FAQ A93 (Price Swing and progressive regime interpretation), FAQ A42 (cost recovery cap sensitivity), FAQ A41 (IRR DCF model specification — reference project parameters).

A95. My investment committee applies a 12–15% hurdle rate, but ORCA computes IRR via a standardized 10% discount rate. Does ORCA’s 10% discount rate affect the IRR figures I see in Explorer and Scenario Builder — and how do I reconcile ORCA’s standardized IRR with my firm’s cost of capital in an IC memo?

Short answer: ORCA’s IRR is not affected by the 10% discount rate assumption. IRR is the rate at which NPV = 0, determined by 60-iteration bisection of the project’s annual cash flows — the computation solves for the rate itself, so no assumed discount rate enters the IRR calculation. Compare ORCA’s IRR directly to your firm’s hurdle rate: if ORCA IRR exceeds your hurdle, the project passes at the standardized reference inputs. The 10% rate does affect ORCA’s NPV and Breakeven figures, which are evaluated at 10% by construction — for NPV-based metrics, disclose the 10% basis and note the approximate adjustment for your firm’s discount rate.

What ORCA’s 10% discount rate affects — and what it does not:

  • IRR (not affected): The Explorer IRR column and Scenario Builder IRR output are the rates at which the project’s discounted cash flows equal zero. The 10% rate is not an input to this computation — it is the output of a bisection that varies the discount rate until NPV = 0. ORCA IRR is directly comparable to your firm’s hurdle rate without any adjustment.
  • NPV (affected): ORCA’s NPV figures are discounted at 10%. At a higher firm discount rate (e.g., 12%), the NPV will be lower. The gap increases for projects with back-loaded cash flows (deepwater PSCs, PRRT-exposed Australia). Rule of thumb: each 1pp increase in discount rate reduces NPV by approximately 3–7% for a 15-year reference project, depending on cash flow timing.
  • Breakeven (affected): ORCA’s Breakeven price is the oil price at which NPV = 0 at a 10% discount rate. At a higher firm discount rate, the true breakeven price will be higher. For long-plateau deepwater projects, each 1pp increase in discount rate adds approximately $1–3/bbl to the breakeven threshold.

4-step IC workflow — reconciling ORCA IRR with firm hurdle rate:

  1. Use ORCA IRR as the regime ranking metric. In Explorer or Fiscal Compare, sort countries by IRR (74/185 countries have IRR data). This ranking is valid regardless of your firm’s discount rate — the regime ordering does not change when the hurdle rate changes, only the pass/fail threshold does.
  2. Apply your firm’s hurdle rate as a binary filter. Any country with ORCA IRR below your hurdle rate fails at standardized reference inputs. Note this does not preclude project-specific inputs from clearing (smaller capex, higher production rate, gas-equivalent pricing). Run Scenario Builder at actual project parameters if the IRR is within 3pp of the hurdle.
  3. For NPV-based IC metrics, note the 10% basis explicitly. If your IC committee requires NPV/barrel or NPV/project at your firm’s discount rate, use the Scenario Builder XLSX export and apply your discount rate to the annual net cash flow column. As an approximation: at [Y]% discount rate, NPV ≈ ORCA NPV × (1 − [(Y − 10%) × 4.5]), where 4.5 reflects the modified duration of a typical 15-year upstream project (adjust for project life and front-loaded vs. back-loaded cash flow profiles).
  4. Disclose both rates in the IC memo. The correct IC framing names the ORCA standardization basis AND your firm’s hurdle rate. See the template below.

Rule of thumb — IRR margin over firm hurdle rate:

  • IRR < hurdle rate: Project does not clear threshold at ORCA’s standardized reference inputs. Run Scenario Builder at project-specific inputs (actual capex, peak rate, opex) before concluding a fail.
  • IRR exceeds hurdle by 1–5pp (marginal): Disclose the margin explicitly. Run Scenario Builder at $60/bbl and +25% capex overrun to confirm the project still clears at downside inputs. See FAQ A88 (capex overrun sensitivity) and FAQ A63 (composite viability screen).
  • IRR exceeds hurdle by 5–10pp (comfortable): Standard IC disclosure. The regime is a viable allocation candidate. Regime ranking by ORCA IRR is the appropriate primary lens for multi-country comparisons.
  • IRR exceeds hurdle by >10pp (robust): Strong regime economics. Focus IC analysis on Price Swing (progressive regime risk at high prices) and Reform Risk — fiscal stability becomes the dominant risk factor at this IRR margin.

IC memo language template: “ORCA IRR for [Country] is [X]% at $75/bbl (10% discount rate basis, standardized Deepwater reference project — ORCA v274, Aug 2026; see FAQ A41 for model specification: $1.2B capex, 50k bbl/d, $15/bbl opex, 60-iteration bisection). This firm applies a [Y]% hurdle rate for [onshore / deepwater / frontier] projects; ORCA IRR exceeds our hurdle rate by [X − Y]pp at the $75/bbl reference price. At $60/bbl (Scenario Builder sensitivity): IRR [Z]% — [clears / fails to clear] the [Y]% hurdle. ORCA NPV at 10% discount rate: $[A]M. For project-specific IRR at actual economics ($[capex]M / [peak rate] bbl/d / $[opex]/bbl opex), see Appendix [K].”

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). See also FAQ A41 (IRR DCF model specification — 60-iteration bisection, 10% discount rate, reference project parameters), FAQ A87 (country risk premium adjustment — how to layer political risk into the discount rate or hurdle), FAQ A63 (Breakeven + IRR composite project viability screen), FAQ A88 (capex overrun sensitivity for marginal projects).

A96. ORCA’s DCF engine computes government take from statutory fiscal parameters — but many upstream deals require a signature bonus or other upfront payment at block award. How do I adjust ORCA’s government take to reflect the all-in fiscal burden including bonuses and upfront payments?

Short answer: ORCA does not model signature bonuses, training bonuses, or capacity-building contributions — these vary by licensing round and contract negotiation, not by statutory fiscal regime, so they cannot be systematically parameterized. To account for them in an IC memo, convert the bonus to a take-equivalent using NPV: divide the bonus payment by project NPV at your price scenario, then add to ORCA’s statutory take. A $200M signature bonus on a $1.2B capex deepwater project adds approximately 2.5–4.5pp to effective take depending on price and project life.

What upfront payments ORCA does and does not capture:

  • Not captured (adjust manually): Signature bonuses (block award payment, $50M–$2B range for major deepwater); training bonuses (common Nigeria/Angola — $5–30M/year); capacity-building contributions (Nigeria NNPC, Iraq INOC — $5–50M lump sum); production bonuses tied to milestone thresholds (e.g., $50M at first oil, $100M at 50k bbl/d — common in West Africa PSCs).
  • Captured (no adjustment needed): Annual surface fees and rentals (included in statutory cost structure where documented); NOC carried working interest (modeled in profit oil split mechanics); cost recovery cap (modeled directly in PSC DCF); income tax on profit oil (modeled in CIT layer); production bonuses defined in the statutory model PSC are captured where sourced.

4-step IC workflow — bonus-adjusted effective take:

  1. Identify the bonus quantum. Source from the signed PSC, IOC press release, or regulatory disclosure. For exploratory comparisons where the specific bonus is unknown, use the country’s historical licensing round range: Nigeria deepwater ($200–600M), Angola deepwater ($100–400M), Iraq TSC ($5–50M), Mozambique Area 1-type ($100–300M).
  2. Convert to NPV-equivalent take uplift. Formula: Bonus Take Uplift (pp) ≈ (Bonus ÷ Project NPV at base price) × 100. Use Scenario Builder at your project-specific inputs to get NPV (export XLSX, or read from the Scenario Builder output panel). A $200M bonus on a project with $1.5B NPV at $75/bbl adds 13.3pp to effective take. A $50M bonus on the same project adds 3.3pp.
  3. Compute all-in effective take. All-In Take ≈ ORCA Government Take + Bonus Take Uplift. For recurring annual payments (training bonus, capacity-building), PV the payment stream at your firm’s discount rate before dividing by NPV. A $20M/year training bonus for 5 years at 12% hurdle rate ≈ $72M PV — treat as equivalent to a $72M signature bonus for the uplift calculation.
  4. Disclose in the IC memo with ORCA as the base. Show ORCA statutory take as the regime baseline and add the bonus uplift as a contract-specific line item with sourcing. This separates regime risk (which ORCA benchmarks against 185 countries) from deal-specific terms (which the IC must vet independently).

Rule of thumb — bonus materiality by deal size:

  • <$50M bonus (<4% of capex on reference project): Generally immaterial (<1pp take uplift on a $1.2B NPV project at $75/bbl). Disclose but do not adjust the headline take figure in the IC summary.
  • $50–$200M bonus (4–17% of capex): Moderate. Adds 1–5pp effective take. Include as a line item in the IC summary table. Countries in this range: most African PSCs, Southeast Asia frontier blocks.
  • >$200M bonus (>17% of capex): Material. Adds 5–15+pp effective take and can shift the regime ranking in a multi-country allocation. Requires explicit all-in take calculation before IC comparison. Common in Nigeria deepwater and Iraq service contracts.

IC memo language template: “ORCA v274 (Aug 2026) reports government take for [Country] of [X]% (standardized Deepwater reference project: $1.2B capex, 50k bbl/d peak, $15/bbl opex). This contract requires a signature bonus of $[B]M payable at block award. Converting to NPV-equivalent at $75/bbl ($[NPV]M project NPV per Scenario Builder): bonus adds approximately [B÷NPV×100]pp to effective take, yielding all-in effective government take of approximately [X + uplift]%. [If training bonus applies:] Annual training bonus of $[T]M/year for [Y] years is valued at $[PV]M (PV at [hurdle]% discount rate) and adds an additional [PV÷NPV×100]pp. All-in effective take including upfront obligations: approximately [total]%. ORCA statutory take of [X]% is used for regime benchmarking; all-in effective take of [total]% reflects this specific contract’s negotiated terms.”

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). See also FAQ A69 (ring-fencing and license-level fiscal structure), FAQ A32 (state equity carried vs. paying WI — the other common PSC uplift not in headline take), FAQ A77 (local content requirements as fiscal uplift), FAQ A63 (composite project viability screen — including all-in take in the three-metric filter), FAQ A41 (IRR DCF model specification — reference project parameters).

A98. An exploration block requires a minimum work program (MWP) of 2 seismic surveys and 3 wells in Years 1–5. ORCA does not model MWP obligations. How do I incorporate the committed exploration spend into government take and IRR analysis for an IC submission on an undrilled block?

Short answer: ORCA models a producing reference project — it does not model sunk exploration or MWP carry costs. For an undrilled block, the MWP is a committed expenditure that must be added to the project capex base before computing all-in IRR. A 3-well MWP at $40M/well ($120M committed) on a $600M development capex block raises effective capex by 20% and reduces IRR by approximately 1.5–3pp depending on success case timing. The IC memo must disclose MWP as a risk-adjusted sunk cost — not a contingent spend.

Three MWP cost structures and how they interact with fiscal take:

  • Firm MWP (non-relinquishable): All wells must be drilled regardless of results. Total committed spend enters the IRR denominator as guaranteed capex. Under a PSC with cost recovery, exploration wells are typically cost-recoverable if a commercial discovery is made — but if the block is relinquished dry, the spent MWP capital is entirely lost with no recovery. Under a concession, exploration costs are capitalized and may generate tax deductions even in a failure scenario (jurisdiction-dependent).
  • Contingent MWP (earn-in / phased): Phase 1 MWP (e.g., 2D seismic + 1 well) must be completed; Phase 2 (2 additional wells) is optional and triggered only if Phase 1 shows hydrocarbons. The firm Phase 1 spend enters all IC scenarios; Phase 2 enters only the success case. This structure allows IC analysis on a probability-weighted basis (P10/P50/P90 well outcome × phase obligation).
  • Cash MWP guarantee (bank letter of credit or cash bond): Some host governments require a cash deposit equal to the estimated MWP cost, which is forfeited if the program is not completed. This is a working capital cost, not a sunk capital cost — it must be modeled as a cash outflow at block award and an inflow at program completion. The timing gap affects NPV even if all wells are drilled.

4-step IC workflow — adjusting ORCA take for MWP obligations:

  1. Identify the MWP structure. Read the PSC/concession agreement MWP clause. Determine: (a) firm vs. contingent; (b) exploration wells vs. seismic-only phases; (c) whether a cash bond or bank guarantee is required. Firm wells at $30–80M each are the primary IRR driver; seismic programs at $5–15M are secondary.
  2. Cost-recover or expense the MWP under the fiscal regime. For PSCs: determine whether exploration costs are cost-recoverable post-discovery (most PSCs: yes, up to the cost recovery cap) and whether the cost recovery begins in Year 1 of production (creates a timing NPV gap even on success). For concessions: determine whether exploration capex is deductible against CIT in the year incurred or capitalized and depreciated (depreciation schedule per A86). ORCA’s reference project starts at plateau production — exploration cost timing is not modeled. Adjust manually.
  3. Run the Scenario Builder with MWP-adjusted capex. Open Scenario Builder, increase Total Capex input by the firm MWP spend (e.g., reference project $1,200M + $120M firm MWP = $1,320M adjusted capex). Run at your base-case oil price. The IRR difference vs. the unadjusted ORCA run is the “MWP IRR drag” — the exploration carry cost embedded in the decision. For PSC blocks, also note the Breakeven uplift: MWP-adjusted Breakeven = ORCA Breakeven + (MWP NPV cost ÷ reference production NPV) × $75/bbl equivalent.
  4. Probability-weight the IC scenarios. The MWP is committed regardless of outcome.
