Present three IC cases: (a) Dry hole / relinquishment — MWP capex fully lost, zero production recovery, IRR = −100%; (b) Sub-commercial discovery — MWP partially recovered depending on regime; (c) Commercial discovery — full cost recovery per ORCA fiscal model + MWP capex recovered under PSC CR cap. Probability-weight using geological risking (Pg) from competent petroleum evaluator. Expected-value IRR = Pg × Success IRR + (1−Pg) × Failure IRR. Disclose Pg assumption in IC memo with source.

Rule of thumb — MWP materiality by block type:

  • Frontier deepwater (high MWP cost, high uncertainty): MWP of 2–3 ultra-deepwater wells at $60–100M each can equal 10–25% of development capex. Exploration risk dominates. IRR drag: 3–6pp at Pg = 30%. Require risk-adjusted IRR ≥15% at base-case price before recommending IC approval.
  • Proven basin near-field (low MWP, high success probability): MWP may be 1 appraisal well at $15–25M into a mapped structure with Pg = 60–80%. IRR drag: 0.5–1.5pp. MWP is not the binding constraint — fiscal take and development economics dominate. ORCA Fiscal Compare is directly applicable with minor MWP adjustment.
  • Cash bond guarantee structures: A $50M cash bond on a $500M NPV project costs approximately 0.3–0.5pp IRR in financing cost (opportunity cost of tied capital, 2–3 year bond term). Disclose as working capital note; do not embed in statutory take figure.
  • PSC vs. concession MWP treatment: Under a PSC with cost recovery, a successful well’s MWP cost enters the cost recovery pool and reduces profit oil the government receives — partially offsetting the MWP IRR drag. Under a concession, the exploration deduction is taken against CIT only, providing less full cost offset. Effective MWP drag is typically 0.5–1.5pp higher for concessions than for PSCs with the same well cost, because the PSC CR mechanism returns more capital to the contractor pre-profit split.

IC memo language template: “Government take for [Country] per ORCA v274 (Aug 2026): [X]% at $75/bbl (standardized 50k bbl/d Deepwater profile, reference project). This block is undrilled with a firm MWP of [N] wells ([estimated cost: $[Y]M]). ORCA take reflects the development-stage fiscal regime only. Adjusted development IRR including MWP capex ($[Y]M added to $1,200M ORCA reference): [W]% at $75/bbl (Scenario Builder run, standardized profile). Geological risking (Pg): [P]% per [Source]. Probability-weighted IRR: [Z]%. Breakeven uplift from MWP: approximately $[B]/bbl. MWP Phase 1 cost-recoverable under PSC CR cap of [CR]% if commercial discovery confirmed [if applicable]. MWP cash bond of $[C]M required at block award [if applicable]; modeled as working capital outflow recovered at [Year N] program completion. Recommend: [proceed / further evaluation / decline] subject to [conditions].”

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). MWP cost benchmarks: Wood Mackenzie Upstream Cost Database (2024); Rystad UCube well cost estimates (2024); IHS Markit Global Exploration Database. Geological risking methodology: SPE-PRMS 2018 §3.4 (resource classification and risking). See also FAQ A41 (IRR DCF model specification — reference project basis); FAQ A86 (depreciation / capital allowance timing — affects exploration cost deductibility); FAQ A96 (signature bonus adjustment — another front-loaded cost not in ORCA statutory take); FAQ A57 (government take exclusions — other off-balance-sheet fiscal burdens).

A97. ORCA computes government take assuming USD realization of all contractor revenues — but several producing countries impose foreign exchange controls that force profit oil conversion at a controlled rate below the market rate. How do I quantify this “FX take equivalent” and disclose it in an IC submission?

Short answer: ORCA does not model FX convertibility risk — the platform assumes USD-equivalent realization of all fiscal cash flows. In countries with hard currency controls, the contractor’s effective take is higher than the statutory ORCA figure because part of contractor revenues are surrendered at a below-market official rate. A 15% parallel-to-official exchange rate spread on 100% profit oil conversion can add 2–6pp to effective government take, depending on oil price and the revenue/cost split.

Two distinct FX risk types for IC disclosure:

  • Conversion risk (affects take directly): Profit oil or export revenue must be surrendered at the central bank official rate. The discount to market rate is a direct reduction in contractor USD-equivalent revenue — equivalent to an additional implicit royalty. Angola (BNA rate), Nigeria (CBN-mandated Naira conversion for domestic crude), and Egypt (CBE repatriation queue) all create conversion risk.
  • Repatriation risk (affects timing/NPV, not take): Revenue is realized in USD but outward remittance is queued or capped. This does not alter the statutory take figure but does increase the effective discount rate required by the IC. Nigeria’s historical FPI queue (2016–2020) and Venezuela’s DICOM restrictions are examples.

Country-by-country FX regime classification (as of mid-2026):

  • USD-settled (no FX adjustment needed): Iraq (IOC payments in USD via SOMO/export pipeline), Guyana (SCC USD-denominated), Mozambique Area 1-type (LNG USD proceeds), most Gulf Cooperation Council concessions (Qatar, UAE, Kuwait).
  • Managed float with convertibility (<2pp adjustment): Norway (NOK/USD — freely convertible, minor hedging cost), UK (GBP/USD — freely convertible), Kazakhstan (KZT — KASE-rate conversion, historically within 3% of Reuters mid), Brazil (BRL — central bank-managed float, convertible).
  • Managed controls with spread (2–5pp effective take uplift): Angola (BNA official vs. informal USD rate — spread has ranged from 10–40% post-2022 kwanza float adjustment); Egypt (EGP CBE official rate — repatriation queue historically 60–180 days); Algeria (Sonatrach USD profit oil settled, but equipment imports subject to dinar controls — indirect cost uplift).
  • Hard controls or parallel market spread (>5pp effective take uplift): Nigeria (pre-2023 dual-rate — NAFEX vs. parallel spread reached 60% in 2022–2023; partially unified mid-2023 but convertibility remains restricted); Venezuela (DICOM rate — parallel spread historically 500%+; operations effectively dollarized but statutory framework retains bolivar conversion requirement); Myanmar (CBM official rate vs. kyat parallel).

4-step IC workflow — quantifying the FX take equivalent:

  1. Classify the FX regime. Determine whether the country is USD-settled, managed float, managed controls, or hard controls using IMF Article IV reports, central bank circulars, and IOC earnings releases (ExxonMobil/TotalEnergies Angola/Nigeria segment disclosures often cite realized FX rates).
  2. Quantify the conversion discount. FX Discount = (Official Rate − Market Rate) ÷ Market Rate. If the official rate is 1,200 NGN/USD and the market rate is 1,600 NGN/USD, the FX discount = 25%. The profit oil share subject to conversion determines the effective cash-flow haircut: FX Haircut = Contractor Profit Oil Revenue (USD) × Conversion Obligation (%) × FX Discount (%).
  3. Convert to take-equivalent uplift. FX Take Uplift (pp) ≈ FX Haircut ÷ Total Revenue × 100. At $75/bbl on a 50,000 bbl/d reference project ($1.37B annual revenue at plateau), a 25% spread on 40% profit oil conversion obligation ≈ $137M/year FX cost — equivalent to approximately 3–5pp on effective government take. Adjust for PSC vs. concession mechanics (profit oil timing, cost recovery offset).
  4. Disclose as a separate line item in the IC memo. Do not embed the FX adjustment in the ORCA take figure — show ORCA statutory take as the regime baseline and add the FX discount as a contract/country-specific adjustment with a sourced assumption. This preserves the cross-country comparability of the regime benchmark.

Rule of thumb — FX regime type to IC action:

  • USD-settled (Iraq, Guyana, most GCC): No adjustment required. Note in IC memo that FX risk is absent for this investment. Use ORCA take directly in capital allocation comparison.
  • Freely convertible (<2pp uplift): Note currency and convertibility; no take adjustment. May apply minor discount rate uplift (+0.5–1.0pp) for currency transaction costs if hedging is required.
  • Managed controls (Angola, Egypt — 2–5pp take uplift): Compute FX haircut using most recent central bank rate data; add to ORCA statutory take as “FX-adjusted effective take.” Flag as a material risk factor requiring IOC Treasury pre-FID sign-off on repatriation structure.
  • Hard controls or parallel market (pre-2023 Nigeria, Venezuela — >5pp uplift): FX risk is deal-defining, not incidental. Require a dedicated repatriation structure (escrow, offshore holding, natural hedge via local opex) before IC submission. Do not present the investment using ORCA take alone — the FX haircut can exceed the statutory take differential between competing jurisdictions.

IC memo language template: “Government take for [Country] per ORCA v274 (Aug 2026): [X]% at $75/bbl (standardized Deepwater profile). [Country] operates under a [USD-settled / managed float / managed controls / hard controls] FX regime. [If applicable:] Contractor profit oil of [Y]% is subject to [Z]% conversion obligation at the CBN/BNA/CBE official rate (current spread to market rate: approximately [N]%). Estimated FX take equivalent: approximately [M]pp, yielding all-in effective take of approximately [X+M]%. The FX-adjusted IRR using Scenario Builder at $[adj]/bbl equivalent realization is [W]%, vs. pre-FX ORCA IRR of [Z]%. All-in FX haircut treated as a financing/treasury risk, not a fiscal regime parameter — ORCA statutory take of [X]% used for cross-country regime benchmarking. Recommend IOC Treasury review of repatriation structure prior to FID.”

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). FX regime data: IMF Article IV Consultation reports (2024–2025); Angola BNA Instrução 3/2020; Nigeria CBN circulars on FX unification (2023); Egypt CBE FX regulations (2024). See also FAQ A57 (government take exclusions — other off-balance-sheet fiscal burdens); FAQ A96 (signature bonus adjustment — another contract-specific take uplift not in ORCA statutory take); FAQ A77 (local content requirements); FAQ A87 (country risk premium / political risk adjustment — complementary to FX repatriation risk).

A99. Norway levies a CO₂ tax (~$195/tonne in 2026) on top of its petroleum CIT and SPT. The UK, Netherlands, Denmark, and Canada also impose carbon pricing on upstream E&P. ORCA does not model carbon levies. How do I quantify the carbon cost overlay on ORCA’s government take figure, and how do I disclose carbon-adjusted effective take in an IC submission?

Short answer: ORCA captures statutory fiscal take (royalties, CIT, SPT/PRRT, profit oil splits, NOC equity) but does not model carbon pricing levies. In Norway, the CO₂ tax adds approximately 2–5pp to effective government take at $75/bbl on a standard offshore project; UK ETS adds roughly 1–3pp; EU ETS in Netherlands/Denmark adds 1–2pp. Carbon costs are material, project-specific, and must be disclosed as a separate line item in any IC submission that benchmarks a carbon-priced jurisdiction against a non-carbon-priced peer.

Four carbon pricing mechanisms relevant to upstream E&P (2026):

  • Norway CO₂ tax (per tonne on combustion + flaring, offshore): NOK 1,140/tonne (~$105) in 2024, rising to approximately NOK 2,000+ (~$195) by 2030 under Norway’s carbon escalation path. Applies to all combustion sources on the NCS (drilling, compression, processing). A 50k bbl/d offshore installation burning 800 tonnes CO₂/day generates ~$56M/year carbon tax at $195/tonne. Combined with Norway’s SPT (56%) and CIT (22%) plus the SPT-based CO₂ tax offset (CO₂ tax is deductible in the SPT base), the net after-SPT-offset CO₂ burden is approximately 44% of the gross CO₂ tax levy (since SPT offsets 56%). Effective incremental take: ~2–4pp at $75/bbl reference project.
  • UK ETS (Emissions Trading Scheme, from Jan 2024, offshore E&P included): UK ETS carbon price ~£35–50/tonne ($44–63) in 2024–2025 for offshore E&P after Offshore Petroleum Regulator for Environment and Decommissioning (OPRED) confirmed E&P inclusion. The UK North Sea Transition Deal target (by 2025: 50% reduction in upstream emissions vs. 2018 baseline) does not reduce the ETS obligation, only the volume of allowances consumed. At £45/tonne and 800 tonnes/day CO₂, annual cost: ~$25M/year. After RFCT/SC/EPL deductibility (~75% combined marginal rate in EPL period), net cost: ~$6M/year. Effective incremental take: ~1–2pp at $75/bbl reference.
  • EU ETS Phase IV (Netherlands, Denmark, Belgium — offshore E&P covered): EU ETS Phase IV carbon price ~€60–80/tonne ($66–88) in 2024. Netherlands and Danish upstream operators purchase allowances through the CSRD/ETS framework. Shell Brunei/NAM and Equinor Denmark operations are covered. Net cost after CIT deductibility (~25% CIT rate): ~75% of gross ETS cost flows through to contractor. Effective incremental take: ~1–2pp on standard offshore reference project.
  • Canada Output-Based Pricing System (OBPS — Alberta/BC offshore and E&P facilities >50k tCO₂/yr): Carbon price CAD $80/tonne (2024), rising to CAD $170/tonne by 2030 under federal schedule. OBPS applies to facilities above the output-based benchmark; efficient operators pay only the marginal above-benchmark emissions. Most major oilsands E&P operations exceed the threshold; conventional E&P varies by facility size. After Alberta CIT deductibility (8% provincial + 15% federal), net incremental take: ~1–3pp for high-emission oilsands; <1pp for conventional offshore-equivalent.

4-step IC workflow — carbon-adjusted effective take:

  1. Identify whether the jurisdiction has upstream carbon pricing. Use ORCA Country Profile as the fiscal baseline; carbon pricing is a separate regulatory layer not captured in the statutory fields. Check: Norway (CO₂ tax law §3 Petroleum Tax Act), UK (ETS Directive 2024 offshore inclusion order), Netherlands (EU ETS Act), Denmark (EU ETS), Canada (Greenhouse Gas Pollution Pricing Act). Most other ORCA jurisdictions (West Africa, Middle East, Southeast Asia) have no upstream carbon price obligation as of 2026.
  2. Estimate the gross carbon cost for your reference project. Gross Carbon Cost ($M/yr) = Project Emissions (tCO₂/yr) × Carbon Price ($/tonne). Project emissions benchmark: offshore deepwater ~300–600 tCO₂/day; North Sea platform ~600–1,200 tCO₂/day (higher gas processing); oilsands in-situ ~0.05–0.12 tCO₂/bbl produced. At ORCA’s 50k bbl/d reference project with an offshore Norway intensity of 18 kg CO₂/bbl (NCS average per NPD): annual emissions ≈ 328k tCO₂ ⇒ gross CO₂ tax at $195/tonne = $64M/year.
  3. Apply the after-tax deductibility offset. Carbon levies are generally deductible against CIT/SPT in the countries where they apply. Net Carbon Cost = Gross Cost × (1 − Marginal Tax Rate on Deductible Expenses). For Norway: SPT + CIT marginal rate = 78%; after offset = 22% of gross. Net annual CO₂ cost at ORCA reference project: $64M × 22% = $14M/year. Carbon Take Uplift (pp) ≈ Net Annual Carbon Cost ÷ Annual Project Revenue × 100. At $75/bbl and 50k bbl/d: annual revenue $1.37B; uplift ≈ $14M ÷ $1,370M = ~1.0pp incremental take. For UK: marginal rate ~75% EPL-era; net cost ~25% of gross; incremental take ~0.5–1.5pp.
  4. Disclose in the IC memo as a separate carbon overlay line. Do not embed the carbon adjustment in the ORCA statutory take figure — preserve cross-country comparability of the regime benchmark. Show: (a) ORCA statutory take baseline; (b) carbon mechanism and price assumption; (c) project emissions estimate and source; (d) after-tax carbon cost; (e) all-in effective take. Flag that carbon prices are escalating in all four jurisdictions and the 2030 price path is material to long-life asset decisions. Request that your Sustainability/HSE team provide a site-specific emissions intensity estimate before FID.

Rule of thumb — carbon pricing impact by jurisdiction (2026 prices):

  • Norway (CO₂ tax ~$195/tonne, 2030 path): After SPT/CIT deductibility, net incremental take: 2–4pp at $75/bbl reference. Rising to 3–6pp if carbon price reaches $300/tonne by 2035 under progressive escalation path. This is the largest carbon pricing impact among ORCA jurisdictions — mandatory disclosure for any Norway comparison.
  • UK ETS (~£45/tonne, included in E&P from 2024): After RFCT/SC/EPL deductibility, net incremental take: 1–2pp at $75/bbl. Less material than Norway given lower carbon price, but note that the EPL creates a 75% marginal rate on deductibles — the deductibility offset is larger than in normal RFCT-only years, actually limiting the net carbon cost during the EPL period.
  • Netherlands / Denmark (EU ETS ~€70/tonne): Net incremental take: 1–2pp at $75/bbl after CIT deductibility. EU ETS price is lower than Norway CO₂ tax on a net basis, but the EU is targeting €150/tonne by 2035 — flag price escalation risk for project life beyond 10 years.
  • Canada OBPS (CAD $80–170/tonne, 2024–2030): Oilsands in-situ high-emission operations: 1–3pp incremental take. Conventional E&P and offshore-equivalent operations: <1pp. OBPS intensity benchmark provides partial relief for efficient operators — only above-benchmark emissions are priced. Do not assume full carbon price applies to all barrel production.
  • All other ORCA jurisdictions (West Africa, Middle East, SE Asia, most LATAM): No mandatory upstream carbon pricing as of 2026. Note: voluntary carbon offset programs in Indonesia, Nigeria, and Brazil do not constitute statutory take and need not be disclosed in ORCA-based IC comparisons.

IC memo language template: “Government take for [Country] per ORCA v274 (Aug 2026): [X]% at $75/bbl (standardized [profile] profile). [Country] imposes [Norway CO₂ tax / UK ETS / EU ETS / Canada OBPS] on upstream operations. At ORCA reference-project emissions intensity ([N] kg CO₂/bbl, [Source]), annual carbon levy (gross): approximately $[G]M at [Year] price of $[P]/tonne. After [SPT+CIT / RFCT+SC / CIT] deductibility ([M]% marginal rate), net annual carbon cost: approximately $[C]M. Carbon take-equivalent uplift: approximately [Y]pp. All-in effective take including carbon overlay: approximately [X+Y]%. Carbon price escalation path ([$P] in [Year] → $[P2] in 2030): flagged as upside fiscal risk for project life beyond 10 years; recommend IC scenario at 2030 carbon price for sensitivity. ORCA statutory take of [X]% used for cross-country regime benchmarking; carbon overlay disclosed as regulatory cost, not statutory fiscal parameter.”

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). Norway CO₂ tax: Norwegian Petroleum Tax Act §3 and Petroleum Activities Act; NPD Norwegian Continental Shelf emissions data (2024). UK ETS: OPRED Offshore Petroleum Regulator ETS inclusion order (Jan 2024); DESNZ UK ETS Authority price data. EU ETS Phase IV: European Commission ETS Directive 2003/87/EC as amended; EEX carbon price data. Canada OBPS: Environment and Climate Change Canada OBPS regulations (SOR/2019-266 as amended); AER Alberta Carbon Competitiveness Incentive Regulation. Emissions intensities: IEA Upstream Oil and Gas Emissions Database (2024). See also FAQ A36 (energy transition fiscal risk — broader transition screening framework); FAQ A43 (windfall profit taxes — price-triggered levies with similar IC disclosure structure); FAQ A56 ($50/bbl stress test — carbon pricing amplifies downside in high-emission regimes); FAQ A87 (country risk premium adjustment — complementary disclosure item in IC submissions).

A100. Several Indonesian and West African PSCs include a First Tranche Petroleum (FTP) clause — a percentage of gross production taken by the government before cost recovery. ORCA does not expose FTP as a separate line item. How does FTP affect contractor economics relative to ORCA’s stated take figure, and how do I adjust for it in an IC submission?

Short answer: FTP is a government “off the top” production share taken before cost recovery commences — it operates economically like an additional royalty applied to gross revenue. ORCA embeds FTP in its statutory take computation where present but does not expose it as a separate parameter. A PSC with 20% FTP is more sensitive to low-price scenarios than a no-FTP PSC with identical profit oil split, because FTP applies whether the project generates profit or not. IC memos for FTP-bearing PSC countries must disclose this above-the-line fiscal burden explicitly.

FTP mechanics by country — how it appears in major PSC jurisdictions:

  • Indonesia (pre-2017 conventional PSC, SKK Migas): Historical Pertamina/SKK Migas standard PSC terms included FTP of 20% of gross production before cost recovery. FTP is split between the government (typically 100% to NOC or 85/15 contractor share depending on contract generation). Post-2017 Gross Split regime (Decree 8/2017) eliminates FTP entirely — a primary reason Gross Split shows lower contractor exposure at low prices despite similar headline take at $75/bbl. ORCA models the dominant mechanic per contract: conventional PSC take includes FTP; the 19 Gross Split contracts in the database have no FTP component.
  • Nigeria (NNPC deepwater PSC, NUPRC): Standard deepwater PSC blocks include FTP of 10–20% of gross production, negotiated contract-by-contract. Older offshore blocks (OPL 209, 210, 211) carry 20% FTP; post-2005 JDZ blocks carry 10%. ORCA’s Nigeria PSC take embeds FTP but does not expose it separately. Cross-check: Nigeria deepwater take of ~65–72% at $75/bbl includes FTP as a component.
  • Angola (Sonangol deepwater PSC, ANPG): Sonangol PSC contracts (offshore pre-salt and Cabinda) typically include FTP of 10–15% of gross. Block 15 (ExxonMobil), Block 17 (TotalEnergies), and Block 31 (BP) all carry FTP layers. ORCA Angola PSC take (~68–72% at $75/bbl) includes FTP.
  • Malaysia (Petronas PSC, standard and marginal field): Petronas standard PSC includes FTP of 10% (standard blocks) or reduced to 5% for marginal field fiscal incentive contracts. R-factor tiers in Malaysia are applied after FTP deduction — meaning FTP effectively reduces the cumulative revenue base used to compute R, slightly accelerating R-factor progression. ORCA Malaysia take includes FTP in statutory computation.
  • No FTP jurisdictions (for comparison): Guyana Stabroek PSC, UK RFCT concession, Norway concession, most OECD concessions, most Latin American concessions, Namibia Orange Basin PSC — no FTP layer. Take comparisons between FTP and no-FTP PSCs overstate the no-FTP PSC’s fiscal attractiveness at low-price scenarios because cost recovery commences from dollar one of gross revenue.

4-step IC workflow — quantifying and disclosing FTP adjustment:

  1. Determine whether the target block carries FTP. Review the ORCA Country Profile source notes (Evidence badge) for “first tranche” or “FTP” references. Cross-reference the PSC term sheet if available from a data room or national regulator publication. For Indonesia: conventional PSC = FTP present (20%); Gross Split = FTP absent. For Nigeria/Angola: check block vintage — deepwater blocks awarded before 2010 typically carry 15–20% FTP; post-2010 blocks 10–15%.
  2. Quantify the FTP take-equivalent impact vs. a no-FTP PSC peer. FTP Take Uplift vs. No-FTP Peer (pp) ≈ FTP% × (Gross Revenue ÷ Total Project Lifecycle Revenue). For a standard 50k bbl/d project at $75/bbl, gross revenue in Year 1 = $1.37B; with 20% FTP, $274M goes to government before cost recovery. Take-equivalent uplift of 20% FTP vs. no-FTP at the reference project: approximately 10–15pp higher effective take for the FTP year — though lifetime take depends on how quickly cost recovery is achieved. Rule of thumb: 10% FTP ≈ +4–7pp lifetime effective take vs. no-FTP PSC peer; 20% FTP ≈ +8–15pp lifetime effective take vs. no-FTP PSC peer (range depends on capex/opex profile and price scenario).
  3. Stress-test at low prices in Scenario Builder. FTP-bearing PSCs are structurally more exposed to low-price scenarios because FTP cannot be deferred when prices fall. Run Scenario Builder at $40/bbl and $50/bbl. A 20% FTP at $40/bbl may exhaust contractor revenue before cost recovery begins in early project years — a situation that would not occur for a no-FTP PSC peer with the same headline take at $75/bbl. Compare IRR at $40/bbl between your FTP target and a no-FTP PSC comparator. If the IRR delta at $40/bbl is >5pp (FTP target lower), this is material for IC downside disclosure.
  4. Disclose in the IC memo as a named fiscal risk factor. FTP should not be hidden within the aggregate take figure for IC purposes. See memo language template below. State: (a) ORCA statutory take includes FTP at [N]%; (b) FTP-equivalent take uplift vs. no-FTP peers; (c) low-price sensitivity at $40/bbl; (d) whether FTP applies to both oil and associated gas (some contracts exempt associated gas from FTP). For Indonesian Gross Split candidates, note that FTP elimination vs. conventional PSC improves contractor low-price protection as a positive fiscal differentiator.

Rule of thumb — FTP impact on contractor economics by FTP level:

  • FTP = 0% (no FTP — Guyana Stabroek, UK, Norway, most OECD, Gross Split Indonesia): ORCA take figure is directly comparable to no-FTP PSC peers. No adjustment needed. At $40/bbl stress: all gross revenue available for cost recovery from Year 1.
  • FTP = 5–10% (standard deepwater PSC — Angola, Nigeria offshore, Malaysia standard): Contractor IRR approximately 1–3pp lower than a no-FTP PSC with identical profit oil split at $75/bbl. At $40/bbl stress: FTP consumes ~$5–10M/yr of additional revenue that would otherwise fund cost recovery. Disclose FTP rate; no separate Scenario Builder adjustment required for $75/bbl base case, but run $40/bbl stress.
  • FTP = 15–20% (high-FTP legacy PSC — Indonesia pre-2017 conventional, some Libya contracts): Contractor IRR approximately 3–6pp lower than a no-FTP PSC peer at $75/bbl. At $40/bbl stress: risk of negative contractor cash flow in plateau years despite positive statutory take regime. Mandatory Scenario Builder stress test at $40/bbl before IC submission. Flag as fiscal risk in IC executive summary.
  • FTP eliminated → Gross Split (Indonesia post-2017 Decree 8/2017): Compared to Indonesia conventional PSC: contractor low-price protection is structurally improved (no above-the-line government take before cost recovery). At $75/bbl headline take is similar; at $40/bbl Gross Split shows 5–10pp higher contractor revenue retention than conventional PSC. Disclose in IC memo as a fiscal quality differentiator for Gross Split blocks.

IC memo language template: “Government take for [Country] per ORCA v274 (Aug 2026): [X]% at $75/bbl (standardized [Deepwater/Onshore] profile). ORCA’s take figure for [Country] PSCs includes First Tranche Petroleum (FTP) of approximately [N]% of gross production, taken prior to cost recovery. FTP operates as an above-the-line government revenue stream that cannot be deferred or avoided through cost optimization — it applies irrespective of project profitability. The FTP-equivalent incremental take burden versus a no-FTP PSC peer is approximately [delta]pp at $75/bbl. At the $50/bbl stress scenario, FTP sensitivity increases to approximately [delta2]pp versus a no-FTP peer (higher sensitivity because FTP compresses the pre-cost-recovery revenue pool in low-price years). Analyst note: ORCA does not expose FTP as a separate parameter in Country Profile or Fiscal Compare views — the [X]% statutory take is the all-in figure including FTP. For a block-specific FTP adjustment, supplement the ORCA baseline with the applicable PSC term sheet FTP rate and run Scenario Builder downside at $40–50/bbl.”

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). Indonesia FTP: SKK Migas standard PSC terms; IHS Markit Indonesia Fiscal Survey (2024); Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources Decree 8/2017 (Gross Split — FTP elimination confirmed); PricewaterhouseCoopers Indonesia oil and gas fiscal guide. Nigeria FTP: NNPC/NUPRC standard PSC terms; Wood Mackenzie Nigeria Upstream Fiscal Study (2024); IHS Markit Nigeria Deepwater Fiscal Review. Angola FTP: Sonangol/ANPG standard deepwater PSC terms; EY Angola Oil & Gas Guide (2024); Wood Mackenzie Angola Fiscal Analysis. Malaysia FTP: Petronas standard PSC terms; Wood Mackenzie Malaysia Fiscal Survey (2024); KPMG Malaysia Petroleum Fiscal Regime (2024). See also FAQ A42 (cost recovery cap — works in tandem with FTP: FTP reduces gross revenue before cost oil calculation, cost cap limits the remaining cost recovery); FAQ A47 (R-factor mechanics — in some PSCs, R-factor cumulative revenue is computed from revenue after FTP deduction); FAQ A59 (cross-project-type capital allocation — PSC vs. concession comparison: FTP amplifies PSC downside risk vs. royalty-concession peers); FAQ A93 (Price Swing — FTP amplifies progressive price sensitivity in high-FTP PSC jurisdictions).

A101. Several concession regimes — including Nigeria OML royalties and some LATAM production contracts — apply royalties on a sliding scale that varies with production volume or price. How does ORCA model sliding-scale royalties, and how should I adjust the stated government take for a production-profile-dependent sliding royalty when preparing an IC submission?

Short answer: Sliding-scale royalties vary the effective royalty rate with production volume tiers, cumulative output thresholds, or oil-price bands — so the government take figure is not fixed but depends on where the asset sits on its production curve. ORCA models a representative rate drawn from the dominant tier at the reference project’s standardised production scale (≈50k bbl/d peak, mid-life decline trajectory). Analysts preparing IC submissions must adjust the stated take for their target asset’s actual production profile, particularly for late-life acquisitions or fast-ramp developments where the effective production-weighted royalty diverges materially from ORCA’s reference-scale rate.

Where sliding-scale royalties apply — regime examples:

  • Nigeria OML (Petroleum Act Cap P10 / PIA 2021): Royalties slide on two axes. By water depth zone: 5% (deep offshore >1,000 m) → 12.5% (shallow offshore 200–1,000 m) → 20% (onshore/shelf ≤200 m). By volume tier for OML onshore: 0–2,000 bbl/d at 20%, 2,001–5,000 bbl/d at 22%, ≥5,001 bbl/d at 20% with various fiscal overlay adjustments under the PIA 2021 schedule. ORCA selects the applicable rate for the block’s water-depth zone and the dominant production tier at reference scale, meaning the take figure assumes sustained plateau-phase output in the highest-volume tranche.
  • Libya EPSA-IV: The royalty equivalent is embedded in the profit-oil split, which varies with the production plateau — early-production years carry a higher contractor share that shifts progressively toward the NOC (LNOC) as cumulative output rises. Government participation also ratchets with production milestones. ORCA models the plateau-phase dominant rate, so the stated take reflects peak-output fiscal terms rather than the blended lifecycle effective rate, which can be 5–10 pp higher for late-life or post-plateau acquisitions.
  • Peru / Colombia / Ecuador (LATAM sliding royalties): Peru applies a 5–20% royalty sliding by field daily production rate (Supreme Decree 017-2003-EM), with the lowest rates reserved for marginal fields producing <200 bbl/d. Colombia’s ANH royalty framework (Decree 4923/2011) imposes 12–25% sliding by production tranche: 8% on the first 5,000 bbl/d, stepping to 25% above 600,000 bbl/d. Ecuador applies a similar volume-tiered structure. ORCA models these at the reference-scale production rate, providing a regional comparator basis — but small-field or marginal-asset IC cases will see materially lower effective royalty than the ORCA figure implies.
  • Flat-royalty contrast (Norway, UK post-2003, most Middle East concessions): No sliding scale — the royalty is a fixed percentage of gross revenue regardless of production rate or price tier. Norway’s royalty was abolished in 2006; the UK abolished PRT for post-2003 licences; Gulf concessions typically levy a fixed 12.5–20% royalty. In these regimes, ORCA’s take figure is directly comparable across peers with no production-profile adjustment required. IC advantage: the government take number is production-profile-invariant.

4-step IC workflow — adjusting ORCA take for sliding-royalty regimes:

  1. Identify the royalty structure. Open the Country Profile tab in ORCA → locate the target block or regime. Check the Evidence badge for “sliding,” “production tier,” or “volume-based” annotations. If the badge shows a flat royalty rate with no tier notation, no adjustment is needed — proceed directly to IC submission with the ORCA take figure.
  2. Determine the production-profile trajectory. Classify the target asset: fast-ramp greenfield (production-weighted toward peak/high-tier phase), steady plateau (aligned with ORCA’s reference assumption), or late-life declining asset (production-weighted toward lower tiers as output falls through successive thresholds). The production-weighting determines whether the effective royalty sits above or below ORCA’s reference-scale rate.
  3. Compute the effective production-weighted royalty. Using the target asset’s year-by-year production forecast, calculate the volume-weighted average royalty rate across tiers over the evaluation period. Compare this to ORCA’s reference-scale rate. If the project peaks below the high-royalty threshold (e.g., a marginal Nigerian onshore field at <2,000 bbl/d), ORCA may overstate take. If the project is a large late-life asset declining through multiple tiers, ORCA may understate effective take because plateau-phase rates no longer apply.
  4. Disclose the adjustment in the IC memo. State ORCA’s reference-rate basis explicitly, the applicable sliding-scale range for the host regime, and your production-weighted effective royalty adjustment. Present the ORCA take as the benchmark and the adjusted take as the asset-specific estimate, with the delta clearly attributed to production-profile divergence from ORCA’s standardised reference project.

Rule of thumb — adjustment magnitude by royalty type:

  • Flat royalty (Norway, UK, most Gulf): No adjustment needed. ORCA take is production-profile-invariant. Use the stated figure directly in IC comparisons.
  • Volume-based sliding scale (Nigeria OML onshore, Peru, Colombia, Ecuador): Adjust take by ±2–6 pp depending on whether the target asset is ramp-up-weighted (effective royalty < ORCA reference, take overstated) or decline-phase-weighted (effective royalty > ORCA reference for assets declining through lower-volume higher-rate tranches, or < ORCA reference for assets declining below the high-tier threshold).
  • Price-based sliding scale (Russia MET pre-reform, some SPT regimes): The take figure moves with the oil-price tier rather than the production profile. Run the Scenario Builder at $50/bbl and $100/bbl to bracket the effective take range; use a price-weighted average aligned with your IC base-case price deck.
  • Complex hybrid (Libya EPSA-IV profit-oil tiers + participation ratchets): ORCA take is plateau-weighted. For late-life acquisitions where production has declined past plateau milestones, effective take may be 5–10 pp higher than the plateau-phase reference figure. Model the acquisition-period production forecast explicitly and adjust.

IC memo language template: “Government take for [Country] [OML/Block] per ORCA v274 (Aug 2026): [X]% at $75/bbl (standardised Deepwater/Onshore profile at ≈50k bbl/d peak). ORCA’s take figure reflects [flat / volume-sliding / price-sliding] royalty at the reference-scale production tier. [Country]’s royalty structure is [flat at N% / volume-based sliding from A% to B% across production tiers / price-linked sliding from A% at <$X/bbl to B% at >$Y/bbl]. For the target asset’s production profile ([describe: fast-ramp greenfield / sustained plateau / late-life declining through tier thresholds]), the effective production-weighted royalty is estimated at [Z]%, [equal to / N pp above / N pp below] the ORCA reference-scale rate. Adjusted take estimate: [adjusted]%. See Appendix [D] for Scenario Builder sensitivity at $50, $75, and $100/bbl.”

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). Nigeria Petroleum Act Cap P10 (2004); Petroleum Industry Act 2021 (PIA 2021 royalty schedule); Wood Mackenzie Nigeria Upstream Fiscal Study (2024); Peru Supreme Decree 017-2003-EM; Colombia ANH royalty regulations (Decree 4923/2011); Wood Mackenzie LATAM Fiscal Survey (2024); IHS Markit Global Upstream Fiscal and Royalty Guide. See also FAQ A41 (IRR DCF model specification), FAQ A61 (production-profile shape impact), FAQ A57 (government take exclusions), FAQ A82 (PRRT/SPT methodology).

A102. My IC committee wants a single government take figure for a country comparison table. ORCA shows government take at $75/bbl, but the country also has a signature bonus, surface rental fees, and a local content training levy. Should I include these in the reported government take, and how does ORCA treat non-tax fiscal costs in its take calculation?

Short answer: ORCA’s government take figure is a statutory take measure — it captures the contractual fiscal instruments that directly share revenue or profit between the contractor and the state: royalties, profit oil/gas splits, income tax, resource rent taxes, and state participation (NOC carried interest at field level). It does not include one-off payments (signature bonuses, work programme bonds), area-based fees (surface rentals, acreage fees), or indirect levies (local content training funds, community development obligations). For a standard country-comparison IC table, ORCA’s take is the right input. For an all-in fiscal burden analysis — where you are computing total value transferred to government including bonuses and levies — you must add those costs as a separate line item above the statutory take figure.

What ORCA government take includes (statutory fiscal take):

  • Royalties: Gross-revenue-based government share. Included in full, whether flat, sliding-scale, or volumetric. For sliding-scale regimes, ORCA models the dominant rate at the reference project’s production scale (see FAQ A101).
  • Cost recovery / profit oil split: In PSCs, the contractor recovers allowable costs before the profit oil split is applied. Both the cost recovery ceiling and the profit oil allocation to the state are captured in the DCF waterfall.
  • Corporate income tax (CIT) / petroleum income tax (PITA): Applied to taxable income after royalty and cost recovery deductions. Included at the statutory rate relevant to the upstream ring-fence.
  • Resource rent taxes (PRRT, SPT, RRT): Profit-uplift-based supplementary taxes triggered above threshold returns. Included in DCF (see FAQ A38 for PRRT/SPT methodology).
  • State participation (NOC carried or paying WI): Government share attributable to the NOC’s working interest in field economics, net of its cost obligations. Included at field level (see FAQ A32 and FAQ A61 for JV and ring-fence treatment).

What ORCA government take excludes (non-statutory fiscal costs):

  • Signature bonuses: One-off upfront payments on block award. These are capital costs to the contractor, not ongoing revenue-sharing instruments. They reduce contractor NPV but are excluded from government take metrics (see FAQ A96 for the NPV-equivalent uplift adjustment).
  • Work programme bonds / minimum work obligations (MWP): Contingent capital costs, not revenue-sharing instruments. Excluded from take (see FAQ A98 for MWP adjustment workflow).
  • Surface rentals / acreage fees: Typically <0.5% of NPV on commercial fields — excluded from government take as per international industry convention (see FAQ A57).
  • Local content levies / training funds / CDF: Indirect operating cost, not a fiscal instrument. Excluded from take but included as an opex uplift in all-in burden analysis (see FAQ A69).
  • Carbon pricing / emissions levies: Operating cost overlay excluded from statutory take. For jurisdictions with CO₂ tax (Norway, UK, EU), add as separate line (see FAQ A99).
  • Withholding taxes on dividends: Shareholder-level tax, not upstream fiscal instrument. Excluded from government take (see FAQ A57).

4-step IC workflow — building the right take figure for your IC table:

  1. Use ORCA take for regime comparison. In any table ranking countries by fiscal burden for bid evaluation or portfolio screening, use the ORCA government take figure directly. This is statutory take on a standardised basis — comparable across all 185 countries and fiscal mechanics on an apples-to-apples basis.
  2. Identify non-statutory items present in your target deal. Review the bid terms or PSA for signature bonus quantum, MWP bond, surface rental schedule, LCR training levy, and CO₂ cost exposure. Quantify each as a PV-equivalent ($ per bbl of project production, or as a percentage of gross revenue) using your project’s production profile and price deck.
  3. Compute all-in fiscal burden separately. Add non-statutory items to ORCA’s statutory take as a separate line in your IC model. Label it clearly: “Statutory take (ORCA): [X]% + Non-statutory items (bonus/levy/LCR): [Y]pp = Effective all-in burden: [X+Y]%.” Keep the two figures separate — combining them obscures the regime comparison.
  4. Report both figures in the IC memo. Statutory take goes in the country-comparison table header; all-in burden goes in the country-specific financial summary section. IC committees expect the distinction — conflating them risks overstating take in low-bonus regimes and understating it in heavy-bonus jurisdictions.

Rule of thumb — materiality of non-statutory items by item type:

  • Signature bonus (frontier block): Can be 2–6pp all-in burden uplift on a $1.2B capex reference project. Always quantify and disclose.
  • Local content / training levy (Nigeria, Angola, Brazil, Indonesia): 0.3–0.8pp IRR impact; 8–15% opex uplift. Sub-1pp for most OECD jurisdictions — generally immaterial for IC ranking but must be noted.
  • Surface rental: <0.5% NPV on commercial fields — exclude from comparison table, footnote only.
  • Carbon price (Norway CO₂ + ETS): 2–4pp effective take-equivalent in Norway; 1–2pp UK ETS; <1pp for most non-EU/non-Nordic jurisdictions. Always add for Norwegian and UK projects (see FAQ A99).

IC memo language template: “Government take for [Country] per ORCA v274 (Aug 2026): [X]% at $75/bbl (standardised profile, statutory fiscal instruments only — royalty, profit oil/CIT/PRRT, and NOC participation). Non-statutory fiscal costs identified for this deal: signature bonus $[N]M (PV-equivalent [A]% of gross revenue over project life); LCR training levy ($[M]M/yr, [B]pp opex uplift); CO₂ tax ($[C]/tonne, [D]pp effective take uplift). All-in effective fiscal burden estimate: [X+A+B+D]%. Country comparison table uses statutory take (ORCA figure) for ranking; all-in burden reported separately in Appendix [E].”

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). Wood Mackenzie Fiscal Take Methodology (2024); Rystad Energy UCube fiscal taxonomy; IHS Markit Global Upstream Fiscal Guide. Cross-reference: FAQ A57 (government take exclusions), FAQ A69 (local content levies), FAQ A96 (signature bonus NPV adjustment), FAQ A98 (MWP obligations), FAQ A99 (carbon pricing overlay).

A103. The PSA for my target country contains a fiscal stabilization clause that locks the contractor’s fiscal terms for 25 years from first commercial production. ORCA shows a government take figure based on the current statutory regime. Does ORCA reflect the stabilized terms, the current regime, or something in between — and how should I disclose the stabilization provision in an IC memo?

Short answer: ORCA models the current statutory fiscal regime for each country — the royalty rates, profit-oil splits, CIT rates, and resource rent tax parameters as codified in the applicable petroleum law and model PSA/concession. It does not model contract-specific stabilization provisions, because these are deal-by-deal negotiated terms that are not publicly disclosed for most assets. For countries where the statutory regime has changed since a major historic contract was signed, ORCA reflects the current law (or the dominant historic structure if the current law postdates most active contracts). Stabilization clauses are therefore a positive adjustment to ORCA’s take figure in regimes that have tightened since your target contract was signed, and a negative adjustment in regimes that have liberalized.

What fiscal stabilization clauses do — three structural types:

  • Full contractual freezing (classic stabilization): All fiscal parameters — royalty rates, cost recovery ceilings, profit-oil splits, CIT rate, and SPT/PRRT triggers — are contractually locked for a defined period (typically 20–30 years from first commercial production). Common in early Caspian PSAs (Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan), older West African PSCs (Angola pre-2004 Blocks, Mozambique Rovuma Area 1 PSA 2006 structure), and legacy Middle East concessions. The contractor pays the fiscal terms written in the original contract regardless of subsequent statutory changes.
  • Economic equilibrium (economic re-balancing): The contract does not freeze specific rates, but commits the government to compensate the contractor if legislative changes reduce the contractor’s after-tax return below a threshold IRR specified in the PSA. Common in LATAM regimes (Peru, Colombia, Brazil pre-salt) and newer East African PSCs. The government can change rates, but must provide fiscal relief (reduced royalty, extended cost recovery, extended contract term) to restore the agreed economics. Less certain than full freezing but still provides meaningful protection.
  • Tax stability agreement (tax treaty equivalent): A separate bilateral agreement between the investor and government guaranteeing specific tax rates (CIT, withholding tax) for the project life. Common where general tax legislation is volatile but the CIT rate is the primary risk (Kazakhstan, Mozambique LNG, some Tanzanian and Ugandan blocks). Does not cover royalty or profit-oil parameters — only CIT-side stability.

How ORCA’s take figure relates to stabilized terms by regime type:

  • Regime tightened since contract signing (most common case): ORCA reflects the current (tighter) regime. A stabilized legacy contract operates under the original lighter terms — the actual contractor take is lower than ORCA implies. Example: Angola Block 15 (signed 1994, cost recovery ceiling 50% under original terms vs. current 65% cap + windfall provisions). For an acquisition of a producing asset operating under a legacy stabilized PSA, ORCA’s take will overstate government burden on the stabilized contract. Adjustment direction: reduce effective take for the acquisition period.
  • Regime liberalized since contract signing: ORCA reflects the current (lighter) regime. The stabilized legacy contract remains on the original heavier terms — the actual contractor take is higher than ORCA implies. Example: some Caspian regimes that reduced CIT rates post-2010 (Kazakhstan flat CIT 20%); a pre-reform legacy contract locked at CIT 30% pays more than the current statutory rate. Adjustment direction: increase effective take for the acquisition period.
  • Current statutory regime matches contract vintage (no reform events): ORCA’s figure is directly applicable. This is the base case for countries with low Stability Scores and few reform events (Norway, UK post-RFCT, Gulf monarchies). No stabilization adjustment needed.
  • Economic equilibrium clauses: ORCA’s take is the government’s starting position. If a reform event reduces contractor return below the equilibrium IRR threshold, the government must provide offsetting relief — but the quantum and timing are uncertain. Treat the ORCA take as the maximum burden under equilibrium protection; disclose in IC memo as a soft floor on contractor returns.

4-step IC workflow — disclosing stabilization in a bid memo:

  1. Identify the stabilization type. Review the target PSA or concession for stabilization language. Classify as: full contractual freeze, economic equilibrium clause, tax stability agreement, or no stabilization. Check the Evidence badge in ORCA’s Country Profile for reform history flags — multiple reform events in a high-take regime often signal that legacy stabilized contracts are operating materially below current statutory rates.
  2. Determine the direction of divergence. Compare ORCA’s current-regime take to the regime in force at contract signing (ORCA’s Reform History tab shows the decade of major fiscal changes). If the regime tightened after signing: current ORCA take > stabilized contract take → adjustment reduces stated burden. If the regime liberalized after signing: current ORCA take < stabilized contract take → adjustment increases stated burden.
  3. Quantify the stabilization delta. Use ORCA’s Scenario Builder to model the original fiscal parameters (if publicly available from the PSA text or Wood Mackenzie field data): set the royalty rate, cost recovery ceiling, and profit-oil split to the original contractual terms. Compare the Scenario Builder take to ORCA’s standard take. The difference (in pp) is the stabilization adjustment. Rule of thumb: full-freeze PSCs in tightened regimes typically run 4–15 pp below current statutory take; economic equilibrium clauses provide a 2–6 pp floor protection.
  4. Disclose in the IC memo. Present ORCA’s statutory take as the country-comparison benchmark, and the stabilization-adjusted take as the asset-specific figure. Label the stabilization type, the contractual lock-in period remaining, and the reform events since signing. If stabilization has expired (or the lock-in period ends during the evaluation horizon), model the step-up to current statutory terms as a fiscal cliff event in the DCF.

Rule of thumb — stabilization impact magnitude by clause type:

  • Full contractual freeze, tightened regime (Angola, Caspian, older West African PSCs): Stabilization benefit typically 4–15 pp below current ORCA take for contracts more than 10 years old in regimes that raised CIT or tightened profit-oil terms. Always model the stabilization expiry date as a fiscal step-up event in the DCF sensitivity.
  • Economic equilibrium (Peru, Colombia, Brazil pre-salt): Provides a 2–6 pp effective floor on take uplift from legislative changes. Less certain than full freeze — disclose as a soft protection in the IC memo, not a hard fiscal lock.
  • Tax stability agreement (Kazakhstan, Mozambique LNG): CIT-side protection only — typically worth 1–4 pp in regimes where CIT has moved materially (e.g., Kazakhstan CIT 30%→20% over 2000–2010). Royalty and profit-oil parameters remain exposed to reform.
  • No stabilization, high Stability Score (Norway, UK, Gulf monarchies): ORCA take is directly applicable. Historical regime stability means current statutory terms closely match legacy contract economics. No adjustment required.

IC memo language template: “Government take for [Country] [Block/Field] per ORCA v274 (Aug 2026): [X]% at $75/bbl (standardised profile, current statutory regime). Target asset operates under a [full contractual freeze / economic equilibrium clause / tax stability agreement] effective from [contract date], covering [describe scope: all fiscal instruments / CIT only] for [N years] from first commercial production (expiry: [year]). The current statutory regime is [tighter / lighter / unchanged] relative to the contract vintage, resulting in an estimated [+/−N pp] stabilization adjustment. Asset-specific effective take (stabilized): approximately [X±N]% at $75/bbl. ORCA statutory take ([X]%) used for cross-country comparison; stabilized take ([X±N]%) reported as the asset-specific figure in the financial model. Stabilization expiry modelled as a fiscal step-up/(step-down) event in DCF year [year]. See Appendix [F] for Scenario Builder sensitivity at stabilized vs. current statutory terms.”

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). Wood Mackenzie Fiscal Stabilization Study (2024); IHS Markit Global PSC Stabilization Survey; Rystad Energy UCube contract-vintage fiscal database; Bowman Gilfillan/Freshfields Bruckhaus Deringer International Petroleum Agreements (3rd ed.). Cross-reference: FAQ A13 (source verification), FAQ A17 (IC-readiness tiers), FAQ A82 (dual-regime environments), FAQ A86 (depreciation and capital allowance timing), FAQ A95 (discount rate reconciliation).

A104. My company structures its upstream investments through a holding company that on-lends capital to the operating subsidiary. How do thin capitalization rules and intercompany interest deductibility affect the effective tax burden — and does ORCA’s government take figure capture these corporate financing effects?

Platform scope: ORCA’s government take figure reflects the statutory upstream fiscal regime applied to a standalone operating entity — royalties, profit oil or gas, income taxes, resource rent taxes, and NOC equity dividends. Intercompany interest deductibility and thin capitalization rules are not captured in the take figure because they operate at the corporate structure level, not the contract level. The financing structure of the operating entity can materially shift the effective CIT burden — and therefore the effective government take — relative to ORCA’s statutory figure.

Why this matters for IC analysis: Many IOC upstream investments are structured through a chain of holding companies with intercompany loans from a treasury entity in a low-tax jurisdiction. If the operating subsidiary can deduct interest on that intercompany debt against its taxable petroleum income, the effective CIT rate falls below the statutory rate — reducing effective government take by 3–12pp in CIT-heavy regimes (Norway, UK, Australia PRRT). However, host countries increasingly impose thin capitalization (thin-cap) rules that cap deductible interest at a fixed debt-to-equity ratio, limiting this benefit.

Three thin-cap rule structures across major petroleum jurisdictions:

  1. Fixed debt-to-equity cap (most common). The operating subsidiary’s deductible interest is capped at a maximum debt-to-equity ratio — typically 2:1 or 3:1. Interest on debt above the cap is non-deductible. Examples: Australia (thin-cap threshold 60% of total assets or 1.5:1 debt-to-equity for general entities; upstream Petroleum Resource Rent Tax ring-fence applies separately); Indonesia (4:1 debt-to-equity, Minister of Finance Regulation 169/PMK.010/2015); Nigeria (debt-to-equity ratio 3:1 for upstream companies per FIRS guidance, CITA amendment); Angola (3:1 cap for PSC contractors, Sonangol approval required for intercompany loans). Rule of thumb: at 3:1 leverage and 5% intercompany interest rate, with 50% of debt above the cap being non-deductible, the CIT tax shield loss is approximately 0.7–1.5pp effective IRR at a 30–35% CIT rate.
  2. Earnings stripping / EBITDA-based cap (OECD BEPS Action 4). Post-2018 OECD BEPS implementation caps net interest deductions at 30% of EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, amortisation). This is more restrictive than a fixed ratio in the early, high-capex phase of a project when EBITDA is low. Examples: Norway (interest limitation rule: deductions capped at 25% of EBITDA for related-party interest, Tax Act §6-41 as amended 2022); UK (corporate interest restriction rule: CIR caps group net interest deductions at 30% EBITDA, TIOPA 2010 Part 10, applies to UK upstream ring-fence if financed via related-party debt); Canada (excessive interest and financing expenses limitation rule: EIFEL, 30% EBITDA cap, effective 2023). In the pre-production phase — when EBITDA is zero or negative — EBITDA-based caps effectively disallow all related-party interest. Carry-forward of disallowed interest is available in most regimes (5–20 years), but the time-value cost is material: 3–6pp effective IRR reduction for a 5-year pre-production period at 8% intercompany interest rates.
  3. PSC ring-fence and cost recovery treatment of interest. In production sharing contract jurisdictions, intercompany interest is typically not a recoverable cost — it sits outside the cost recovery ring-fence by contract definition. The contractor may be able to deduct interest for CIT purposes separately from the PSC cost recovery mechanism, but many PSCs explicitly prohibit intercompany financing costs from entering the cost oil pool. Examples: Indonesia (intercompany interest not recoverable under PTK 007/BPMIGAS/PTK/IX/2009 cost recovery guidelines); Angola ANPG model PSC (related-party financing charges excluded from cost oil); Malaysia Petronas PSC (intercompany financing excluded from cost oil by standard contract clause). Practical implication: even where CIT deductibility is permitted, the cash flow benefit is deferred relative to a third-party debt structure because CIT is paid on profit oil share (after cost recovery), not on gross revenue.

4-step IC adjustment workflow for intercompany debt structures:

  1. Identify the applicable thin-cap rule. Look up the host country’s thin-cap regime: fixed D/E ratio vs. EBITDA cap vs. PSC ring-fence. Consult ORCA’s Country Profile evidence sources (primary tax legislation cited in Evidence A/B fields) for the current rule. For OECD members, BEPS Action 4 EBITDA-based caps are now standard. For non-OECD members, fixed D/E ratios remain more common.
  2. Estimate the deductible interest tax shield. If the operating structure carries [D] of intercompany debt at rate [r], and the thin-cap cap limits deductible debt to [D_cap]: tax shield = [D_cap × r × CIT rate]. Compare against uncapped tax shield = [D × r × CIT rate]. The delta is the cost of the thin-cap constraint. At Norway’s marginal upstream rate (78%: 22% CIT + 56% SPT), the tax shield value of interest deductibility is very high — and Norway’s EBITDA-based cap for related-party interest (25% EBITDA, Tax Act §6-41) can materially restrict this for intercompany-funded development projects in years 1–5 when EBITDA is suppressed by capital write-offs.
  3. Apply effective CIT rate adjustment in the Scenario Builder. Reduce the CIT rate input by the estimated tax shield benefit (net of thin-cap restriction) to model the financing-adjusted effective take. Example: Nigeria statutory CIT 30% + PPT 85% blended rate; if intercompany interest at 5% on a $500M loan is 50% disallowed by thin-cap: effective CIT reduction = 0.50 × $25M interest × 30% CIT = $3.75M/year → approximately 0.4pp IRR benefit from the deductible portion, offset by the disallowed portion which adds 0.4pp effective take back. Net impact at 50% thin-cap disallowance: near-zero. The key insight: thin-cap rules in oil-producing nations are calibrated to neutralize most of the financing tax shield at high D/E ratios.
  4. IC memo disclosure language: “Government take of [X]% per ORCA v274 (Aug 2026) reflects statutory upstream fiscal terms applied to a standalone operating entity. Intercompany financing adjustment: [Country] [thin-cap rule type] limits related-party interest deductibility to [D/E ratio or EBITDA%]. At the proposed [$Xm intercompany facility / Y% interest rate], estimated financing tax shield: $[Z]M NPV (net of thin-cap restriction); effective take adjustment: [+/−N]pp. Detailed financing structure analysis available in Appendix [G] — consult tax counsel for final treaty position and transfer pricing documentation requirements.”

Rule of thumb by jurisdiction:

  • Norway (78% marginal rate, EBITDA-based cap): Intercompany interest deductibility is the single most valuable financing tool available, but restricted by 25% EBITDA cap post-2022. For pre-production years, carry-forward preserves the benefit. Net financing tax shield at $1B intercompany loan = $15–25M NPV over 25-year project. Disclose thin-cap carry-forward as a timing risk.
  • UK (40–75% blended EPL-era rate, CIR 30% EBITDA cap): Corporate Interest Restriction applies to ring-fence upstream income. Third-party debt secured on North Sea assets is exempt from CIR; related-party intercompany debt is subject. Effective benefit of $500M intercompany loan: $8–12M NPV at current CIR application — material but thin-cap-constrained for pure intercompany structures.
  • Indonesia, Nigeria, Angola (fixed D/E cap, 3:1–4:1): High statutory rates (30–50% CIT + profit oil) but fixed-ratio thin-cap rules are well-established and broadly honored. For a 3:1 leverage structure: approximately 60–70% of optimal tax shield is recoverable. Net IRR benefit: 0.8–1.5pp at reference project scale.
  • UAE, Qatar, Saudi Arabia (low or zero upstream CIT for IOC JV partners): Intercompany interest deductibility is largely irrelevant because the effective CIT burden is already minimal for IOC working interest holders. Government take comes predominantly from profit oil/gas splitting and royalties — financing structure does not affect these. No thin-cap adjustment needed.
  • PSC regimes with hard ring-fence on cost recovery: Assume zero benefit from intercompany interest in the cost oil pool; model any CIT deductibility benefit separately and at a discounted probability (50–70%) reflecting PSC contract interpretation risk.

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). OECD BEPS Action 4 Final Report (2015, updated 2021); PwC Global Tax Summaries — Oil & Gas (2024); Norway Petroleum Tax Act §6-41 (interest limitation rule); UK TIOPA 2010 Part 10 (Corporate Interest Restriction); Indonesia MoF Regulation 169/PMK.010/2015; Nigeria CITA thin-cap guidance (FIRS 2020); Angola ANPG Model PSC — cost recovery cost categories. Cross-reference: FAQ A38 (PRRT/SPT methodology — Norway/UK high-rate regimes where financing structure matters most); FAQ A41 (IRR DCF model — intercompany debt timing effects on pre-production EBITDA); FAQ A57 (government take exclusions — financing costs are excluded from take but affect contractor IRR); FAQ A82 (dual-regime environments — thin-cap rules can differ between licence classes in the same jurisdiction); FAQ A95 (discount rate reconciliation — intercompany financing cost vs. WACC).

A105. We are evaluating a farm-in to a deepwater exploration block where we would acquire 30% working interest and carry the farmor through a two-well appraisal program. The fiscal regime is a PSC. How does ORCA’s government take figure apply to a farmed-in working interest, and how should I model the carry structure in the DCF and IC submission?

Platform scope: ORCA’s government take figure reflects the statutory fiscal regime applied to the full contract — royalties, cost recovery/profit oil split, CIT/PITA, and NOC participation — for a standardized reference project. ORCA does not model farm-in consideration, carry obligations, or working interest allocation between co-venturers. The stated government take applies at the contract level; the allocation between farmor and farmee of the contractor’s net share is a commercial arrangement outside the fiscal regime. For IC purposes, you must model the carry as a modification to the farmee’s effective cost basis, then apply ORCA’s take to the resulting contractor net cash flow.

Why the carry structure matters for effective IRR: In a carried-interest farm-in, the farmee funds 100% of the appraisal program cost in exchange for a working interest share. The farmor gets a “free carry” through exploration/appraisal without contributing cash. From the farmee’s perspective, the economic cost of the carry is a premium on top of the stated working interest acquisition price — it raises the effective cost basis and reduces IRR relative to a simple proportionate cost-share. Three carry structures appear in upstream M&A, each with different fiscal treatment:

  1. Gross carry (most common in frontier/appraisal). The farmee pays 100% of the work program cost for N% working interest. The carry obligation sits outside the PSC cost recovery ring-fence — it is not a recoverable cost against the contractor cost oil pool. Fiscal treatment: the farmee recovers its own working interest share of costs through cost oil in the normal way; the additional carry premium is written off as a pre-production exploration expense (deductible for CIT in most concession regimes; typically not recoverable in PSC cost oil). Effective take uplift: carry premium ÷ project NPV × 100, typically 2–8pp IRR reduction for a two-well deepwater appraisal carry at frontier exploration acreage. Example: at $120M two-well program, 30% WI farmee funding 100% = $84M carry premium on top of proportionate $36M cost share. At $75/bbl reference project NPV of $400M: carry uplift ≈ 21pp gross, but NPV-adjusted carry cost (discounted at 10%) ≈ 6–10pp effective IRR drag.
  2. Net profits carry (earn-in structure). The farmee earns its working interest by funding the work program; once production is established, the farmor’s costs are recovered from production revenues before the farmor shares in net profits. This structure is common in PSC regimes where carry reimbursement can be tied to production milestones (e.g., first commercial production + payout). Fiscal treatment: the earn-in cost is typically capitalized to the farmee’s cost pool and recovered through cost oil; the farmor’s reimbursement from production is treated as a payment by the farmee — not a recoverable PSC cost. Key risk: payout definition often excludes certain cost recovery caps, meaning the farmor’s reimbursement may extend beyond the DCF’s expected payout date. Disclose as a timing risk in the IC submission.
  3. Cash consideration + partial carry (hybrid). The farmee pays upfront cash for working interest and carries the farmor through Phase 1 of the work program only, with proportionate cost-sharing thereafter. This is the most balanced structure and the most common in conventional basin farm-ins (e.g., North Sea, West Africa offshore). The upfront cash component may be treated as a signature payment for PSC purposes — confirm with the host government whether the bonus is payable to the government (triggering a fiscal disclosure per FAQ A96) or directly to the farmor (purely commercial, no fiscal overlay). The carry component is modeled as in structure (1) above but only for Phase 1 capital.

4-step IC adjustment workflow for carried-interest farm-ins:

  1. Confirm the farmee’s effective working interest and carry obligation. The fiscal regime (ORCA government take) applies at the contract level. The farmee’s DCF is computed on: (a) its WI% share of gross production revenues, (b) its WI% share of cost oil entitlement (for PSC), (c) its WI% share of profit oil, (d) its WI% share of CIT/PITA liability, plus (e) 100% of the carry obligation (or the agreed percentage of carry) as an incremental capex line in years 1–N of the work program.
  2. Model the carry as upfront capex in the farmee’s DCF. Run ORCA’s Scenario Builder at the host country’s fiscal terms. Set capex = (farmee’s WI% × total project capex) + carry obligation. The carry is expensed/capitalized at cost; it does not change the government take percentage (that is fixed by the fiscal regime), but it increases the cost basis and therefore reduces contractor IRR. Compare farmee-adjusted IRR against ORCA’s reference-project contractor IRR to quantify the carry cost in IRR points.
  3. Check PSC cost recovery eligibility of the carry premium. In PSC regimes, only “contract costs” as defined in the PSC are recoverable through cost oil. Carry obligations to a third-party farmor are almost universally excluded from the recoverable cost pool — they sit outside the ring-fence. This means the farmee recovers its WI-proportionate development costs through cost oil in the normal way, but the carry premium is lost to the ring-fence and reduces effective contractor economics by the full amount. Confirm by reviewing the Evidence A sources for the country in ORCA’s Country Profile (cost recovery eligible cost categories are typically enumerated in Annex A of the PSC).
  4. IC memo disclosure for carry structures: “Government take of [X]% per ORCA v274 (Aug 2026) reflects statutory [country] PSC terms applied to the full contract at standardized reference project parameters. Farmee effective take (including carry obligation): all-in contractor economics modeled at [farmee WI]% working interest with $[Y]M gross carry obligation in years [1–N]; carry premium is not recoverable from cost oil under [country] PSC terms. Farmee IRR: [Z]% (vs. ORCA reference contractor IRR at full WI: [W]%); carry drag: [Z−W]pp. Farmor fiscal position: not modeled — farmor has zero economic cost through Phase [N]; farmor effective take materially below statutory regime until [payout event]. Detailed co-venturer economic split available in Appendix [F].”

Fiscal treatment of farm-in consideration (tax on disposal/acquisition):

  • For the farmor (seller): In many upstream jurisdictions, the cash consideration received on farm-out is taxable as a capital gain or license disposal gain. Examples: UK (ring-fence allowable loss treatment; farm-out proceeds reduce the farmor’s cost pool for ring-fence CT purposes — HMRC PD6 treatment); Norway (farm-out gain is taxable at 78% marginal rate, but NORM SPE regime allows special allowances); Australia PRRT (farm-in consideration is a project receipt for PRRT purposes; reduces farmee’s deductible starting base). ORCA does not model the tax on farm-out proceeds — this is a transaction-level tax that sits above the production fiscal regime. Disclose as a separate tax due diligence line.
  • For the farmee (buyer): In most jurisdictions, the farm-in acquisition cost (WI purchase price + carry obligation) is capitalized as an exploration or development asset and enters the normal cost recovery / tax depreciation schedule. In PRRT regimes (Australia), the farm-in cost forms part of the farmee’s starting base for the PRRT uplift calculation — a significant benefit. In PSC regimes, the acquisition cost is typically non-recoverable from cost oil (it is a commercial transaction, not a contract cost); only subsequent capital expenditure on the work program enters the cost pool.
  • Rule of thumb by regime type: Concession regimes (Norway, UK, Angola): farm-in acquisition cost deductible for CIT; carry premium non-recoverable but CIT-deductible. PSC regimes (Indonesia, Nigeria, Guyana): acquisition cost non-recoverable from cost oil; carry premium non-recoverable; only new capital (WI% of development program) enters cost pool. PRRT regimes (Australia, Timor-Leste): farm-in cost forms starting base for PRRT uplift — high value if the project is long-lived; acquisition premium drives superior after-PRRT returns vs. concession structures.

Rule of thumb for carry cost by block type:

  • Frontier deepwater appraisal carry ($80–200M program, Pg=20–35%): Carry cost dominates effective IRR. At 30% WI, full-carry two-well program: 5–10pp IRR drag vs. proportionate cost-share. DCF almost always negative at P50 on standalone basis; carries economic value only at P90 resource or with portfolio diversification credit.
  • Near-field appraisal / development farm-in ($20–80M program, Pg=50–70%): Carry cost modest relative to project NPV. 1–3pp IRR drag is typical. Farm-in is often accretive vs. greenfield if the farmee acquires fiscal cost recovery attributes of advanced project (Norway SDFI-type carry structures: near-zero drag due to 78% tax refundability of exploration costs).
  • Producing asset farm-in (no carry, pure WI acquisition): No carry modeling required. Apply ORCA take directly at farmee WI%; only acquisition premium and working capital enter effective cost basis adjustment.

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). IHS Markit Upstream Farm-in Valuation (2022); Wood Mackenzie Farm-in Market Monitor (2024 Q1); UK HMRC PD6 Petroleum Revenue Tax Technical Notes — farm-out treatment; Norway Petroleum Tax Act §3(c) (farm-in/farm-out; exploration refund scheme for unlisted companies); Australia PRRT Assessment Act 1987 §22B (starting base); Guyana PPT model PSC (Section 8 — cost recovery eligible costs, farm-in exclusion). Cross-reference: FAQ A57 (government take exclusions — acquisition cost sits above the production fiscal regime); FAQ A63 (composite viability screen — frontier carry structures require P90 resource for positive expected-value screen); FAQ A82 (dual-regime environments — farm-in across PSC and concession tranche in same basin); FAQ A95 (discount rate reconciliation — carry structures increase project risk profile and may warrant a higher project-specific discount rate); FAQ A96 (signature bonus adjustment — confirm whether farm-in cash consideration triggers a government bonus obligation).

A106. We are acquiring a mature North Sea block with approximately 15 years of production remaining. The operator estimates gross decommissioning costs of $350–400M. ORCA does not include decommissioning in its DCF output. How do I incorporate the decommissioning liability into the government take analysis and IC submission?

Platform scope: ORCA models a standardized 15-year reference project with no explicit decommissioning phase — the project cash flows terminate at year 15 without an abandonment cost tail. ORCA’s government take figure therefore excludes decommissioning costs and the associated fiscal relief. For late-life acquisitions where the decommissioning obligation is material relative to project NPV, the decommissioning liability must be modeled separately and disclosed as a named IC line item distinct from the ORCA take figure.

Why decommissioning matters for late-life IC analysis: Decommissioning costs are a real, legally enforceable liability from the date of acquisition. In most upstream jurisdictions, the buyer (farmee or acquirer) inherits joint and several liability for decommissioning as operator of record or co-venturer. The NPV of a $350M gross decommissioning obligation discounted at 10% over 15 years is approximately $84M — equivalent to 7–14pp of government take at $75/bbl for a mid-tier field, or a 2–4pp IRR reduction on a $1.2B capex reference project. In mature basin acquisitions (UK, Norway, US GoM), the decommissioning liability routinely exceeds the residual field NPV in downside price scenarios, making it a deal-defining variable.

Regime-specific fiscal treatment of decommissioning costs:

  • UK (Ring-fence CT + PRT — most favorable). HMRC provides decommissioning relief under Sections 3D and 3DA of the Taxes and Capital Allowances Act 2010. Key features: (1) decommissioning costs are 100% deductible against ring-fence profits in the year incurred; (2) if the acquirer has insufficient ring-fence profits to absorb the full deduction, HMRC provides a “decommissioning relief undertaking” (DRU) — a government-backed guarantee that the relief will be available at a floor rate of 50% regardless of future tax law changes; (3) PRT (Petroleum Revenue Tax, historic fields only) provides a separate decommissioning supplement. Effective net-of-tax decommissioning obligation: approximately 20–30% of gross cost at current RFCT rate (30% ring-fence CT + 10% supplementary charge = 40% combined rate, recently adjusted under Energy Profits Levy). Rule of thumb: UK North Sea fixed platform $150–400M gross → $45–120M net after tax relief. The DRU is a transferable asset — its value must be disclosed in the acquisition price negotiation.
  • Norway (PTA Section 22 — highly favorable with refund mechanism). Under the Norwegian Petroleum Tax Act §22, decommissioning costs are deductible at the full 78% marginal tax rate (ordinary CIT 22% + Special Petroleum Tax 56%). Critically, companies with insufficient taxable income to absorb the deduction receive a direct cash refund from the Norwegian government at the 78% rate — effectively transferring 78% of the gross decommissioning cost to the state. This makes decommissioning obligations in Norway uniquely well-hedged: the contractor retains approximately 22% net exposure on the gross decommissioning cost. For a $300M gross obligation: net contractor obligation ≈ $66M. Equinor and the Norwegian government maintain an equalization scheme for decommissioning timing; verify applicability for the specific license. Rule of thumb: Norway North Sea $100–300M gross → $22–66M net after 78% relief.
  • Australia (PRRT — deductible with GDP uplift). Decommissioning costs are “PRRT deductible expenditures” under the Petroleum Resource Rent Tax Assessment Act 1987. Undeducted abandonment costs at project end receive the GDP uplift (Long Term Bond Rate + 5%, compounding) applied retroactively, making late-project decommissioning relatively low-NPV cost on an after-PRRT basis. The PRRT rate is 40%; combined with CIT at 30%, effective total decommissioning relief can reach 58–62% of gross cost for a PRRT-liable project. Farm-in cost (including decommissioning liability assumption) may increase the farmee’s starting base for PRRT uplift purposes (per §22B). Rule of thumb: $100–250M gross Australian offshore decommissioning → $40–95M net of combined PRRT + CIT relief.
  • US GoM (no specific decommissioning relief — ordinary CIT only). The US provides no special decommissioning fiscal relief. Costs are deducted as operating expenses in the year incurred against the 21% federal CIT rate plus applicable state taxes. BSEE (Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement) regulations require operators to post supplemental financial assurance bonds covering decommissioning obligations — these bonds typically equal the estimated gross decommissioning cost and represent an off-balance-sheet working capital requirement that reduces project IRR. Rule of thumb: US GoM deepwater subsea well P&A $30–80M; platform $80–250M; net after CIT deduction ≈ 78–80% of gross. BSEE bond requirement adds 2–4% annual carry cost on the full gross obligation.
  • West Africa PSC (decommissioning split by working interest share). In standard West African PSC structures (Nigeria, Angola, Gabon, Ghana), the host government and NOC participate as WI holders, so the contractor’s decommissioning obligation is limited to its proportionate WI% share. For a standard 40% NOC carried interest structure, the contractor bears 60% of gross decommissioning costs. However, most West African PSCs explicitly exclude post-production decommissioning costs from the recoverable cost oil pool — meaning the contractor cannot recover its decommissioning share through cost oil; the cost is borne entirely from the contractor’s post-production cash. Applicable CIT provides a partial offset (30–35% in most West African jurisdictions). Rule of thumb: Nigeria/Angola deepwater $200–400M gross; 60% contractor share = $120–240M; net after CIT ≈ $78–156M. No ring-fence decommissioning guarantee equivalent exists — full disclosure in IC memo required.
  • Indonesia Gross Split PSC (contractor bears 100% — no government cost-sharing). The 2017 Indonesian Gross Split regime eliminates cost recovery entirely. Contractors receive a larger split of gross production (fixed + variable) in lieu of cost recovery. This means decommissioning costs are fully contractor-borne with no government cost-sharing mechanism. The only fiscal offset is Indonesian CIT (22%) applied to decommissioning when expensed. For a production sharing legacy contract (pre-2017), standard PSC decommissioning applies (shared via cost oil if within the recovery period; otherwise contractor-borne). Gross Split decommissioning is a material deal risk: the all-in net obligation equals 78% of gross cost with no ring-fence or refund mechanism.
