  • FTP vs. no-FTP: If the PSC has a First Tranche Petroleum (FTP = 10–20% of gross production allocated to government before cost recovery), the effective take will be higher than a no-FTP PSC with the same profit oil split. The Scenario Builder FTP field captures this — leave at 0% if not contractually required.

Rule of thumb by mechanic for Scenario Builder vs. country default divergence: Concession: divergence typically under 5pp (royalty and CIT rates are statutory — country default is usually accurate). PSC: divergence can be 5–15pp if block-specific cost recovery cap or FTP differs from country norm. TSC: use Scenario Builder whenever the contract fee differs from ORCA's TSC basis (Iraq TSC country average ≈$2.50/bbl; a specific block may offer $1.80 or $3.20). PRRT: always use country default for Australia unless you are modeling a specific project above threshold with a known development cost base — PRRT output is highly sensitive to project IRR trajectory. Cross-reference: FAQ A70 (R-factor mechanics); FAQ A100 (FTP/first tranche petroleum); FAQ A128 (production decline curve shape and take interaction); FAQ A41 (DCF model specification and IC disclosure requirements).

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). Johnston, D., International Petroleum Fiscal Systems and Production Sharing Contracts (PennWell, 1994): Chapter 4 (PSC parameter calibration). EY, Global Oil and Gas Tax Guide (2024): CIT/ring-fence rates by jurisdiction. Wood Mackenzie, Upstream Fiscal Benchmarking Methodology (2024 subscription). SPE, Petroleum Economics and Risk Analysis, 2nd ed. (2021): field-level fiscal calibration workflow. Cross-reference: FAQ A37 (IC capital allocation memo workflow); FAQ A41 (IRR DCF model specification); FAQ A70 (R-factor mechanics — profit oil tier calibration); FAQ A100 (FTP first tranche petroleum); FAQ A128 (production decline curve shape interaction with fiscal mechanics).

A134. Our upstream portfolio spans positions in 14 countries across PSC, Concession, and TSC regimes. A single renegotiation wave in West African PSCs would hit 70% of our positions simultaneously. How do I use ORCA to quantify fiscal mechanic concentration risk and present it in a portfolio review?

Why mechanic concentration matters: Government take is not just a country-level variable — it is a mechanic-level variable. PSC profit oil splits, Concession royalty rates, and TSC fee schedules are each vulnerable to distinct policy risks. A portfolio concentrated in PSCs in Sub-Saharan Africa (Nigeria, Angola, Ghana, Tanzania, Mozambique) faces correlated renegotiation risk: a regional PSC reform wave — as occurred in 2011–2014 (Nigeria Petroleum Industry Bill, Angola's PREDD reforms, Mozambique's 2014 taxation changes) — can simultaneously increase effective take across all PSC positions. This systemic fiscal risk is distinct from country-specific political risk and does not diversify within a single mechanic type. Concession regimes face analogous windfall profit tax exposure in high-price environments (e.g., UK EPL 2022, Norway SPT increase 2022). A balanced portfolio identifies where mechanic clustering exceeds tolerable systemic thresholds.

4-step concentration audit workflow using ORCA:

  1. Map your mechanic distribution (IOC Portfolio tab): Load your company on the IOC Portfolio tab. The stats bar shows your mechanic count and weighted average take by country. Read the Mechanic column in the results table and tally the contract-count weight by mechanic type. Rule of thumb thresholds: >60% of contracts in one mechanic type = concentrated; >70% = high concentration risk. The IOC Portfolio tab exports to XLSX (↓ XLSX button) — use this to build the concentration audit table in Excel.
  2. Stress-test your PSC positions (Fiscal Compare + Screener): Run Fiscal Compare at $50/bbl and sort by Swing. PSC regimes in Sub-Saharan Africa show the highest Swing (typically 15–28pp), because R-factor acceleration and high profit oil splits amplify price sensitivity. Filter the Screener to Mechanic = PSC + Region = Africa + Swing > 15pp to identify your highest-concentration/highest-sensitivity cluster. A cluster where 8 of 14 positions share PSC mechanic + Africa region + Swing >15pp is a portfolio-level stress scenario, not just individual country risk.
  3. Identify reform correlation risk (Reform Risk tab): On the Reform Risk tab, check the Regional Reform Tilt panel — it shows whether a region is net-tightening or net-liberalizing. Africa has historically been net-tightening (5–7 tightening events vs. 1–2 liberalizing per 5-year period, 2010–2023). For each country in your PSC cluster, check the Stability Score (0–5 dot scale). A cluster where >3 of 5 PSC countries have Stability Score ≤ 2 means correlated reform risk is not diversified away by geography — it is amplified by regional policy contagion.
  4. Build the IC memo concentration matrix: Report three metrics for the portfolio: (a) Mechanic concentration ratio = % of total contracts (or production-weighted WI%) in the dominant mechanic; (b) Systemic sensitivity = weighted-average Swing for positions in the dominant mechanic cluster (use Screener export for the underlying data); (c) Reform correlation score = % of dominant-mechanic positions in regions with net-tightening reform trend × (1 − average Stability Score). IC memo disclosure template: "Portfolio fiscal mechanic analysis (ORCA v274): [PSC] concentration [X]% of contracts (production-weighted: [Y]%). Systemic price sensitivity (weighted avg Swing, PSC cluster): [Z]pp. Reform correlation risk: [N] of [M] PSC positions in net-tightening regions with Stability Score ≤ 2. Recommended portfolio rebalancing: [target mechanic allocation] to reduce systemic sensitivity below [threshold]pp."

What ORCA does and does not capture for concentration analysis: ORCA captures statutory fiscal mechanic (Concession, PSC, TSC, PRRT, RSC, Buy-back, Revenue Share, Gross Split) at the country level using the dominant mechanic by contract count. It does not model: (a) specific block-level contractual terms that may diverge from country norms (use Scenario Builder per block); (b) hedging instruments or fiscal stabilization clauses that may dampen reform exposure (see FAQ A103); (c) production-weighted WI shares (the IOC Portfolio table shows contract counts, not WI% — weight by your actual WI% in the XLSX output for a production-adjusted view). The concentration analysis using ORCA is a first-order screen. Second-order analysis (which stabilization clauses actually hedge the PSC positions; what prior reform events affected which specific blocks) requires data room materials and contract-by-contract review.

Rule of thumb by mechanic type for systemic risk: PSC (especially Sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia): highest reform risk, highest Swing — systemic threshold >50% of contracts warrants a portfolio-level mitigation plan (Scenario Builder stress-test at tightened terms; identify Stability Score ≥4 PSC alternatives). Concession (OECD): low reform risk in normal environments, but windfall profit tax exposure in high-price scenarios — apply UK EPL or Norway SPT analogy if Swing >10pp and price >$90/bbl. TSC (Iraq, Kuwait): structurally low take (fee per barrel) and low Swing — diversifying concentration with TSC positions reduces both average take and systemic sensitivity. PRRT (Australia): reform stable since 2012 uplift amendment; concentration risk low for portfolios with Woodside/Santos-type exposure. Rule: the systemic risk score (concentration ratio × average Swing) should not exceed 15 for any mechanic cluster in a healthy portfolio (e.g., 60% PSC × 25pp avg Swing = 15 — borderline; 70% × 22pp = 15.4 — exceeds threshold).

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). IMF Fiscal Affairs Department (2012), “Fiscal Regimes for Extractive Industries: Design and Implementation.” IEA, “World Energy Investment” (2023): IOC portfolio allocation and regime-type diversification. Wood Mackenzie (2022), “West African Upstream Fiscal Reform Risk: PSC Renegotiation Wave Assessment.” Nigeria Petroleum Industry Act 2021 (fiscal reform context). Angola Presidential Decree 55/18 (2018 PSC fiscal adjustment). Tanzania Natural Resources (Permanent Sovereignty) Act 2017. Mozambique Law 27/2014 (petroleum taxation reform). ORCA Reform History database: regional tightening/liberalizing event counts 2010–2023. Cross-reference: FAQ A24 (portfolio fiscal risk triage — 3-layer screen: exposure mapping + $50 stress test + reform risk overlay); FAQ A51 (reform risk classification by Stability Score tier); FAQ A71 (IOC Portfolio tab 4-step capital allocation pre-screening); FAQ A73 (stabilization clause vs. Reform Risk Stability Score); FAQ A93 (Price Swing interpretation — 3-tier thresholds); FAQ A117 (portfolio asset review triage framework).

A135. The platform shows country-level fiscal parameters. Before I cite any ORCA figure in an IC submission, I need to know: are these current-law statutory terms, block-specific contractual terms from individual PSAs, or modeled estimates — and when were the parameters last verified?

What ORCA reports — current-law statutory terms as of August 2026: Every fiscal parameter in ORCA is sourced from current legislation, presidential decrees, petroleum acts, model contracts, or official government publications — not from block-specific PSA or concession agreement text. This distinction matters: the Nigerian PIA 2021 sets a statutory deepwater royalty of 5–7.5%. A specific OML awarded in 2003 may still operate under its original royalty ring-fence at 0%. ORCA shows the PIA 2021 statutory rate. The block-specific 2003 terms require a data room review.

Evidence badge tells you the source tier:

  • A badge (Primary — green): Parameter sourced from primary legislation or official decree (e.g., Nigerian PIA 2021, Norwegian Petroleum Taxation Act §5, Indonesian MoEMR Decree 8/2017). This is the most reliable tier. Cite directly in IC memos with the statutory source.
  • B badge (Verified — amber): Parameter sourced from a verified secondary source — operator annual report (SEC 20-F, ASX filing), NOC disclosure, or a cross-checked industry database (S&P Global, Wood Mackenzie, Rystad). Use with "verified secondary source" qualifier in IC memo footnotes.
  • C badge (Modeled — red): Parameter estimated from a comparable regime or modeled from secondary sources where primary data is unavailable. Flag as "modeled estimate" in all IC submissions and verify with in-country legal counsel or operator data room before FID.

What ORCA does NOT capture (adjust separately in Scenario Builder):

  • Block-specific contractual terms: If your block was awarded under legacy PSA terms predating the current model contract, ORCA shows the current model contract. Use Scenario Builder to enter block-specific royalty, cost recovery cap, and profit oil split from the data room PSA (FAQ A133 covers Scenario Builder calibration step-by-step).
  • Stabilization clauses: A PSA stabilization clause freezes fiscal terms at the contract date, making the block immune to subsequent statutory reforms. ORCA shows current-law statutory terms — if your block is stabilized at 2008 terms, the difference between 2008 and 2026 statutory rates is the stabilization benefit (see FAQ A103).
  • Sub-national levies: State, provincial, and municipal petroleum taxes (US severance taxes, Canadian Crown royalties, Brazilian state ICMS) are not in ORCA's country-level take figure (see FAQ A126).
  • Non-statutory fiscal costs: Signature bonuses, training levies, surface rentals, and community development contributions are not modeled in ORCA's DCF take calculation (see FAQ A102 for how to adjust).

Data vintage and reform cutoff: The platform data is compiled through August 2026. Fiscal reforms enacted after this date are not reflected. To check whether a material reform occurred near the cutoff: (1) Go to Reform Risk tab and check the country's most recent reform event date in the timeline. (2) If a reform event appears as "2026" or "2025-Q4," cross-check the Evidence badge source citation for the affected parameter — an A-badge source with a 2026 legislative reference indicates the reform IS captured; a B-badge or C-badge with a 2024 or earlier date indicates the reform may postdate the sourcing. (3) For active reform jurisdictions (Angola, Nigeria, Indonesia, Kazakhstan), assume a 6–12 month data lag for regulatory guidance and ministerial decrees even when the legislation is captured.

4-step IC citation workflow:

  1. Check Evidence badge tier: Open Country Profile for your target country. Review the A/B/C badge for each parameter you plan to cite. Flag all C-badge parameters as requiring verification before use in IC submissions.
  2. Check reform recency: On Reform Risk tab, verify whether any reform event appears within 18 months of August 2026. If yes, verify whether the reform is pre- or post-cutoff via the source citation. A recent reform not reflected in ORCA will show as a stale parameter until the next data update.
  3. Identify block-specific deviations: Obtain the PSA or concession agreement from the data room. Compare royalty, cost recovery cap, and profit oil split to ORCA's country-level statutory parameters. If deviations exist, model block-specific terms in Scenario Builder and report both: "Statutory take per ORCA v274: [X]%; contract-specific take (Scenario Builder): [Y]%."
  4. Disclose in IC memo: Use this language: "Fiscal benchmarking based on current-law statutory parameters as of August 2026 (ORCA Petroleum Fiscal Intelligence Platform, v233 — yoburgqs.github.io/petroleum-fiscal-db/). Evidence quality: [A/B/C badge tier for key parameters]. Block-specific contractual terms modeled separately using ORCA Scenario Builder where material deviations from statutory regime are identified."

Rule of thumb by source tier and IC use case:

  • All A-badge parameters, stable regime: Cite ORCA directly. No additional verification required for IC screening. Add "statutory terms as of Aug 2026" qualifier.
  • B-badge parameters, established producer: Cite with "verified secondary source" qualifier. Cross-check one key parameter against the operator's most recent annual report before FID submission.
  • C-badge parameters, any use case: Flag as "modeled estimate — requires legal/in-country verification before FID." Do not present as verified fact in IC submissions. Use Scenario Builder to sensitize the key uncertain parameter ±5pp and present as a range.
  • Any parameter, recent reform country: Check Reform Risk tab for 2025–2026 events before citing. If reform found: obtain primary source and verify whether ORCA's August 2026 data captures it.

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). Evidence quality framework: ORCA Methodology, Section 3 (Evidence Tiers A/B/C). Reform history methodology: ORCA Reform History Database sourcing protocol (primary legislation dates verified against EITI country reports, IEA World Energy Legislation Database, and operator 20-F disclosures). Cross-reference: FAQ A57 (what ORCA government take includes and excludes from the statutory calculation); FAQ A103 (stabilization clauses and how they diverge from current-law statutory take); FAQ A126 (sub-national fiscal takes — US severance, Canadian Crown royalties, Brazilian state levies); FAQ A102 (non-statutory fiscal costs: signature bonuses, training levies, surface rentals); FAQ A133 (Scenario Builder calibration for block-specific PSA terms).

A136. ORCA shows government take as a percentage of gross revenue. But our IC model tracks entitlement barrels and working interest production separately. How do I reconcile ORCA's take figure with our WI-basis reserves booking and entitlement-volume production forecast?

The core reconciliation: ORCA take is a gross revenue fraction; your IC model needs a net entitlement fraction. These are structurally different metrics and cannot be compared directly without adjustment. Government take in ORCA measures what fraction of gross project revenue flows to the state across all fiscal instruments (royalties, taxes, profit oil/gas). Your IC model's entitlement barrel count measures what fraction of physical production you book as contractor equity — a different denominator and a different economic concept.

How entitlement differs by fiscal mechanic:

  • Concession (royalty-tax): Contractor holds working interest (WI) title to all production. Entitlement = WI% × gross production. Government take is paid as royalty and CIT from WI revenue. Your WI-basis reserves booking and ORCA's take figure operate on the same gross production base — no adjustment needed beyond WI% scaling. Rule of thumb: Concession take is WI-invariant (A39 covers this).
  • PSC — cost oil + profit oil: Contractor's entitlement = cost oil (up to the cap) + profit oil share. This is typically 20–50% of gross production, not 100%. If ORCA reports 65% government take for an Indonesian PSC, the contractor entitlement is approximately 35% of gross production — but expressed as entitlement barrels, not WI barrels. Under SEC ASC 932-10-55-11 and IFRS 6, PSC reserves are booked on the entitlement basis (cost oil + profit oil attributable to the contractor). A take of 65% does NOT mean WI = 35% — see FAQ A119 for the full SEC reserves booking framework by mechanic.
  • TSC / RSC: Contractor has no entitlement to production. Reserves are not bookable under SEC/IFRS because the contractor receives a fee, not a production interest. Your IC model should treat TSC cashflow as a service fee stream, not an equity production stream (FAQ A119).
  • PRRT (Australia): Contractor holds WI title (same as Concession). Entitlement = WI%. PRRT is a cash-flow based profit tax — it does not alter the production entitlement fraction. Reserves booking is WI-basis.

4-step reconciliation workflow for an IC model:

  1. Identify mechanic and WI%: From ORCA Country Profile, confirm the fiscal mechanic (Concession, PSC, TSC, PRRT). Confirm your WI% from the JOA or bid round award. For PSC, identify the cost recovery cap and profit oil split from the block-specific PSA (use Scenario Builder to enter these if different from statutory defaults — FAQ A133).
  2. Compute entitlement production: For Concession: entitlement = WI% × gross production (straightforward). For PSC: entitlement = (cost oil recovered ÷ gross production) + (profit oil contractor share). Cost oil recovered = min(gross production × opex + capex amortization, cap%). Run this through the Scenario Builder with your production profile to get the annual entitlement split. For PRRT: same as Concession (WI-basis).
  3. Map ORCA take to IC model cashflow, not to entitlement %: Use ORCA's take figure to calibrate the total fiscal burden on contractor cashflow — not to derive entitlement production. In your IC DCF, the revenue line is: entitlement barrels × price × (1 − contractor fiscal burden%). The contractor fiscal burden% = 1 − contractor revenue share, which for a PSC is approximately (1 − take%). Do not apply ORCA take directly to WI production — this double-counts the entitlement adjustment.
  4. IC memo disclosure: Report both metrics. "ORCA statutory government take: [X]% of gross project revenue (Deepwater $75/bbl Scenario Builder basis). Contractor entitlement production: [Y]% of gross production (cost oil + profit oil, modeled on block-specific PSA terms). WI%: [Z]%. SEC/IFRS reserves booking basis: entitlement-volume (PSC) / WI-volume (Concession)." See FAQ A119 for full SEC reserves booking language by mechanic type.

Rule of thumb by mechanic type:

  • Concession: ORCA take applies directly to WI revenue. Entitlement = WI%. No reconciliation gap between take% and production entitlement%.
  • PSC with 60% cost recovery cap and 65/35 profit split: At $75/bbl Deepwater, typical entitlement ≈ 28–38% of gross production (cost oil + profit oil combined). ORCA's ~63–68% take figure represents the state's revenue fraction — not the inverse of your entitlement fraction (because cost oil recovery reduces the effective take basis).
  • PSC with high FTP (20%+): FTP is allocated before cost oil recovery and accrues directly to the state. High FTP compresses contractor entitlement at low prices while take appears similar to a no-FTP peer. IRR impact 3–6pp at $50/bbl (FAQ A100). Adjust your IC model's entitlement production forecast to reflect FTP as a first-deduction before cost oil.
  • TSC / RSC: No production entitlement. ORCA take is essentially 100% minus the remuneration fee as a fraction of gross revenue. IC model: model cashflow as fee income, not production revenue.

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). Cross-reference: FAQ A39 (government take is WI-invariant in concessions); FAQ A100 (FTP first tranche petroleum — impact on PSC entitlement at low prices); FAQ A119 (SEC proved reserves booking by fiscal mechanic — entitlement vs. WI basis); FAQ A120 (non-operator WI analysis); FAQ A133 (Scenario Builder calibration for block-specific PSA terms). SEC ASC 932-10-55-11 (entitlement-volume booking for PSC/RSC); IFRS 6 (exploration for and evaluation of mineral resources — production-sharing accounting basis).

A137. ORCA's IRR model uses a 10% discount rate. Our IC committee uses a project-specific WACC. How do I adjust ORCA's IRR and NPV figures for a different discount rate, and what discount rate should I use for upstream petroleum projects?

The 10% discount rate in ORCA is a standardized benchmarking basis, not a project-specific recommendation. ORCA's IRR is calculated using a 10% nominal discount rate applied to a standardized reference project ($1.2B capex, 50k bbl/d peak, $15/bbl opex for the Deepwater profile — see FAQ A41 for full DCF specification). This allows direct comparison of government take and contractor returns across 185 countries on a consistent basis. Your IC committee's WACC will differ based on your firm's capital structure, country risk premium, and project financing.

Discount rate benchmarks for upstream petroleum:

  • Major IOC (Tier 1 — ExxonMobil, Shell, TotalEnergies, BP, Chevron, Equinor): 8–10% nominal WACC. Lower country risk premium due to portfolio diversification and investment-grade credit. ORCA's 10% basis is consistent with Tier 1 project screening.
  • Independent E&P (Tier 2 — Tullow, Kosmos, Vaalco): 12–15% nominal WACC. Higher equity cost and single-country concentration premium. ORCA's 10% overstates contractor returns for independents in high-risk jurisdictions.
  • National Oil Company (NOC) joint ventures: 8–12% nominal WACC, depending on host government's cost of capital and NOC mandate (commercial vs. strategic). NOC carry provisions (FAQ A32) may reduce effective WACC below commercial benchmarks.
  • Country risk premium (sovereign floor): Add 2–4pp for Sub-Saharan Africa frontier, 1–3pp for Middle East/MENA, 0–1pp for OECD/Norway/Australia. Rule of thumb: if ORCA's Stability Score is <3 (volatile), add 1–2pp to your discount rate.

How to adjust ORCA's IRR for your WACC: ORCA reports project IRR — the discount rate at which contractor NPV = 0. IRR is discount-rate-independent by definition. To evaluate a project against your WACC: if ORCA IRR > your WACC, the project clears your hurdle rate under the standardized profile. To compute NPV at your specific WACC, use the Scenario Builder (FAQ A41) — it calculates contractor NPV at the 10% ORCA basis. For a different discount rate, scale NPV directionally: for every 1pp increase in discount rate above 10%, expect NPV to decline approximately 4–8% for a 15-year project (duration-dependent; longer-lived projects have higher discount rate sensitivity).

4-step IC workflow for discount rate adjustment:

  1. Establish your firm's WACC: Use your treasury / corporate finance team's project-specific WACC. Upstream projects typically use nominal, post-tax WACC. Note whether your WACC is real or nominal — ORCA uses nominal (no inflation adjustment).
  2. Compare ORCA IRR to your WACC: If ORCA IRR > WACC, the project clears the hurdle under standardized assumptions. If ORCA IRR is near your WACC (within 3pp), run the Scenario Builder with your specific project parameters before drawing conclusions.
  3. Apply country risk overlay: For frontier or politically volatile jurisdictions (Stability Score <3), add 1–3pp to your hurdle rate and recheck the IRR screen. ORCA's Reform Risk tab and Stability Score provide the primary inputs for this adjustment.
  4. IC memo language: "ORCA reports IRR of [X]% for [Country] at $75/bbl Deepwater basis (10% discount rate, standardized profile — FAQ A41). At our [Y]% WACC, the project [clears / misses] the IC hurdle by [Z]pp. Country risk premium of [P]pp applied for [sovereign rationale]."

Rule of thumb by project type: Deepwater projects have high upfront capex and are more sensitive to discount rate than onshore mature plays. A 2pp increase in discount rate reduces IRR-to-WACC spread by approximately 2pp for onshore projects and 3–4pp for deepwater due to longer payback periods. LNG projects are the most discount-rate-sensitive due to 20–25 year project life.

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). Cross-reference: FAQ A41 (IRR DCF model specification — full reference project parameters); FAQ A63 (Breakeven + IRR composite project viability screen); FAQ A117 (portfolio asset review — 4-metric triage framework); FAQ A133 (Scenario Builder calibration). Industry benchmarks: Wood Mackenzie Upstream Cost of Capital Report (2024); EY Global Oil & Gas Transactions Review (2025); IOC public WACC disclosures (annual reports, 2024–2025).

A138. How should I interpret ORCA government take figures in the context of our company's energy transition strategy? We need to identify which countries in our portfolio carry the highest fiscal risk as demand shifts over the next decade.

ORCA's three transition-sensitive metrics — Price Swing, Breakeven, and Reform Risk — form a trifecta for fiscal transition screening. Government take alone is insufficient for transition-era portfolio analysis. A 60% take regime with a $35/bbl breakeven and a Stability Score of 5 is fundamentally different from a 60% take regime with an $80/bbl breakeven and three fiscal law changes in the past decade. The latter is the higher transition risk.

The transition-screening trifecta:

  • Price Swing (take at $75 minus take at $50): Measures fiscal amplification of price volatility. A Swing >20pp means the government captures a large share of price upside but the contractor absorbs a disproportionate share of price downside — directly relevant in a $50–70/bbl energy transition demand-shock scenario. See FAQ A56 for the $50/bbl stress-test workflow.
  • Breakeven price: The oil price at which contractor NPV reaches zero. Countries with Breakeven >$65/bbl are structurally vulnerable to a sustained low-price environment driven by demand substitution. Breakeven Map (FAQ A127) provides a direct visual scan. Coverage: 68 of 185 countries.
  • Reform Risk (Stability Score + Reform History): Countries with Stability Score <3 and a history of government-favorable reforms are statistically more likely to tighten terms in a revenue-constrained environment. High-take + low-stability is the worst-case transition combination. Use the Reform Risk tab to scan your portfolio countries. See FAQ A73 for stabilization clause vs. Stability Score reconciliation.

4-step decarbonization exposure audit using ORCA:

  1. Run Fiscal Compare at $50/bbl: Use the Custom price and sort by Govt Take ascending. Flag all countries where take at $50 exceeds 65% — these regimes leave minimal contractor margin in a demand-driven price shock.
  2. Cross-filter by Price Swing >20pp: Export to XLSX, add a Swing column filter. Countries with both high take at $50 AND high Swing are doubly exposed — they deliver less to the contractor when prices fall and more to the government when prices rise.
  3. Apply the Reform Risk overlay: For each flagged country, check the Stability Score in Country Profile. Score <3 + recent hostile reform in Reform History = highest transition exposure. Score 4–5 + no recent reform = lower transition risk despite high statutory take.
  4. IC memo presentation: Build a 3-column portfolio table: Country / Take@$50 / Swing / Stability Score / Transition Flag (High/Medium/Low). Use ORCA XLSX export for the base data and add the Transition Flag column manually using the three-metric framework above.

Rule of thumb by IOC transition strategy type:

  • Net-zero committed IOC (BP/Shell trajectory): Focus on Breakeven <$45 + Swing <15pp + Stability Score ≥4. Short-cycle, low-cost assets in stable regimes. Norway PRRT and Gulf of Mexico Concession are benchmarks.
  • Production-volume IOC (TotalEnergies/Equinor trajectory): Breakeven <$55 + Swing <20pp acceptable. Focus on frontier PSC regimes with strong stabilization clauses (Angola, UAE) and transparent reform risk.
  • NOC/resource-nationalist priority: Fiscal metrics secondary to political mandate. Transition fiscal risk may actually increase government share as revenues fall — budget pressure triggers upstream tax reform faster in commodity-dependent states (Nigeria, Angola, Iraq, Algeria).

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). Cross-reference: FAQ A56 ($50/bbl energy-transition demand-shock stress test); FAQ A73 (stabilization clause vs. Reform Risk Stability Score); FAQ A99 (carbon pricing overlay); FAQ A117 (portfolio asset review triage); FAQ A127 (Breakeven Map vs. Fiscal Compare differentiation); FAQ A134 (portfolio fiscal mechanic concentration risk). Industry context: IEA World Energy Outlook 2024 (demand scenarios); Wood Mackenzie Energy Transition Outlook (2024); IRENA Renewable Power Generation Costs (2024).

A139. ORCA's DCF is unlevered (100% equity). Our IC models typically use 60–70% debt financing. How do I reconcile ORCA's government take and IRR figures with a levered project model for an IC submission?

ORCA uses an unlevered (all-equity) DCF by design — this ensures government take is comparable across all 185 countries regardless of each company's financing structure. A levered IRR is project-company specific, not regime-specific. For IC submissions, you apply a levered adjustment on top of ORCA's unlevered baseline rather than replacing it.

Why the distinction matters by fiscal mechanic:

  • Concession regimes (royalty + CIT): Interest expense is typically deductible against CIT, creating a tax shield. At 65% debt, a 30% CIT regime yields a ~6–9pp IRR uplift from the interest tax shield on a standard $1.2B Deepwater project. CIT deductibility is confirmed in most OECD concession regimes (Norway, UK, Australia, Netherlands).
  • PSC regimes (cost recovery + profit oil): Debt service is generally recoverable under cost oil, but interest deductibility rules vary. In Angola, Nigeria, and Malaysia, interest on shareholder loans is often capped or ring-fenced at the license level, limiting the tax shield value. In Indonesia Gross Split PSCs, there is no cost recovery at all — leverage provides no fiscal benefit. Levered uplift: 2–5pp IRR vs. 6–9pp for concessions.
  • PRRT and SPT regimes (Australia / Norway): PRRT uplift rates on unrecovered costs (currently 13.4% for exploration, 5% + LTBR for development) act as a form of implicit interest deductibility at the regime level. Additional explicit interest deductibility against PRRT is limited. Norway SPT: interest deductible at the standard CIT layer but not the SPT layer. Net levered uplift: 3–5pp IRR.

Thin-cap rules — country matrix:

  • Nigeria: 3:1 debt-to-equity cap; interest on shareholder loans exceeding the cap is non-deductible under CITA Section 27. Post-PIA 2021: ring-fencing at field level limits interest allocation across licenses.
  • Angola: Sonangol approval required for shareholder loan structures; interest deductibility at Decree-Law 07/11 CIT (25%) layer only, not cost oil.
  • Kazakhstan: 4:1 thin-cap ratio under Tax Code Article 246. For PSA/PSC projects governed by subsoil use agreements, contractual stabilization may override the code — verify contract terms.
  • UAE / Qatar / Iraq TSC: IOC financing structure largely irrelevant — government take is determined by TSC/RSC fee, not CIT on contractor profit. Leverage provides no material fiscal benefit in these regimes.
  • Norway / UK / Australia / Netherlands: Full interest deductibility at CIT layer; transfer pricing arm's-length requirement applies to related-party debt.

4-step levered IRR adjustment workflow for IC submissions:

  1. Establish the ORCA unlevered IRR baseline: Run Scenario Builder with your project parameters (capex, opex, peak rate, price). Record the unlevered contractor IRR. This is your regime-comparable baseline — cite it as "ORCA unlevered IRR" in the IC memo.
  2. Apply the interest tax shield: Calculate the annual interest payment (debt amount × rate). Multiply by the effective deductible tax rate (CIT for concessions; zero for most PSCs without cost oil interest recovery). Discount the tax shield at the cost of debt. Add to unlevered project NPV to get levered NPV, then re-derive levered IRR.
  3. Check thin-cap and ring-fencing constraints: For Nigeria, Angola, Kazakhstan — cap the deductible interest at the applicable debt-to-equity ratio. For PSC regimes — confirm whether interest is recoverable under cost oil or excluded. Adjust the tax shield value accordingly.
  4. IC memo disclosure: Present both metrics: "ORCA unlevered IRR: [X]% (regime-comparable, 100% equity basis) | Company levered IRR: [Y]% (60% debt at [rate]%, [country] thin-cap rules applied)." Do not replace the unlevered figure — include both for comparability.

Rule of thumb by financing structure:

  • 60% debt, OECD concession, 30% CIT: Levered IRR ≈ Unlevered IRR + 6–9pp (strong tax shield)
  • 60% debt, West Africa PSC, ring-fenced: Levered IRR ≈ Unlevered IRR + 2–4pp (limited cost oil recovery)
  • 60% debt, Indonesia Gross Split: Levered IRR ≈ Unlevered IRR (no cost recovery layer — leverage fiscally neutral)
  • TSC/RSC Gulf (UAE, Iraq, Qatar): Levered IRR ≈ Unlevered IRR (fee-based regime — financing structure irrelevant to government take)

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). Cross-reference: FAQ A8 (DCF methodology and discount rate); FAQ A41 (IRR DCF model specification); FAQ A69 (fiscal ring-fencing); FAQ A80 (cost recovery cap mechanics). Industry context: Wood Mackenzie Project Economics Guide (2024); EY Global Oil & Gas Tax Guide (2025); IHS Markit Upstream Fiscal Terms Database (2025).

A140. ORCA shows a 60% government take for both a PSC country and a Concession country. Are they economically equivalent for the contractor? How do I adjust for mechanic-specific distortions in cross-regime comparisons?

A 60% take in a PSC and a 60% take in a Concession are not economically equivalent — ORCA's take% is a standardized output metric computed on the same reference project, but the underlying fiscal mechanics create different contractor cashflow profiles even at the same headline take. Three structural differences drive this:

  • Cost recovery timing (PSC only): In a PSC, the contractor recovers capital and operating costs from cost oil before any profit oil split. This front-loads contractor cashflows — recovery happens in years 1–4 of production, before government profit oil. In a concession, royalties are paid from first production (day one), and CIT is paid on profits. A PSC at 60% take will typically have a higher early IRR than a concession at 60% take because government revenue is deferred to the back end. The Scenario Builder IRR accounts for this timing difference — use it to compare, not the take% alone.
  • Price-sensitivity asymmetry (progressive vs. flat mechanics): A concession with a flat 20% royalty + 35% CIT has take that rises only modestly with price (mostly through higher taxable profit). A PSC with an R-factor profit oil tier jumps from 55% at $50/bbl to 72% at $125/bbl — the same "60% take at $75" hides a 17pp swing. Use the Swing column in the Explorer or the 4-price view in Fiscal Compare to assess price-sensitivity alongside the headline take.
  • Cost recovery cap (PSC regimes with a cap): If a PSC limits cost oil to 60% of gross revenue (Nigeria deepwater, Angola Block 17, Malaysia), contractors in high-cost projects may be unable to recover all costs in the first production years. Uncovered costs carry forward, but this delays recovery and reduces effective IRR. A 60% take PSC with an 80% cost recovery cap is materially better than a 60% take PSC with a 50% cap. Use the Evidence tab on Country Profile to verify the cap rate — it appears as cost_recovery_cap in the fiscal facts table.

4-step IC workflow for cross-mechanic take comparisons:

  1. Use IRR, not take, as the primary ranking metric when comparing across mechanics. Run Scenario Builder with the same project parameters in each target country. IRR captures cashflow timing, cost recovery, and price path — take% does not. Countries where IRR data is unavailable (111/185) should be ranked by take with an explicit caveat in the IC memo.
  2. Check the Swing column (take@$125 − take@$50). A PSC with >20pp swing will look competitive at $75 but punishing at $100+. Flag high-swing regimes in the IC memo if the project NPV is sensitive to price upside.
  3. Note the cost recovery cap for any PSC: 80% cap is standard for most deepwater PSCs; 50–60% cap materially reduces early cash flows in high-capex projects. The cap appears in the Country Profile fiscal facts table if sourced.
  4. IC memo disclosure: "Government take figures are computed on a standardized basis (ORCA Deepwater reference project, $75/bbl). Concession and PSC takes are not directly comparable at the cashflow level — see IRR and Swing columns for a timing-adjusted and price-sensitivity-adjusted comparison (ORCA v274)."

Rule of thumb by mechanic pair:

  • PSC vs. Concession at equal take%: PSC typically shows 1–3pp higher IRR due to cost recovery front-loading. If both show the same IRR, the concession is economically equivalent or better (no cap risk).
  • Flat Concession vs. R-factor PSC at equal take%: At $75 base case they look equal; above $100/bbl the PSC can become 10–20pp higher take. Prefer flat concession if your price deck goes to $100+.
  • TSC/RSC (Iraq/UAE model) vs. PSC: TSC/RSC take is mechanically different — contractor receives a fixed remuneration fee per barrel, not a share of profit oil. At low prices, TSC/RSC appears high-take (small denominator); at high prices it looks low-take. The TSC/RSC Swing column is the most useful diagnostic — it directly shows price sensitivity of the remuneration structure.

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). Cross-reference: FAQ A8 (DCF methodology); FAQ A42 (cost recovery cap mechanics); FAQ A47 (R-factor mechanics); FAQ A70 (R-factor PSCs and price sensitivity); FAQ A139 (levered vs. unlevered IRR). Industry context: Johnston, D. (2003) International Exploration Economics, Risk, and Contract Analysis; Wood Mackenzie Fiscal Terms Primer (2024).

A141. ORCA reports take at the country level. When our company holds multiple blocks in the same country under different PSAs, how does fiscal ring-fencing affect our effective consolidated take — and how should we present this in an IC memo?

ORCA's country-level take is a per-contract benchmark, not a consolidated multi-block figure. When an IOC holds multiple blocks in the same jurisdiction, the fiscal ring-fence structure determines whether losses, cost pools, and production from different blocks can be consolidated for tax purposes — directly affecting the effective take on the portfolio.

Three ring-fence structures and their IC implications:

  • License-level ring-fence (Nigeria, Angola, Libya): Each PSA is a separate fiscal ring. Cost oil from Block A cannot offset the profit oil base on Block B. A low-production or pre-production block generates no cross-block tax relief. Effective consolidated take approaches the sum of per-block takes — no inter-block uplift. For a portfolio with one producing and two appraisal blocks, the IC effective take equals the producing block's take; the appraisals are pure cost with no offset. ORCA's per-contract take is the correct per-block benchmark.
  • Company-level ring-fence (UK, Norway, Australia): All blocks are consolidated for tax purposes at the company level. Exploration costs, development capex, and decommissioning provisions on non-producing blocks reduce the taxable base on producing blocks. In Norway, this is particularly powerful: a company with three blocks — one producing, two in exploration — effectively receives a 78% uplift on its exploration costs against the producing block's SPT base. IC effective take falls below ORCA's per-block benchmark whenever the company has pre-production costs to offset.
  • Field-level ring-fence (USA GoM, Malaysia Petronas PSC): Each field (not license area) is ring-fenced. Relevant for unitized fields straddling multiple PSA areas. Contractor entitlement is computed field-by-field; cross-field consolidation is not permitted. ORCA's country-level take applies at the field level — no adjustment required for multi-block portfolios unless blocks straddle a field unit.

4-step IC workflow for multi-block consolidated take:

  1. Identify the ring-fence type from the Country Profile fiscal facts table (ring_fence_type) and the Evidence badge. If not sourced, classify by country: Nigeria/Angola/Libya/Kazakhstan = license-level; UK/Norway/Australia/Denmark = company-level; USA GoM/Malaysia = field-level.
  2. For license-level countries: use ORCA's per-contract take as-is for each block. Present a weighted-average effective take across your block portfolio using production volumes as weights. Example IC memo language: "Effective consolidated take across three blocks (weighted by gross production): 64.2% — consistent with ORCA per-contract benchmark of 62–67% for this jurisdiction (ORCA v274)."
  3. For company-level countries: use ORCA's take as the producing-block baseline, then compute an explicit exploration cost offset. Rule of thumb: each $100M of pre-production costs in a company-ring-fence jurisdiction reduces effective take by ~0.3–0.8pp on a 50k bbl/d producing block over 10 years. Model this in Scenario Builder by reducing the effective opex + capex base for the producing block by the annual exploration cost amortized over the project life.
  4. IC memo disclosure: State the ring-fence type, the block count, and whether the consolidation produces a material difference from the per-block benchmark. Threshold for materiality: >1pp difference in effective consolidated take vs. ORCA benchmark. Example: "Fiscal ring-fence: license-level (Nigeria). Each of our three blocks is independently ring-fenced; no cross-block consolidation applies. Consolidated effective take approximates per-block average of 63.5% (ORCA v274, Deepwater $75/bbl)."

Rule of thumb by ring-fence type:

  • License-level (Nigeria, Angola, Libya, Congo): ORCA per-contract take = correct effective take per block. Consolidated take = production-weighted average. No cross-block adjustment.
  • Company-level (UK, Norway, Australia, Denmark): ORCA per-contract take understates effective take for a company with only producing assets; overstates effective take for a company with significant pre-production costs. Adjust by ~0.3–0.8pp per $100M exploration cost in the same jurisdiction.
  • Field-level (USA GoM, Malaysia): ORCA = per-field take. Multi-block portfolios aggregate at the field level; no cross-field adjustment unless a unitized field straddles contract areas.

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). Cross-reference: FAQ A69 (ring-fencing structural types); FAQ A39 (working interest and take invariance); FAQ A57 (exclusions from ORCA take); FAQ A131 (NOC working interest). Industry context: Johnston, D. (2003) International Exploration Economics, Risk, and Contract Analysis; KPMG Global Oil and Gas Tax Guide (2024); Wood Mackenzie Fiscal Terms Primer (2024).

A142. A target country's PSC has a First Tranche Petroleum (FTP) provision of 20%. How does FTP change the government take calculation, and why does it matter more than the headline profit oil split?

FTP is the most distorting single term in a PSC fiscal structure — it directly reduces the cost recovery pool before cost oil is allocated. A PSC with 20% FTP and 60/40 profit oil split is materially worse for the contractor than the same split without FTP — even though the profit oil percentages look identical. Understanding this distinction is mandatory for any IC memo involving a PSC jurisdiction.

How FTP works in the DCF mechanics:

  1. Gross revenue is divided first. Under a PSC with FTP, the host government (or NOC) receives FTP% of gross production before any cost recovery allocation. This is a "royalty-equivalent" carve-out at the top of the cashflow waterfall.
  2. Remaining revenue enters cost recovery. The contractor recovers allowable costs from the post-FTP revenue pool (subject to the cost recovery cap — typically 60–80% of post-FTP revenue).
  3. Profit oil is then split. Post-cost-recovery revenue is shared per the profit oil split. The contractor's total take includes: (a) cost oil recovery; (b) contractor share of profit oil; minus (c) CIT on contractor profit.
  4. The FTP belongs to the government. In most jurisdictions (Indonesia, Malaysia, Libya), the NOC or government receives FTP directly. In some regimes, the NOC shares FTP pro-rata to its working interest (Angola Sonangol structure). ORCA models FTP as a government-side allocation in all cases; it is included in the government take figure.

Why FTP matters more than the profit oil split at low oil prices:

  • FTP compresses early-life contractor cashflow. In the first 3–5 years of production, when cost oil recovery is largest, FTP reduces the recoverable base — effectively delaying cost recovery by the same proportion as the FTP rate. A 20% FTP on a $500M/yr revenue project removes $100M/yr from the cost recovery pool before the contractor sees any cashflow.
  • IRR impact is front-loaded. Because FTP hits Year-1 through Year-5 most severely, its IRR impact is larger than its steady-state take impact would suggest. Rule of thumb: a 20% FTP in a typical deepwater PSC reduces contractor IRR by 2–4pp relative to the equivalent no-FTP structure — at the same stated profit oil split and same CIT rate.
  • At low prices, FTP can create negative contractor cashflow. When oil prices fall below the cost recovery breakeven (opex + capex amortization), the contractor's post-FTP cost recovery may be insufficient to recover costs. The contractor pays FTP but cannot recover costs because the post-FTP revenue pool is too small. This is the structural reason why high-FTP PSCs show compressed IRR at $50/bbl — the take figure at $75/bbl understates the downside risk.

FTP rate benchmarks by jurisdiction:

  • Indonesia (Gross Split replaces FTP since 2017): Pre-2017 PSC contracts carried 20% FTP. New Gross Split contracts have no FTP; the contractor receives a fixed gross revenue share instead. For legacy contracts, ORCA reflects the pre-2017 FTP-PSC terms; new blocks use Gross Split.
  • Malaysia (Petronas PSC): 10% FTP standard, with NOC cost recovery rights. Effective FTP rate slightly lower than statutory due to NOC cost share structure.
  • Libya (EPSA-IV model): 20–25% FTP in recent bid rounds; historically up to 35% for mature fields. Libya's high FTP + high profit oil split produces one of the most front-loaded contractor cost structures in Africa.
  • Angola (Sonangol PSC): No FTP in most production contracts; cost recovery cap of 50% applies instead. Angola's structure is more favorable to contractors than Nigeria's in early-field-life cashflow terms.
  • Nigeria (DPR PSC): No FTP; 60% cost recovery cap. Profit oil split is the primary government take variable. ORCA's Nigeria figure reflects the cost-recovery cap structure, not an FTP carve-out.
  • Iraq KRG (PSC): No FTP; royalty of 10% + profit oil split + CIT. The royalty functions as an FTP-equivalent but is structured differently (it applies to gross production but is a flat royalty, not a cost-pool carve-out).

4-step IC workflow for FTP-bearing PSCs:

  1. Confirm FTP presence and rate from Country Profile. Check the ftp_rate and ftp_applies fields in the Evidence panel. A non-zero FTP rate means the contractor's effective cost recovery base is (1 − FTP%) × gross revenue — not gross revenue.
  2. Run Scenario Builder at the FTP-adjusted cost recovery base. In the Scenario Builder, the cost recovery cap input should reflect the post-FTP pool. If the country's cost recovery cap is 60% and FTP is 20%, the effective cost recovery available to the contractor is 60% × (1 − 20%) = 48% of gross revenue. Enter this effective cap when calibrating a custom regime.
  3. Run a $50/bbl stress test. If the ORCA $75/bbl IRR is <15% for a high-FTP PSC (Libya, legacy Indonesia, Malaysia deepwater), the $50/bbl scenario often turns IRR negative — the contractor's FTP obligation exceeds recoverable cost oil at low prices. Model this explicitly and disclose in the IC memo.
  4. IC memo disclosure: Always disclose FTP rate alongside the take and IRR figures. Example: "Government take 68.3% at $75/bbl (ORCA v274, standardized Deepwater profile). PSC includes 20% FTP — effective cost recovery base is post-FTP gross revenue. At $50/bbl, contractor IRR is estimated at [X]% using Scenario Builder with FTP-adjusted cost recovery cap (see Appendix H). The FTP structure creates asymmetric downside risk vs. a no-FTP concession at equivalent headline take."

Rule of thumb for IC memo language: "Jurisdiction X operates a PSC with [Y]% FTP (ORCA v274, source: [PSA text/Wood Mac/EY]). FTP is a pre-cost-recovery carve-out that reduces the contractor's cost recovery pool to [1−Y]% of gross revenue before cost oil allocation. At the ORCA Deepwater reference project ($1.2B capex, 50k bbl/d, $15/bbl opex), the FTP-adjusted contractor IRR is [Z]% at $75/bbl and [W]% at $50/bbl — compare to the no-FTP equivalent IRR of [A]% and [B]% respectively. The [Y]pp FTP rate represents an incremental [delta]pp IRR penalty vs. an equivalent concession structure at the same headline profit oil split."

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). Cross-reference: FAQ A42 (cost recovery cap mechanics); FAQ A100 (FTP PSC entitlement barrels); FAQ A136 (entitlement reconciliation); FAQ A84 (gas-weighted adjustment). Industry context: Johnston, D. (2003) International Exploration Economics, Risk, and Contract Analysis; Wood Mackenzie Fiscal Terms Primer (2024); Rystad Energy UCube Indonesia Gross Split (2024).

A143. A gas condensate field produces both dry gas (sold to a domestic market at regulated prices) and condensate (sold at international oil prices). How does this split affect the government take calculation, and how should I adjust the ORCA figure for an IC memo on a gas-condensate project?

ORCA's government take figures are calibrated to a crude oil reference project — they require explicit adjustment for gas-condensate fields where a significant share of revenue comes from regulated-price gas. The degree of adjustment depends on the gas/condensate split, the domestic market pricing structure, and whether the fiscal regime applies separate royalty or cost recovery rules to gas vs. liquids.

Why gas-condensate take differs from crude oil take:

  • Regulated gas prices reduce gross revenue. In most producing jurisdictions (Nigeria, Indonesia, Egypt, Malaysia, Algeria, Bangladesh), domestic gas is sold at a regulated price — typically $1–4/MMBtu — while international LNG or export prices are $7–15/MMBtu. A field that earns $3/MMBtu on 60% of its revenue is structurally different from a crude oil field at $75/bbl equivalent, even if the statutory take % is identical.
  • Cost recovery is split by product in many PSC regimes. Indonesia PTK 007, Malaysia Petronas PSC, and Egypt EGPC agreements maintain separate cost recovery and profit-sharing accounts for gas and oil. Condensate typically follows oil terms; dry gas follows gas terms. Cross-subsidization between pools is generally not permitted — cost recovery shortfalls in the gas pool cannot be recovered from the oil/condensate profit pool.
  • R-factor PSCs reset faster on condensate. Because condensate revenues accrue to the cost recovery pool at a higher realized price than regulated gas, the R-factor (cumulative revenue ÷ cumulative cost) rises faster for condensate-dominant production — triggering higher-tier government profit oil shares earlier in field life than a dry-gas profile would.
  • PRRT (Australia) has explicit gas ring-fence provisions. The Petroleum Resource Rent Tax applies separately to gas projects vs. oil projects in most jurisdictions, with separate uplift rates and augmented bond provisions for LNG. Offshore gas projects under PRRT require explicit separation of LNG vs. condensate cashflows in the assessable petroleum revenue calculation.

4-step IC adjustment workflow for gas-condensate projects:

  1. Identify the gas/condensate/crude split from your project economics. Express each product as a % of total revenue (not production volume) at your reference price assumption. For a field with 60% domestic gas at $2/MMBtu, 15% condensate at $70/bbl, and 25% crude at $75/bbl, revenue-weighted pricing is materially below the ORCA $75/bbl crude oil basis.
  2. Apply ORCA's country take as a ceiling for the condensate and crude component. Use Fiscal Compare to screen the country; the ORCA figure correctly describes the condensate and crude take. For the gas component, reduce gross revenue by the ratio of regulated price to international price (e.g. $2/$8 = 25%) before applying the same take structure — this is a conservative approximation that understates the true effective take because cost recovery and profit oil calculations are cumulative, not per-product-per-year.
  3. Run the Scenario Builder with a revenue-weighted effective price. If your gas/condensate field has a blended revenue-weighted price of $45/bbl equivalent (reflecting low domestic gas pricing), run the Scenario Builder at $45 to generate a take and IRR that better approximates the project's actual revenue profile. Compare to the ORCA $75 result to calibrate the downward adjustment.
  4. IC memo disclosure: Always disclose the product split and pricing assumption alongside the ORCA take figure. Example: "ORCA government take of 58.3% at $75/bbl crude applies to condensate and oil revenue. Domestic gas (60% of revenue) is sold at regulated tariff of $2/MMBtu; blended project revenue is ~$38/bbl crude equivalent at current gas pricing. Field-specific effective take is estimated at [X]% using Scenario Builder at $38/bbl. See Appendix G for full product-weighted take decomposition." Cross-reference FAQ A60 for additional gas-specific fiscal adjustment methodology.

Rule of thumb by jurisdiction and gas pricing structure:

  • Indonesia (PTK 007 PSC, DMO): Domestic Market Obligation gas at government-set price ($2–3/MMBtu); typically 25% of production at regulated price for the first 5 years of production. Use ORCA figure for the export/condensate component; reduce gas-stream revenue by 65–75% relative to export price for DMO-obligated volumes.
  • Nigeria (DPR PSC, gas ring-fence): Gas is subject to separate ring-fence; condensate follows oil terms. For associated gas projects, ORCA crude take understates the all-in burden — Nigeria's gas fiscal terms are less contractor-favorable than oil for most block types.
  • Malaysia (Petronas PSC): Gas and liquids share the same PSC cost recovery pool but are metered and priced separately. Condensate at international price; pipeline gas at Petronas offtake price (~$3.5/MMBtu). Revenue-weighted adjustment required for fields with >30% gas by energy content.
  • Australia (PRRT + condensate): Condensate is taxed under PRRT alongside oil; dry gas project PRRT is assessed separately with higher uplift (150% vs 125% for exploration wells). For integrated LNG projects, the gas and condensate PRRT pools are typically ring-fenced at the project level. ORCA's Australia figure reflects condensate/oil PRRT; LNG stream requires separate PRRT modeling.
  • Norway (SPT + condensate): Condensate is treated as crude for SPT purposes; associated gas sold domestically follows separate tariff rules that are typically revenue-neutral at Norwegian hub prices (TTF-linked). ORCA's Norway figure is appropriate for condensate-dominant fields; gas-dominant Barents Sea assets require Norwegian Petroleum Tax Office gas tariff review.

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). Cross-reference: FAQ A60 (gas-weighted country adjustment); FAQ A84 (gas condensate DMO pricing); FAQ A126 (sub-national fiscal levies on gas production); FAQ A132 (PRRT pre-development treatment). Industry context: Johnston, D. (2003) International Exploration Economics, Risk, and Contract Analysis; IEA (2023) Upstream Oil and Gas Investment Handbook; Wood Mackenzie Gas Fiscal Terms Review (2024); Indonesia PTK 007 Rev.3 (SKK Migas, 2018).

A144. A PSC has a sliding-scale profit oil split based on the R-factor. The contract tiers are: R < 1.0 = 70/30 (govt/contractor); 1.0–2.0 = 80/20; > 2.0 = 90/10. How does ORCA approximate this, and how do I calculate the weighted-average R-factor trajectory for a project to determine which tier dominates?

ORCA approximates sliding-scale R-factor PSCs using the mid-tier profit oil split — typically the Tier 2 split — as the representative government take figure. This approximation is conservative for high-price scenarios (where actual take is higher) and optimistic for low-price scenarios (where actual take is lower, but cost recovery is still ongoing). For a three-tier PSC, the mid-tier approximation is usually within 3–6pp of the project-life-weighted average effective take at $75/bbl on the ORCA reference project.

How the R-factor is defined and calculated:

  • R-factor = cumulative revenue ÷ cumulative cost. R = (cumulative contractor gross revenue, including cost oil receipts) ÷ (cumulative contractor capital expenditure + operating expenditure). R starts at zero (before any production revenue), rises as cumulative receipts grow, and crosses each tier threshold at a specific field-life year.
  • The most common definition uses cumulative contractor receipts. "Contractor gross revenue" in most PSC definitions includes: (a) all cost oil recovered (used to pay back capex and opex); (b) contractor's profit oil share at the current tier. FTP, royalty, and NOC WI share are excluded from the contractor's cumulative receipts — they belong to the government side of the ledger.
  • Each year's profit oil split is determined by that year's R-factor. R is recalculated annually. In early years (R < 1.0), the 70/30 split applies. Once cumulative receipts exceed cumulative cost (R > 1.0), the split shifts to 80/20 — typically in Year 4–7 for a $1.2B deepwater project at $75/bbl. R crosses 2.0 (90/10 tier) in Year 8–12 for the same project, after all capital is recovered and OPEX cash flows are steady.
  • Lower oil prices delay R-factor progression. At $50/bbl, cumulative revenue grows more slowly — R may not cross the 1.0 threshold until Year 6–9, meaning the contractor spends more years in the favorable Tier 1 (70/30) — but this benefit is more than offset by the lower total revenue. The R-factor system is inherently price-progressive: at high prices, the contractor reaches Tier 3 (90/10) faster, locking in high government take for more of the project's productive life.

How to calculate the project-life-weighted average take for a specific R-factor PSC:

  1. Build the annual R-factor trajectory. In your project DCF, compute cumulative contractor receipts (cost oil + contractor profit oil) and cumulative costs (capex + opex) year-by-year. Calculate R for each year. Identify the year in which R crosses each tier threshold (1.0, 2.0, etc.).
  2. Apply the correct profit oil split to each year. For years where R < 1.0, use Tier 1 split (30% contractor). For R = 1.0–2.0, use Tier 2 (20% contractor). For R > 2.0, use Tier 3 (10% contractor). The transition is typically a step function, not gradual — the split changes in the year R crosses the threshold.
  3. Compute production-weighted effective take. Weight each year's effective government take (cost oil allocation + government profit oil + royalty + CIT) by that year's production volume. The production-weighted average is the "project-life government take" — the comparable metric to ORCA's single-number take figure.
  4. Compare to ORCA's approximation and adjust the IC memo accordingly. If the ORCA figure is 72% (mid-tier approximation), but your trajectory shows the project spends 8 of 15 years in Tier 3 (R > 2.0), the actual effective take at $75/bbl may be 76–79%. Disclose the deviation in the IC memo: "ORCA reports 72% take (mid-tier R-factor approximation). Project-specific weighted-average take is estimated at 77% based on ORCA v274 Scenario Builder trajectory at $75/bbl Deepwater profile."

Common R-factor PSC countries and their ORCA approximation accuracy:

  • Indonesia (pre-2017 legacy PSC, 3-tier R-factor): ORCA mid-tier approximation typically 3–5pp below actual high-price take. Legacy contracts vary; check Country Profile for block-specific tier schedule.
  • Angola (Sonangol PSC, 2-tier or 3-tier by area): ORCA approximation within 2–4pp for standard deepwater blocks. High-FTP blocks (Block 32/33/17) diverge more — see FAQ A142 for FTP interaction with R-factor timing.
  • Malaysia (Petronas PSC, 2-tier R-factor): R-factor threshold typically at 1.5; ORCA mid-tier approximation usually within 2pp. Gas cost-recovery ring-fence can shift the effective R-factor trajectory — see FAQ A143 for gas-condensate treatment.
  • Kazakhstan (Subsoil Use Agreements, 3-tier R-factor + export customs duty): R-factor divergence from ORCA approximation can be 5–10pp at high prices — Kazakhstan's export customs duty adds a price-progressive fiscal layer on top of the PSC split that ORCA does not fully capture in the headline take.
  • Papua New Guinea (PNGL PSC): 2-tier R-factor; ORCA mid-tier approximation within 2–3pp for standard offshore projects.

Rule of thumb for IC memo language: "Government take per ORCA v274 (standardized reference project) is [X]%. This figure uses a mid-tier R-factor approximation. At $75/bbl, the reference project's R-factor is estimated to cross R = 1.0 in Year [Y] and R = 2.0 in Year [Z] — implying the production-weighted take at $75/bbl is approximately [X + delta]%, with additional upside to [X + max_delta]% at $100/bbl where Tier 3 is reached earlier. A project-specific R-factor schedule analysis is recommended for investment committee submission." Cross-reference FAQ A47 for R-factor mechanics overview and ORCA's `profit_oil_tier_schedule` field in the Country Profile API output.

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). Cross-reference: FAQ A47 (R-factor mechanics overview); FAQ A70 (R-factor in PSC context); FAQ A142 (FTP interaction with cost recovery); FAQ A100 (PSC entitlement barrels). Industry context: Johnston, D. (2003) International Exploration Economics, Risk, and Contract Analysis; Rystad Energy UCube R-Factor Tier Methodology Note (2023); Wood Mackenzie Fiscal Terms Primer — R-Factor PSC chapter (2024).

A145. A NOC holds a 30% state equity interest in a PSC alongside an IOC operator. ORCA reports government take as 72%. Does the NOC's equity participation affect the contractor's effective take, and how do I adjust the ORCA figure for an IC analysis that separates NOC equity from fiscal take?

This is one of the most common IC memo errors: conflating fiscal take (royalties, taxes, profit oil) with NOC equity participation (the government's working interest share in the contractor consortium). ORCA reports government take on a contractor barrel basis — it does not deduct or adjust for NOC equity participation. Understanding the interaction is critical for correct IC framing.

Two distinct channels of government capture:

  • Fiscal take (what ORCA reports): royalties, corporate income tax, profit oil split, resource rent taxes — all extracted from the total project cashflow regardless of who holds working interest. ORCA's take% is calculated on this basis: what fraction of gross project revenue is captured by the state via fiscal mechanisms.
  • NOC equity participation: the government's pro-rata share of contractor net cashflow via its working interest. If the NOC holds 30% WI on a carried or paying basis, it receives 30% of the contractor's net profit oil — but this is already inside the contractor-side portion of the fiscal split.

The critical distinction — carried vs. paying NOC interest:

  • Carried interest (exploration phase only, then converts to paying): During exploration, the IOC carries the NOC's share — the IOC funds 100% of exploration capex and recovers the NOC's share from future cost recovery oil. Once commercial discovery is made and the NOC converts to a paying interest, it funds its pro-rata share of development and operating costs. Net effect on IOC economics: exploration phase is effectively diluted, but the post-conversion structure is equivalent to a standard WI arrangement. See FAQ A32 for carried interest quantification methodology.
  • Fully paying NOC WI (from day one): NOC funds its pro-rata share of all costs from exploration through production. The IOC's net cashflow is simply its WI fraction of the contractor net profit oil. ORCA take is unaffected — the fiscal split applies to the combined contractor position.
  • Permanently carried (state equity backed by cost oil recovery but no cash calls): Less common; effectively increases the IOC's real cost burden and reduces its net entitlement vs. the stated WI. Angola's Sonangol has historically operated in this mode on some pre-2018 PSC contracts.

4-step IC adjustment workflow:

  1. Identify the NOC WI structure using the Country Profile (ORCA shows NOC WI where available) and confirm whether the interest is carried (exploration only) or paying (from inception). The contract text or operator annual reports are authoritative.
  2. Determine the IOC's net WI after the NOC share. If the IOC holds 70% WI in a paying NOC arrangement, the IOC's cashflow is 70% × (1 − fiscal take%) × gross revenue. ORCA's take figure applies to the combined contractor group — it does not change based on WI split.
  3. Quantify the carry cost if applicable. Under carried exploration, the IOC effectively funds 100/70 = 143% of the exploration cost to cover the NOC's 30% share. Model this as an incremental capex burden in the Scenario Builder: increase exploration capex by 1/(1−NOC carry%) to reflect the gross-up.
  4. IC memo disclosure: State "ORCA government take of [X]% reflects fiscal mechanisms (royalty/CIT/profit oil) applied to the gross contractor position. The NOC holds [Y]% [carried/paying] working interest. IOC net WI is [Z]%. All IRR and NPV figures are presented on a [100% WI / IOC net WI] basis." Specify which basis clearly — IC committees regularly misread WI-basis vs. 100% basis returns.

Country-specific benchmarks (NOC WI structures):

  • Nigeria (NNPC/NUPRC PSC): NNPC typically holds 55–60% WI in JV concessions (paying); in deepwater PSCs, NOC back-in rights at commerciality are 30–40%. IOC net WI in deepwater can be as low as 30–45% depending on block vintage.
  • Angola (Sonangol PSC): Sonangol holds 20–30% WI; historically carried through exploration on pre-2018 blocks, converting to paying after first commercial production. Post-2018 blocks under new petroleum law operate on more conventional paying-WI terms.
  • Malaysia (Petronas RSC/PSC): Petronas retains 15% carried through exploration on most PSC blocks. IOC effective WI at development: 85% of the contractor position (before profit oil split). RSC contracts may have different participation structures — verify per contract.
  • Brazil (Petrobras pre-salt PSC): Under the 2010 pre-salt law, Petrobras was mandatory operator with minimum 30% WI on all pre-salt blocks. This structure was reformed in 2016; post-2016 pre-salt rounds allow minority Petrobras or no-Petrobras participation. Check block vintage carefully.
  • Kazakhstan (Kazmunaygaz JV agreements): KMG typically holds 16–40% WI depending on the asset; most interests are paying from inception. KMG's right of first refusal on WI transfers is a key M&A consideration — see FAQ A46 on upstream M&A due diligence.
  • Iraq-KRG (PSC with KRG back-in): KRG holds 25–30% back-in rights at commerciality on most PSC blocks; these convert from carried to paying at development FID. ORCA's KRG take (43.5%) reflects the fiscal layer; the back-in right is a separate economic event.

Rule of thumb for IC memo language: "ORCA government take of [X]% (ORCA v274, standardized reference project) reflects fiscal mechanisms applied to the gross contractor position. This figure does not adjust for NOC equity participation. IOC net WI is [Z]% ([carried/paying] NOC basis). All returns presented on IOC net WI basis. A NOC carry adjustment of [+W]pp effective capex is applied in the Scenario Builder model for exploration-phase carry."

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). Cross-reference: FAQ A32 (state equity carried vs. paying working interest — quantification); FAQ A46 (upstream M&A due diligence — WI transfer and KMG ROFR); FAQ A69 (fiscal ring-fencing and how NOC WI interacts with license-level ring-fences); FAQ A100 (PSC entitlement barrels and cost recovery). Industry context: Johnston, D. (2003) International Exploration Economics, Risk, and Contract Analysis; Bindemann, K. (1999) Production-Sharing Agreements: An Economic Analysis; Wood Mackenzie NOC Participation Study (2023); Nigeria Upstream Petroleum Regulations 2021 (NUPRC).

A146. Our candidate country is an OPEC member currently under a production quota constraint. ORCA's government take figure is based on a standardized production profile. How do I adjust the ORCA fiscal take for a project that will be subject to voluntary production curtailment — and what does the quota risk mean for IRR?

ORCA's standardized reference project assumes uninhibited plateau production — the DCF engine does not model OPEC quota curtailment because quota allocation is a sovereign decision made at the country level, not embedded in the fiscal terms of any single block. For IC analysis in OPEC member states, a two-layer adjustment is required: a quota-curtailment volume adjustment layered above the ORCA fiscal take, and an IRR impact assessment for the resulting extended payback period.

Why ORCA does not model OPEC quota: OPEC production quotas are country-level agreements, not block-level fiscal terms. The fiscal regime (royalty, CIT, profit oil) is unaffected by quota — a barrel produced still faces the same take. The economic impact is entirely on the volume profile: curtailment delays cost recovery, reduces early-year revenues, and extends the payback period of the reference project. ORCA captures the fiscal layer correctly; the quota layer is a project-level risk adjustment that belongs in the analyst's DCF model, not in a cross-country fiscal comparison tool.

How quota curtailment affects project economics:

  • Extended cost recovery (PSC countries): If production plateau is cut from 50k bbl/d to 35k bbl/d by quota, cost recovery takes proportionally longer — the cost oil pool fills more slowly. Under Indonesia's pre-2017 PSC structure, a 30% plateau cut can extend cost recovery by 2–3 years, reducing IRR by 2–4pp. Nigeria NLNG allocations have historically been ring-fenced from OPEC oil quotas, but upstream block curtailments affect cost recovery timing.
  • NPV impact (all mechanics): A 30% plateau curtailment (e.g. 50k → 35k bbl/d) in Year 1–5 shifts cash flows rightward by 2–3 years. At 10% discount rate, this reduces NPV by approximately 15–25% vs. the uninhibited base case. The take% itself does not change — the same fraction of each barrel goes to the government — but the absolute contractor NPV shrinks because future cash flows are worth less.
  • IRR impact: IRR is particularly sensitive to early-year cash flow delays. A 30% plateau curtailment in Years 1–3 of production typically reduces unlevered IRR by 3–6pp for a deepwater project. The exact impact depends on the cost recovery profile: high-capex projects (deepwater, LNG) with back-loaded recovery are most affected; low-capex onshore projects with fast payback are least affected.

4-step IC adjustment workflow:

  1. Establish the curtailment scenario. Use the country's OPEC quota history (IEA Monthly Oil Market Report, OPEC Monthly Oil Market Report) to determine the typical curtailment depth and duration for that member. Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait, and Iraq have all operated at significant curtailment in 2022–2025 (+500k–2M bbl/d cuts). Estimate the block-level curtailment as a percentage of plateau rate — typically 15–35% for OPEC+ members under the 2022–2024 Vienna agreement structure.
  2. Model the curtailed production profile in Scenario Builder. Use the Scenario Builder with a custom project: reduce the peak rate by the curtailment factor (e.g. set peak rate to 35k bbl/d instead of 50k bbl/d) and extend the plateau by an equivalent period (maintain total ultimate recovery). Run both uncurtailed and curtailed DCFs and compare IRR and NPV — this quantifies the quota discount without changing the fiscal terms.
  3. Compute the IRR corridor. Present three scenarios: (a) uninhibited plateau (ORCA standard basis), (b) 15% curtailment (moderate OPEC discipline), (c) 30% curtailment (deep cut comparable to 2020 COVID or 2024 voluntary cuts). The corridor gives the IC committee a range rather than a false point estimate. For PSC countries, also note the cost recovery delay impact explicitly.
  4. IC memo disclosure. State: "ORCA government take of [X]% (v251, standardized 50k bbl/d deepwater reference project, uninhibited plateau) applies uniformly regardless of quota curtailment — the fiscal terms are unchanged by OPEC allocation. However, the IOC net project IRR is [Y–Z]% depending on curtailment depth ([base case uninhibited] / [15% cut] / [30% cut]) modeled in the Scenario Builder. All three scenarios use the same ORCA fiscal parameters applied to the corresponding production profile."

Country-specific curtailment context:

  • Saudi Arabia (Concession): Aramco's operational flexibility means curtailment is managed at company level — individual upstream contractors are generally shielded from pro-rata allocation. New IOC-operated blocks (e.g. unconventional gas under Vision 2030) may not face same curtailment exposure. Verify per contract whether the block is subject to national allocation.
  • Iraq (TSC): TSC fee-per-barrel structure means curtailment directly reduces IOC revenue (IOC earns a fixed $/bbl on produced barrels). A 30% curtailment is a 30% revenue cut. IRR impact in early production years is severe — 4–7pp reduction. Iraq's OPEC compliance has historically been poor (underdelivering on cuts), which paradoxically protects IOC volumes in some periods.
  • UAE / ADNOC (Concession): ADNOC-managed fields; IOC participating interests are generally structured to buffer operators from pro-rata curtailment. IOC net take is contractually protected in most concession agreements, but verify per block.
  • Nigeria (PSC): Nigeria has historically under-complied with OPEC quotas due to security incidents and production decline — quota risk is lower than compliance-driven members. PSC cost recovery is the main risk driver when curtailments do occur.
  • Kazakhstan (PSC/Concession): Kashagan and Tengiz have been selectively exempt from OPEC+ cuts as new production ramp-ups. Verify whether the specific development falls under the Kazakh exemption or is subject to quota.

Rule of thumb for IC memo: "For OPEC member states, ORCA take figures are presented on an uninhibited-plateau basis. Quota curtailment risk is modeled separately: a [X]% plateau curtailment for [Y] years reduces project IRR by approximately [2–6]pp and NPV by [15–25]% relative to the ORCA reference case. IC committee should review the curtailment corridor alongside the base-case ORCA fiscal comparison."

Source: ORCA v274 (Aug 2026). Cross-reference: FAQ A84 (production profile shape and fiscal regime interaction); FAQ A90 (price sensitivity at different production scales); FAQ A117 (portfolio-level asset review triage using ORCA metrics); FAQ A128 (production decline curve shape interaction with fiscal mechanics). Industry context: OPEC Monthly Oil Market Reports (2022–2025); IEA Monthly Oil Market Reports (2022–2025); Johnston, D. (2003) International Exploration Economics, Risk, and Contract Analysis; Wood Mackenzie OPEC+ Production Tracker (2024); Rystad Energy UCube OPEC Compliance Monitor (2024).

A147. When I compare two countries with the same headline government take percentage, one uses a royalty-based system and the other a profit-based system. Our IC committee says these are not economically equivalent — how do I explain the difference and which regime is actually better for the contractor at different oil prices?

Your IC committee is correct. Two regimes with identical headline take at $75/bbl can have dramatically different economics depending on whether the government captures its share from gross revenue (royalty-first) or from profits after cost recovery (profit-based). The distinction is not cosmetic — it affects the payback period, the exposure to low-price environments, and the value of cost efficiency to the contractor.

Royalty-based take (Concession): The government takes a percentage of gross revenue before any costs are deducted. A 20% royalty means 20 cents of every dollar of oil revenue goes to the government regardless of whether the project is profitable. This is a first-mover claim on revenue. At low oil prices, royalties can make projects sub-economic even when the contractor's costs are fixed — the government takes 20% of a small pie, the contractor's net is even smaller. The contractor bears the full cost risk. However, royalty regimes are generally transparent and predictable: the government take calculation is simple and auditable.

Profit-based take (PSC — Production Sharing Contract): The contractor first recovers costs from a cost oil pool (typically 60–80% of gross revenue), then splits the remaining profit oil with the government. At low oil prices, a higher fraction of revenue goes to cost recovery, leaving less for the profit split — the contractor's effective take can actually improve at low prices because the government's share of a smaller profit pool is smaller. At high prices, the profit pool is large and the government captures a higher fraction. This is the PSC "fiscal leverage" effect — PSCs are inherently progressive.

The ORCA Price Swing column quantifies this difference: A country with a high Price Swing (e.g. 25pp) means the government take at $125/bbl is 25pp higher than at $50/bbl — this is a hallmark of profit-based systems (R-factor PSCs, PRRT, sliding-scale royalties). A country with a low Price Swing (e.g. 5pp) typically has a flat royalty structure — the government takes roughly the same percentage regardless of price. Two countries at 60% take at $75/bbl with Swings of 5pp vs. 25pp have very different risk profiles for the contractor.

IRR impact at different price scenarios:

  • At $50/bbl (stress scenario): The royalty-based regime still takes 20% of gross revenue even as the project margins collapse.
